_ HELP 'TIS HITMLNITY'S Olt?. Ye bate heard in the streets, while the bright stars above Binned down into eyes gazing heavenward in love, The mad moans of torture from drink-befouled lips, (Which learned their sad art by initiative sips), And ye pitied the wretches who tottering fled To a drunkard's dark home, to a drunkard's foul bed, But came not the thoualat so ye saw them pass by: "Help, help! I will help, 'tis humanity's cry !" Ye have seen at the bars in the palaces grand, While the publican stood with the cash in his hand, The drinkers who pass from the gaudy-made trap O'ercome by their passions—oh! fatal mishap! Have wa' ched them indulge in the potions which hurl Them victims, alas! into sin's giddy whirl; Been them drift into vice with remorseless eye, Nor thought, "1 will help! 'Lis humanity's cry !" Ye have seen strange pollutions defiling the fair, Oh! so horribly marring God's handiwork there! Beheld the shamed light of the beautiful sun Expose the black work with which drinking begun; And, shuddering, marvelled at creatures so vile, Bo terribly lost_ that your grief made them smile Then, passing along, with a sorrowful sigh Ye thought of their guilt, not "humanity" cry 0, men! do not gaze with an apathist's sight On scenes so appalling to Christian light; Do not look with an eye of the pitiless type On iniquity's harvest around you so ripe! But think of the crimes, and the griefs, and the tears, The woe and the want, of sad home with their fears Of all the fell ills that have sprung from this curse, Our nation will foster, our statemen will nurse. Then ask If your duty be not to reply : " Help! here is help !" to " HUMS.NITY'S CRY !" Warrington, April sth, 1882. BENJ. SAWDON.
AN APRIL DAY.

The April rain falls slowly, Like tears that follow sighs. And fleecy clouds glide lightly Over the azure skies; The soft south wind is wooing The pale clematis vine, Dallying with its tendrils As trustingly they twine. The east a rainbow. spstnheth,

Promise of watchful care— A glowing, gorgeous banner, That fairies might prepare With rays of gold and purple, • With emerald's flashing light With tints from deep blue sapphires, And hearts of rubies bright. From sward that spreads before me The crocus lifts its head, And pale and starry flowers Peep from their winter bed; And o'er the latticed trellis The clinging vine doth creep, While down amid the mossy turf The harebell lies asleep. I love the gentle April— Her soft and balmy sighs; Her smiles are ofttimes tearful, But hope's in her earnest eyes I Sweet in truth is the lesson That grief may learn alway, For, ever, weeping April Is followed by joyous May. Mrs. BLoomprixs MOORE.

Persons should be careful about dropping remarks; they may be picked up. Many a man who thinks himself a great gun is nothing more than a big bore. A useful hint is wrapped up in the following:—" Died of thin shoes, January, 18—." Politeness is like an air cushion. There may be nothing solid in it, but it eases the jolts of the world wonderfully. "I thought you took an interest in my welfare," said William. "No,sir," replied Susan, "only in your farewell." Jones thinks a man fortunate who has his will contested after death only. He says his will has been contested ever Since he married Mrs. Jones. When we hear a man boast of the length of his ancestry we are reminded of the quaint saying of the farmers, " The older the seed, the worse the crop." "Say," said the city youth to the modest countryman, "hay seed out o' your hair yet ?" " %Val," was the deliber- ate reply, "I jedge not from the way the calves run after me." A young officer thought to puzzle the Editor of La Figaro by asking him, when two men of equal age and rank met, which should be the first to bow. The editor replied, "The more polite of the two." 0. W. Holmes says: "The true girl has to be sought for." Exactly; and the good-for-nothing young scamp who sponges his way through the world too often does the seeking, and gets the girl who ought to be married to the young man of sense who has no time or inclination to hunt her up. Three travellers, stopping at an inn, ordered a brace of partridges for dinner. When they were served, the logician of the company quietly helped himself to one and left the other for his comp " Hold! " they cried, • " that is not a fair division." "There is one for you two, and here, on my plate, is one for me, too. Isn't that fair." He was at breakfast, wrestling with a piece of remark- ably t)ugh veal. His wife said to him, "You always say there's something to be thankful for in every thing. I fancy you'd be puzzled to find something to be thankful for in that veal." "Not at all," he cheerfully responded, stop- ping to breathe; "I was just thinking how grateful we shoull be that we met it when it was young." THE DESERT REGIONS OF THE WOHLD.—That the pre- sence or absence of moisture has a great influence in deter- mining the chr:racter of vegetation cannot be denied; and that the distribution of forests over the earth's surface is largely connected with the amount of rainfall in different regions, is beyond a doubt. An inspection of a rain-chart of the earth, and a comparison of the position of the rain- leas and drier areas with that of the belts or tracts destitute
of trees, will be sufficient to show at once that, in a general way, regions where the rainfall is dtficient are those where

_ trees are least developed; and also that a vigorous growth -of grasses may be found where the precipitation is quite moderate in amount. That the desert regions of the world are the rainless ones cannot for a moment be doubted. Ab- solute deserts, however, if by the term desert is meant a region entirely destitute of vegetation, are not by any means of frequent occurrence; and when such tracts do occur they rarely extend over large areas. The amount of desert on the earth is exceedingly small when compared with that of the region to which the name steppe may pro- perly be applied. Moving zands form the surface least favourable to vegetation; for even a rock surface, entirely destitute of soil, may be more or less encrusted with lichens. Hence the fact that a considerable portion of the Sahara is underlain with a sandstone whichleasily disintegrates on weathering, giving rise to great masses of pure sand, is re- garded as one of the reasons for the utter barrenness of such large areas in Ncrthern Africa. Since moisture is essential to the vigorous growth of trees, so that very dry regions are, as a general rule, not covered with forests, it will not be difficalt to understand why treeless areas etre usually found in the interior of continental muses, as is so well illustrated by the position of the plains of North America, and that of the pampas and lianos of the southern division of the New World. The edges of the continents are the rsgions where the larger portion of the rainfall on the land takes place. To this rule there are but few exceptions; the most striking one is the existence of a rainless belt along a Considerable part of the west coast of South America, a con- dition of things depending on the position of the chain of the Andes in that region with reference to the trade-winds. —Science for All. MARINO A ROAD IN A DAY.—This road, which leaves the western extremity of Princes-street at a right angle, and runs southward towards Bruntsfield Links, had long been projected, but owing to the objections raised by the proprietors of many barns, byres, and sheds which stood in the way, the plan could not be matured, till after several years of trouble and speculation; and when at last the pro- posal was about to be agreed to by the opposing parties, the broad and stately road was—to the surprise, of the public and mortification of the opposition—made in one day! It so happened that a gentleman, said to be Sir John Clerk, Bart., of Pennicuik (an officer of the royal navy, who suc- ceeded his father, Sir George, in 1784), laid a bet with a e friend to the effect "That he would, between sunrise and sunset, execute the lice of road, extending nearly a mile in length by twenty paces in breadth." This scheme he con- tertesi with address, and executed with nautical prompti- tude. It happened to be the winter season, when many men were unemployed. He had no difficulty ia collecting several hundreds of these at the liirkbraehead upon the ap- pointed morning before sunrise, when he gave them all a plentiful breakfast of porter, whisky, and bread and cheese, after which, just as the sun rose, he ordered them to set to work; "some to tear down enclosures, others to unroof and demolish cottages, and a considerable portion to bring earth wherewith to fill up the natural hollow (near the church- yard gate) to the required height. The inhabitants dis- mayed at so vast a force and so summary a mode of pro- cedure, made no resistance; and so active were the workmen that before sunset the road was sufficiently formed to allow the bettor to drive his carriage trinnophatly over it, which he did amidst the acclamations of a great multitude of per. tons, who flocked from the town to witnees the issue of this extraordinary undertaking. Amongst the instances of tem- porary distressoccasioned to the inhabitants, the most laughable was that of a poor simple woman who had a cot- tage and small cow-feeding establishment upon the spot. It appeare that this good creature had risen early, as usual, milked her cows, smoked her pipe, taken her ordinary matutinal tea, and lastly, recollecting that she had some friends invited to dine with her upon sheep-head and hail about noon, placed the pot upon the fire, In order that it might simmer peaceably till she sheuld return from town, where she had to supply a numerous set of customers with the produe ee her dairy. Our readers may judge the con. nternaticn i this poor woman when, upon her return from the duties of the morning, she found neither house, nor byre, nor cows, nor fire, nor pipe,•nor pot, nor anything that was here upon the spot where she had left them but a f!ve hours before. All had vanished, like the palace of Aladdie, lesving not a wrack behind." Such was the origin of that broad and handsome street which now leads to where the Castle Barns stood of old.—Cassell',, Old and New Edin- burjh.

Mr. J. R. Green is announced to be at work upon "Eng- land and the Northmen," which is to complete his " Making of England." We take the following from the AthencPum :—MM. Bran have, Les frlandes informs us, greatly improved the manu- facture of oxygen by Baussingault's process of peroxidising and reoxidising barium. This material after being used 400 was found not to be deteriorated. MM. Brin expect to be able to supply oxygen on a large scale at twelve to fifteen centimes per cubic metre. The Academy says that a picture by Mr. Edwin Long, R.A., which will hardly fail to be a principal attraction at the Royal Academy, has been suggested by the line in the fifth chapter of Judges—" Why do his chariots stay ?" The mother who makes, in the anxiety of one waiting, the in- quiry. thus formed, sits in Mr. Long's picture, within sight of the road that leads homeward, and watches the road, as yet empty. The sentiment of most anxious waiting—of a I waiting already far too prolonged—is expressed with com- plete force' both in the face and attitude of the principal figure, and it is expressed again, or echoed, in the faces and gestures of the women who wait with her. Continental railway engineers, says Iron, have for some time past noticed the rapid destruction of rails laid in tun- nels and at their approaches, which is attributed to the sand used for ensuring the adhesion of the locomotive. The use of sand is the more necessary in turnels on account of the formation and deposit on the rails of a coating of a fatty nature, due to the oil used in lubrication and the water re - suiting from the exhaust steam which is more condensed in the confined space of a tunnel than in the open air. The grains of sand become gradually encrusted in the slightest superficial scratches of the table of the rails, and at last act as wedges under the repeated pressure of the wheels. A remedy for this evil has recently been employed with success in the Hauenstein tunnel, Switzerland, after replacing the worn-out rails. Instead of sand, a jet of hot water from the locomotive was used, which freed the surface of the rail from the fatty deposit, ensuring perfect adhesion of the wheels. ASBESTOS AS A CARRIAGE LINING.—It was probably not generally known, until the Spuyten Duyvil railway disaster' in the United States, that it is the practice of lining the floors of American passenger carriages with shavings. The inquiry subsequent to that disastrous occurrence disclosed the fact that the shavings set fire to the carriages in the late collision with such suddenness that it was impossible for passengers to escape who were rendered incapable of extricating themselves by the first shock. Asbestos, which Is non-combustible and an excellent non-conductor, is just the material for lining cars. It is, therefore, a satisfaction to know that, from information supplied by the United States Mineral Wool Company, of 16, Courtlandt-street, New York, there are now about 700,000 pounds of this material in use in American passenger cars. The method is simply to pack three or four inches of the ordinary descrip- tion between the floor proper and a false bottom made of tongued and grooved half-inch stuff. But great beneit would be gained by using one inch of the extra description on all other parts of the carriage, thus preventing the cold draughts through cracks and making the carriage more comfortable in the heat oisummer. The whole expense for lining an American railway car in this fashion, it is stated, would be about thirty dollars. UNSUSPECTED POISONS.— The Pharmaceutical Journal quotes the opinion of an eminent analyst, from which it ap- pears that decided symptoms of poisoning result more fre- quently than we are aware of from any considerable con- sumption of potatoes. Among the poorer classes, who live largely on potatoes, such symptoms are said to be common, more particularly when the tubers are very young or very old. such potatoes, we are told, contain considerable quan- tities of solanine. This poison was found in very unmis- takable quantities in the stomach of a man who had bees for two or three days previous to his death living on nothing but raw unripe potatoes, and there seems to have been no room for doubt that this diet accounted for the presence of the poison. It is said to be found chiefly, if not entirely, is the skin of the potato, and is soluble in boiling water, and we may, we suppose, assume therefore that a very young or a very old potato boiled in its skin must be to some extent permeated by solanine, and must be unwholesome to an ex- tent that may become serious if partaken of in large quan- tities. Another unsuspected source of poison is said to be maize or Indian corn. A disease as fatal in Italy as con- sumption is in this country is attributed entirely to the ex- clusive use of this cereal, which is thought to be especially dangerous if ground in a damaged condition—damaged, we suppose, by incipient decay, though that is not stated. There is said to be one remarkable fact connected with the disease which is thought to have its origin in this source— the disease known as pellagra. Sufferers from it who cona- mit suicide always do so by drowning, a fact explained by the pleasure afforded by the sight or touch of water, which constitutes a symptom of this disorder.—Globe. NOVELTIES IN PHOTOGRAPHY.—To tourists desiring as easily taken pictorial souvenir of places visited, an arrange- ment described in La Nature should be welcome. It con- sists of a large opera-glass which is readily transformed into a photographic apparatus. When this is desired, the object- glasses (which are fixed similarly to bayonets) are detached and the eye-glasses unscrewed. For the latter photographic Object-glasses are substituted, one of these being provided ilkith a rocking shutter. For the object-glasses of the opera- glass are substituted a photographic frame to hold a sensi- tised dry plate and a frame for ground glass, the former on that tube which carries the shutter. A screen before a cir- cular aperture in the photograph-frame is. easily removed when the plate is in position by pressing a latch outside. To obtain the proper focus one screws the instrument till a good image appears on the ground glass; as the two tubes corre- spond optically, the plate adapted to the other tube is then In the right position. A momentary touch, by which the rocking shutter is displaced, gives sufficient exposure; the screen is replaced, the frame detached, the negative re- moved, and a fresh plate substituted. The shifting of plates within the frame is done with the hands within a bag im- permeable to light, and having two bracelets of caoutchouc. The photographic apparatus should be steadily supported on some object (e q. a wail or a trunk of a tree) when a view is to be taken. The plates need not be developed at once, but may he kept for months before this is done. Simple direc- tions for the process and for printing on paper are given. The various items required for this mode of photography are neatly packed in a small bag. A recent photographic achievement by M. Marcy is an apparatus which pointed like a fowling-piece at a bird in flight, gives 12 pictures in a second, each picture having had an exposure of 1-700th of a second. The pictures combined in Plateau's phenakis- tiscope, exhibit the flight of a bird in such a way that analysis is possible, and some interesting results may thus be looked for. ASTRONOMICIL OCCURRENCES FOR APRIL.

The Mom is near Mercury on the morning of the 17th, Vie day of New Moon. She is near both Venus and Saturn during the evening hours of the 18th, and at some distance left of these two planets during the evening hours of the 19th, Venus being the higher of the two planets. She is to the right of Jupiter during the evening hours of the 19th, and to the left of him during the evening hours of the 20th. She is to the right of Mars during the evening hours of the 23rd, and to his left during the evening hours of the 24th. She is nearest the Earth on the afternoon of the 15th, and most distant on the afternoon of the 27th. MERCURY iS a morning star, rising on the Ist at sh. 9m. a.m., or 29 minutes before sunrise, and on the last day of the month at 4h. 34m. a.m. He is near the Moon cn the 17th. _ _ _

VENUS is an evening star, setting on the Ist at 7h 24m. p.m., and on the last day at Bh. 58m. p.m. She is near the Moon on the 18th, near Saturn on the 19th, and in her ascending node on the 26th. MARS sets an the 2nd at 2h. 43m. a.m., or 2h. 53m. before sunrise; on the 22nd at lh. 53m. a.m., or 3h. before sunrise; and on the last day at lh. 36m. a.m. He is due south on the let at 6h. 14m. p.m., and on the last day at sh. 19m. p.m. He is quadrature with the Sun on the 2nd, and near the Moon on the 24th. JUPITER is an evening star, setting on the let at 10h. 38m. p.m., and en the last day at 9h. 19m. p.m., or 2h. after sunset. He is due south on the Ist at 2h. 55m. p.m., and on the last day at lh. 26m. p.m. He is near the Moon on the 20th. SATURN is an evening star, setting on the Ist at 911. lire. p.m., and on the last day at 7b. 40m. p.m., or 21m. after sunset. He is due south on the Ist at 111. 59m. p.m., and on the last day at Oh. 19m. p.m. He is near the Moon on the 19th, and near Venus on the same day. On February 24, Grand Duchess Nancy, of the Underley herd, belonging to Earl Bective, produced a roan heifer calf, by Duke of Ormskirk (36,526). In reference to the weight of calves, about a year ago a heifer calf in this herd weighed 1121 b. at birth. On Monday morning, the farm buildings in the occupa- tion of a man named Scott were burned down near Chard. This makes the sixth such fire that has recently occurred in the district. After the last a public meeting was called, the conflagration denounced as the work of an incendiary, and a reward of £lOO offered, but no clue to the perpetrator has yet been obtained. Farmers will be glad to learn that Miss E. A. Ormerod, of Minster Lodge, Isllwortb, is about to make that worst of all field pests, the wire-worm, the subject of a special inquiry, similar to that recently published in relation to the turnip- fly. Readers who are willing to make observations and re- port to Miss Ormerod, during the spring and summer, would do well to communicate with her at once, as this will enable her to save much of the valuable time which will otherwise be occupied in obtaining correspondents. Some very important remarks on the subject of security for tenants' improvements were made by Mr. J. J. Clark, of Goldstone Farm, Brighton, at the Robertabridge m eeting of the East Sussex Branch of the Farmers' Alliance, last week. Mr. Clark had exceptional security for his capital; but he had to pay an exorbitant rent in order to get it. That is to say, he paid £4 an acre where the preceding tenant paid £2 108 , in order to get a lease of twenty-one years and •compensation for improvements. If the Law had been just he would not have had to pay a heavy fine to protect his property from confiscation. Having obtained security, he improved his.holding to such an extent that, whereas his returns four years ago were £2,000, last year they were £6,000. As his landlord recently required fifteen acres of the farm, the improvements had to be valued. He had con- verted ordinary farm land into rich market-garden ground, , and the valuers awarded him no less than £BO an acre, which he actually received from his landlord. Hundreds of market gardeners raise the value of land in this way, and get no compensation whatever. RICE MEAL.-I have used rice meal very extensively for three ?mations for my milking cows. I have a large contract for new milk, and keep thirty cows to supply it. The food given them during winter, in addition to hay and turnips, is invariably rice meal and about 21b. decorticated cotton cake each per day. The rice meal is placed, with chopped

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, APRIL t57'14247
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, APRIL t57'14247

hay or straw, in a large trough, well mixed up with water, - and a good tubful given morning and evening, immediately after milking, the cotton cake being distributed previous to milking. My cows have milked very well upon this diet, and are in good condition. The milk is remarkably rich, and when churned yields a large amount of butter, though sometimes long in churning. In passing, I may say I have never experienced any disagreeable taste or odour. from the use of the cotton cake, nor has any complaint ever been made to me. When, on chance occasions, I have been un- able to obtain rice meal, and have substituted Indian meal, I have found a dimiaution in the quantity of milk. I can- not find any article that will produce equal results at any- thing near the price. I pay 133. per 2401 b., always using the best kind, as I find the second quality very much in- ferior. Some cattle are rather diffident about taking it at first, but soon take to it. I have also used it for fattening beasts, but in such cases mix in oatmeal, as I find the flesh thus is more solid. My horses use it, preferring it to Indian meal. I have also fed pigs with it, and am well satisfied with the results. I begin my young pigs with it, and use nothing else until about the last month, .when I substitute oatmeal. My calves, too, are brought up on it. On wean- in.' them from new milk, some rice meal is taken, and scalded and well stirred, to prevent its becoming lumpy; then it is thinned to the proper state by water and a little new milk added. Gradually the new milk is taken away, and then rice meal porridge becomes their sole diet night and morning, with plenty of hay or grass, according to the time of year. In this way, while selling all my new milk, as nearly as possible, I bring up fifteen to twenty calves annually, and they are in good, healthy, growing condition. Holleth.

the words of the Great Teacher, uttered in Judea eighteen centuries ago, are true today :—" There is nothing covered that shall not be revealed, neither hid that shall not be known. Therefore, whatsoever ye have spoken in dark- ness shall be heard in the light, and that which ye have spoken in the ear shall be proclaimed upon the house-tops." The case before us supplies an illustration of these wotds. In the Secret Service Accounts appears the following item, under date of June 20th, 1798 :—" F.H., for the discovery of L.E.F., M,000." This was the first gleam of intelligence that was shed upon the mystery. Still the darkness had not all been rolled away. Everybody knew who " L.E.F." was, but the question remained—who was " F.H. ?" That ques- tion was answered when the "Memoirs and Correspondence of Lord Cornwallis" was published, in 1860. There we read in a communication to the Secretary of State:—" Francis Higgins, of the Freeman's Journal, was the person who pro- cured for me all the intelligence respecting Lord Edward Fitzgerald." Francis Higgins was dead when the secret of his infamy leaped into the light of day, but his memory will be branded by every true Irishman wii a mark as opprobrious as that which the first murderer wore. On the 27th of July, 1798, a bill was brought forward by the Attorney-General for the attainder of Lord Edward Fitzgerald. After a long discussion and examination of witnesses in both Houses, the bill passed the House of Lords in the month of September and received the Royal assent in the October following. This Act of Attainder was known to have been considered by the Irish Government as a mea- sure which could not be defended upon legal or Constitu- tional grounds, but which had been rendered necessary by the state of the country and as a Means of striking terror into the disaffected. No sooner had they attained this object than a disposition to relax into a humaner policy showed itself. It was not, however, until 1803 that the bill was repealed, and mainly through the Prince Regent, who recommended this act of justice. For this an the Prince was well rewarded, He received from independent minds two tributet as flattering and at honourable as Sovereign has ever won. Lord Holland, in the House of Lords, declared that "it was an act of a wise and gracious and high-minded Prince," while the following laudatory verses were penned by Lord Byron:—

To be the father of the fatherless, To stretch the hand from the throne's height and raise His offspring, who expired in other days, To make thy sire's sway a kingdom less, This is to be a monarch and repress Envy into unutterable praise; Dismiss thy guard and trust thee to such traits, For who would lift a hand except to bless? Were it not easy, sir, and is't not sweet To make thyself beloved and to be Omnipotent by mercy's beams ') For thilS Thy Sovereignty would grow but more complete. A despot thou, and yet thy people free, And by the heart, not hand, enslaving us.

We would not have our raaders suppose that we approve the methods adopted by Lord Edward and his coadjutors for the accomplishment of their purposes, however much we may and do admire their patrioasm. Lord Edward might not have been a very prudent man, but he was a patriot, pre- pared to make the most costly sacrifices for the vreal of his native land. Had he been a prudent man—a shrewd human pence-table—he might have lived a life of ease and affluence, and died in the bosom of his friends. Had he in political life been actuated by dishonourable ambition, he might have clung to his great family connections and Parliamentary in- fluence, and they unquestionably would have advanced his fortunes and gratified his desires. But the voluntary sacri- fices he made, and the magnanimous manner in which he devoted himself to the idependence of Ireland, are incon- testable proofs of the purity of his soul. Of the first family in Ireland, with an easy fortune, beautiful wife, and family of lovely children, the certainty of a splendid appointment under Government if he would condescend to support their measures, he devoted himself wholly to the emancipation of his country, and sacrificed everything to it, even to his blood. Pitt, Castlereagh, and Camden branded Lord Edward as a rebel and a traitor, because he resisted their tyranny; but we feel, with Grattan, that "the treason of the Minister against the liberties of the people was infinitely worse than the rebellion of the people against the Minister." Certain it is that the memory of Lord Edward Fitzgerald will live in the heart of every honest Irishman, and in the history of the future his name will be bracketed with those of Wash- ington of America, and Garibaldi of Italy.

compromised himself in his demonstration against Cosham, but had clung, with most of his battalion, to the crest of the hill. It is a disputed point who had the best of it but I am inclined to think that if the action had lasted another half hour the invaders under Higginson would have hurled the enemy back on his original position by weight of numbers. It is true that Pakenham's right had by a weak line of skirmishers come practic illy into touch with the force occupying Cosham, but he was weak on the crest, and on the south of it, and not only would Wood have broken into his centre but Newdigate was swinging Kent round and would have forced Pakenham's left out of the valley and on to the defender's centre. The fact is that the key of the position was the high ground where Pakenham had placed his two 40-pounders, and to defend that point he had at hand only about 8,000 men opposed to 22,000. In short, Pakenham fought an offensive battle all along the line, though he bad inferior numbers. I think he ought to hare remained on the defensive on his left to have pushed on that flank, and to have swung two brigades, supported by the fire of the gunboats, of Hilsea lines, and the infantry in Cosham, round so as to fall on the left of Higginson's army. The battle altogether was interesting, but the ground was cramped and the pace was necessarily hurried. The rival commanders showed that they knew their work, and they were well seconded by their divisional generals. The troops behaved with steadiness and were well in hand; but there were certaip defects and some absurdities almost unavoidable on occasions like Easter Monday fights. Notwithstanding these, I wish to record my opinion to-day that the efficie icy of the volunteers has increased during the last two or three years in a very marked manner.

div.head: ILLUSTRIOUS IRISH \UN,
div.p: ILLUSTRIOUS IRISH \UN,

No. XV.—LORD EDWARD FITZGERALD. "We're fallen upon gloomy days Star after star decays, Every bright name that shed Light o'er the land is fled, Dark falls the tear of him who mourneth, Last joy or hope that ne'er returneth But brightly flows the tear Wept o'er the hero's bier."—Thomas Moore. Lord Edward Fitzgerald was nobly born. He came of a good stock. His forefathers had been distinguished as patriots, ever ready to do and dare for the land of their birth. More than one of his ancestors came to an untimely end in consequence. Lord Thomas Fitzgerald lost his head on Tower Hill for a gallant but fruitless attempt to recover the independence of Ireland. There is no name in the Irish peerage which has been so frequently and prominently con- nected with the political destinies of Ireland as that of the illustrious race from whom Lord Edward descended. This illustrious Irishman was born in 1763. He was the fifth son of the Duke of Leinster—the duke who addressed a memorial to George 11., denouncing the political Primate Stone as "a greedy Churchman, investing himself with the temporal power and affecting to be a second Wolsey in the State." Ten years after the birth of his son Edward, the Duke died. The son, who was educated for the military profession, in course of time became a lieutenant in the 96th Regiment of Foot. As one of Flood's "armed nego- tiators,' he went to America, where be won laurels in his profession, and where his career nearly came to an abrupt termination. He was engaged at Eutaw Springs one of the best fighting engagements during the war. So close indeed and desperate was the encounter that every officer engdged is said to have had, personally, and hand to hand, the op- portunity of distinguishing himself. Lord Edward received a severe wound in the thigh, which left him insensible on the field. In this helpless situation he was found by a poor negro, who carried him off the field on his back to his hut, and there nursed him most tenderly, till he was well enough of his wound to bear removing to Charlestown. This negro was no other than the faithful Tony, whom, in gratitude for the honest creature's kindness, he now took into his ser- vice, and who continued devotedly attached to his noble master to the end of his career. Another incident may be here mentioned, as it is somewhat connected with this military expedition. It is said that when Lord Edward lay suffering under the fatal wounds of which he died in 1793, a military man connected with the Government, who had known him at this time, happening to allude during a visit to him in prison to the circumstances under which they were brought together, the gallant sufferer exclaimed— " Ah ! I was wounded then in a very different cause; that was in fighting against liberty—this in fighting for it."

On his return to Ireland he became a member of Parlia- ment, and formed one of that band of patriots who laboured, through good and evil report, to uphold the independence of Ireland. When at last, despairing of obtaining any good for Ireland from the English Government and from the Irish Parliament as then constituted, Grattan announced his determination to retire from political strife, Lord Edward was one of the patriots who formed the same resolution, and, with Arthur O'Conner, threw in his lot with the United Irishmen. He soon became one of the most promi- nent members of that society, and went to the Continent to negotiate with the French Directory for assistance in the attempt about to be made to secure the liberties of Ireland. It was he who planned the military operations for the gene- ral rising which was fixed for the 23rd of May. When the arrest of the Committee was made in Bond's horme, Lord Edward was not present, and there were many, even in high quarters, who were anxious to spare the life of this noble chief. "Will nobody," wrote Lord Clare to a friend of Lord Edward's, "reason with that rash young man? Will no- body induce him to leave the kingdom? I pledge myself every port shall be left open to him." But the answer Lord Edward gave was the only answer which a noble chief could give. "It is now out of the question," said he. "I am too deeply pledged to these men to be able .0 withdraw with honour." Indeed, the very calamity that had just be- fallen the cause but bound a spirit like his more ardently to its service. To repair the breaches made in the organisa- tion by these arrests was now the first great object of Lord Edward and his friends. The Government offered a reward for his apprehension, and the Castle authorities did their best to discover his whereabouts. For several weeks their efforts were in vain. Lady Fitzgerald, on the disappearance of her husband, removed from the Duke of Leinster's house in Denzel-street to a private house, taking with her an at- tached female servant and her husband's 'favourite Tony. To this house Lord Edward found his way. He had not been long there, however, when one of those slight accidents which seem to defy all caution made the secret known to the whole family. The name he went by was Jackson. A pair of boots having been left outside his door to be cleaned, the man servant to whom they had been given for that pur- pose told his mistress afterwards that he knew who the gentleman was upstairs, but that she need not fear, for he would die to save him. He then showed her Lord Edward's name written at full length in one of the boots. The lady mentioned the circumstance to Lord Edward. "What a noble fellow," he exclaimed. "I should like to have some talk with him." In the hope that it might be some incite- ment to the man's fidelity, the lady told him his lordship's wish. But he answered, "No; I will no look at him; for if they should take use up, I can then, you know, swear that I never saw him."

At length his pursuers discovered his retreat. Major Swan and others made their way to Thomas-street, where he was hiding. Having placed soldiers round the house to prevent his escape, the Major mounted the stairs and made his way to Lord Edward's room. Scarcely had he time to mention the object of his visit when Lord Edward jumped up, as Murphy, who was also present, describes him "like a tiger from the bed," on seeing which, Major Swan fired a small pocket pistol at him, but without effect. Lord Edward struck at Swan with a dagger and immediately after, Ryan, armed only with a sword cane, entered the room. In the meantime Major Sirr, hearing the report of Swan's pistol, hastened up stairs, and saw within the room Lord Edward struggling between Swan and Ryan, the latter down on the floor weltering in his blood, and both clinging to their powerful adversary, who was now dragging them towards the door. Sirr took a deli- berate aim and fired, lodging the contents of his pistol in Lord Edward's right arm, near the shoulder. For a moment the wound staggered him, but he rallied immediately and struggled so violently that the soldiers who had come upon the scene found it necessary to lay their firelccks across him before he could be disarmed or bound so as to prevent far- ther mischief. At once, a doctor was sent for. The wounds of Major Swan, though numerous, were found not to be severe but Ryan's gave little hope. The wound which Lord Edward had received was pronounced by the doctor not to be dangerous, upon hearing of which his lordship calmly said, "I am sorry for that." From Thomas-street he was conveyed in a sedan chair to the Castle. There his wounds were dressed, and to one who was going to his wife with the news, he said, "Break it tenderly to her." We have spoken of Lord Clare terms in such terms that we are bound to mention here one incident to his credit. While Lord Edward lay in INewgate delirious from the wound which he had received, his aunt, Lady Louisa Connolly, applied in vain to the Lord-Lieutenant (Lord Camden) and the Chief Secretary (Lord Castlereagh) for an order to see him. In her despair she thought of the Lord Chancellor, and drove to his house. He had a large dinner party, and dinner was hardly off the table. He went to her directly, and heard her request. "Lady Louisa," he said, after a pause for deliberation, "to grant an order is impossible. We have decided in Council that none shall be given, but you are a woman and a near relative. I know of no decision which prohibits my taking you with me." He went with her at once, and remained three hours in an outer apartment, during her interview with her nephew. On the night of the 3rd of June, it having become manifest that the noble prisoner could not survive many hours, the hearts of those in authority at length relented, and his brother was permitted to see him. "It is Heaven to see you," said the sufferer. These were about the last intelligible words he uttered. He relapsed into delirium, and on the 4th of June, 1798, the best, the noblest, and the bravest of the band of United Irishmen passed over to the great majority. It was clear that the arrest of Lord Edward had been the result of treachery. Some one had sold the noble lord for money. For 62 years the secret of the name of the blood. money recipient who sold the setting of Lord Edward Fitz- gerald to the Irish Government for £l,OOO prompt payment was carefully preserved. Numbers of innocent persons were suspected of the infamy of this transaction. Peter Finnerty was suspected. Lawrence Tighe was suspected. Murphy's servant woman was suspected. Felix Rourke was suspected. Walter Cox was publicly denounced by Dr. Brenan, in his " Milesian Magazine," as the betrayer. Even Samuel Neil- son was suspected. The memories of several of Lord Edward's followers—nay, even of some who were his bosom friends—have been cruelly wronged by imputations of treachery; by inuendoes and whisperings of authentic reve- lations of discoveries of their perfidy, which have sur- rounded their graves with hateful snspicions of their honour- Inflicting pain and anguish on their wives and children. But

div.head: TEMPORARY RELEASE OF MR. PARNELL, M.P.
div.p: TEMPORARY RELEASE OF MR. PARNELL, M.P.

Mr. Parnell, M.P., the Irish Land League leader, was released from Kilmainham at six o'clock on Monday morn- ing, and left at once by mail steamer for Holyhead. The hon. member is released on parole for ten days, in order that he may attend the funeral of a nephew who died in Paris on Saturday. No one in Dublin was aware of the impending event, and there was no demonstration of any character as Mr. Parnell drove through the city to the Westland-row terminus, where he booked through to London. The news of Mr. Parnell's releas3 spread like wildfire throughout the country, and for some time it was generally believed that he had been unconditionally liberated. The Castle authorities refused all information on the subject, and allowed the above rumour to spread and grow in volume until it was confidently reported that the prison gates were about to be opened, and the suspects generally to be released. Acting on the strength of these rumours, 'great rejoicings were manifested among Mr. Parnell's followers throughout the kingdom, and high hopes were raised, only to be dashed again, when the true facts of the case leaked out, as they did in the evening. Mr. Parnell pledged his word not to take part in any politi- cal demonstration during the period he is at large. The hon. member spent Monday night in London, at the residence of Mr. Justin M'Carthy, and ofi Tuesday morning left London for Paris, and succeeded in giving most of his friends the slip. By some it is said that he has most carefully avoided everything in the way of demonstration, and has refused during his absence in Paris to hold any communication with his Parliamentary colleagues relating to political affairs. From another source we gather that despite Mr. Parnell's desire to avoid all political matter, he has been induced to suggest what he thinks the best means of improving the desperate situation in Ireland. He says that some provision should be made to take away the load of arrears from poor tenants, and that the purchasing powers of the Land Act should be rendered operative. Mr. Parnell, it may be added, has now been nearly six months in gaol. He was arrested in Dublin on the 13th October last, and conveyed at once to Kilmainham, where he remained till Monday morning. The two warrants issued by the Lord-Lieutenant, on which he was arrested, charged him with inciting and intimidating people from paying their just debts in the shape of rents, and also from availing themselves of the benefit of the Land Act. Immediately on his arrest,.Mr. Egan, the Land League treasurer, and other officials, hastily left Dublin and betook themselves to Paris. His release, exactly stated, is for a week or such further time, not exceedinc, ten days, as will enable him to attend his nephew's funeral'.

div.head: EASTER MONDAY VOLUNTEER REVIEW.
div.p: THE EASTER MONDAY VOLUNTEER REVIEW.

The Easter Monday volunteer review and sham fight at Portsmouth was attended with complete success. According to the pre-arranged plan, the 27,000 men engaged in the operations, under the supreme command of Prince Edward of Saxe-Weimar, were divided into attacking and defending forces, the former under Major-General Higginson and Sir E. Wood, while Major-Generals Pakenham and Gage com- manding the defending force. The signal to open was fired about noon, when about a quarter of a million of spectators had assembled to watch the manceuvres from the surround- ing hills. The invaders, having landed at Brighton with the intention of marching 'upon London, had detached a force to mask Portsmouth, and were engaged by the defen- ders on Portsdown Hills and the Hilsea lines. In endeavour- ing to obtain possession of the heights in the rear and to the south of Fort Widley the invaders were successfully met by Pakenham's third brigade and the fire of gunboats in har- bour, and were consequently unable to occupy Cosham and the line of hills. The contest lasted an hour and a half, when the attacking force, having no prospect of making good their hold upon Portsmouth, the Duke of Cambridge gave the order to cease firing. The Prince of Wales, the Commander-in-Chief, the Duke and Duchess of Teek, and numerous foreign officers were present. It was half-past five when the review was concluded. Before leaving the ground the Prince of Wales expressed his entire satisfaction with the day's proceedings. The limes in a description of the mimic battle, says The plan of attack of General Higginson, commanding the invaders, was merely to mask Cosham, occupying the atten- tion of any troops met with by a false attack conducted by only one battalion, and to destroy Cosham with his heavy guns, which were also to silence, or, at least, occupy the attention of, the defenders of Hilsea lines; while with Nevrdigate's division marching close to the northern limit of the manceuvre ground, an attempt was to be made on the enemy's left to hustle them off the hill. At noon the signal gun was fired, and Sprot's brigade of Wood's division, cover- ing his front witl. Ist Surrey Rifles, showed along the ridge and soon began to dip down in the valley in order to im- press any troops in Cosham with the idea that an attack on the village was intended. The 92nd and the 2nd battalion of the Black Watch were sent to occupy this village as soon as noon had passed, but beyond a bickering ccmbat at long range Sprot's brigade had no part in the battle. He, how- ever, carried out his instructions mist exactly. The de- fending force under General Pakenham had been equally prompt, and pushing rapidly forward had established a bat- tery of eight 40-pounders on a high knoll into which the ridge rises a little to the eastward of Fort Southwick, and about 12-35 the gunboats if Porchester, the blended guns in Hilsea lines together with the 40-pounders above mentioned, opened fire, and almost immediately General Higginson's four 40-poun- ders replied from a support a little to the westward of Fort Purbrook. About 1.30 p.m. the fight. was very hot. Paken- ham's line ran from north-west to sonth-east, and he was gradually impelling the enemy back towards Ford Widley. Along a considerable portion of the line of Gough's and Ranelagh's brigades were opposed at a distance of only 100 yards, and, had there been ballets in the rifles, no one at the end of five minutes would have been left alive in that part lof the field. The volunteers, however, were animated by the gallantry of their respective brigadiers, one of whom roae a few yards in front and the other a few yards in rear of their firing lines. No wonder, then, that some bodies of Ranelagh's brigade almost strolled up to the firing line, while others who were ordered to retire did so at a leisurely pace. It was magnificent, but was certainly not war. In the meantime Kent being reinforced, surged forward with irresistible might and thrust back Pakenham's left brigade. At this critical moment Wood had collected the best part of two of his brigades, for Sprot, in obedience to orders, had

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: THE STATE OF IRELAND.
On Tuesday Lord Carlingford was invested a Knight o St. Patrick at Dublin Castle.

Mr. P. J. Smyth, M.P., has received an address from the labourers of Moycalla, county Tipperary, conveying tht assurance of their support in his oppositi94 to the Land League. Placards were posted at Castleisland on Monday, offering a reward of £5OO to any person who would murder five land- lords to be named to him in a manner similar to that in which Mr. Herbert was shot. The placards were immediately torn down.

In the case of the your's; man Kinsella, who was convicted in Dublin of causing the death Of an acquaintance named Andrews in a house in Tighe-street in that city, Chief Justice Morris on Saturday passed a sentence of 20 years' penal servitude. At a soirée at Waterford, on Tuescikiy, Mr. Leamy, M.P., , stigmatised the present Government at: mean and con- temptible; and said that if Parliamentary azitation failed, Irishmen would resort to another and surer meano of bring- ing back their freedom.

The Times publishes a letter from Mr. Goldwin Smith advocating stringent repressive measures in Ireland, and says that, whatever embarrasment may be felt, there is one thing which statesmen should refuse to do and that is to beat a hasty retreat before the agressiona of organised crime.

Two ex-suspects, named John Riorden, secretary of the late Land League, and Thomas 31‘Carthy, teacher of a Land League school, who were released from Clonrael and Limerick Gaols on Saturday, were on Tuesday morning arrested on a charge of treason-felony, and remanded for eight days. Farther investigation into the attempt to blow up Bally- cooney police barricks on Sunday night .shows that a quantity of powder must have been deposited at the butt of the side- walk, with the fusee concealed in a cutting in the earth. The explosion tore up the floor and considerably damaged the walls and roof.

The Dorset-street shooting caso—another supposed Fenian murder—cams before the Dublin Commission Court on Saturday. There was such a small response to the call of the jury panel that counsel for the Crown applied for the postponement of the trial till the nest Commission, and the application was granted. In connection with a seizure of arms and ammunition in Halston-street, Dublin, on Saturday, the two men Byrne and Colgan were brought up at the police court on Wednes- day charged with the possession of arms in a proclaimed district. Byrne, who admitted having been concerned in the Fenian troubles of 1867, was sentenced to three months' imprisonment. The other was released on bail. The presence of Lord Carlingford and the Marquis of Hartington, as well as of the Chief Secretary, in Ireland at this juncture has given rise to rumours as to prospective changes in the personnel of the Irish Government. The most distinct rumour is that Earl Cowper is about to resign the office of Lord Lieutenant.

Mr. Smythe, whose sister-in-law was shot on the occasion of the attempt of his own life, has addressed a letter to his tenants on the Barbaville estate, in the course of which he says that most of them by their silence assented to the deed of blood. Those liable to rent would in future pay to a non- resident agent, who could make no further allowance, nor do anything on the property not strictly required by law. He regarded many of the tenants-as guilty of complicity, directly or indirectly, in the plot o( murder, which they might now regret, because of the fatal mistake. It will be remembered that when an attack was made by a number of young men said to be returning from a dance party neat Dundrum, county Tipperary, on the 26th Decerft- ber, on the house of an unpopular blacksmith named Dwyer, the blacksmith rushed out and put them to flight, and, overtaking one of them, felled him with a billhook or hedge slasher, inflicting a mortal wound. Dwyer surrendered to the police, but the grand jury at the aBslz3s threw out the bill of indictment. On Tuesday evening Dwyer's house was burnt-to the ground. Dr. Gillooly, Roman Catholic Bishop of Elphin, speaking in the Cathedral at Sligo on Sunday, referred to the way Ire- land was being disgraced by foul murders and the system of "Boycotting" certain people, and denounced all illegal and unconstitutional combinations. The vengeance of Heaven, he said, would fall upon a country which used such diaboli- cal means to forward even the best objects. He also con- demned the teaching of those who urged the people not to pay their just and lawful debts. They should avoid all con- nection with tho!e who taught such wild and un-Christian doctrines. If there were wrongs to be redressed they should be redressed in a constitutional manner.

The Dublin Gazette of Tuesday night offers a reward of £lOO for the arrest of Dennis Ryan and Patrick Lonney, for the murder of Patrick Sullivan at Cork, and £5O for any in- formation that will lead to their arrest. Also a reward of £lOO for information regarding the persons who posted boy- cotting notices at Mullough, county Clare. A reward of £2OO isoffered for any information that will lead to the arrest of the persons who attacked the house of a farmer named Patrick Muggar, at Skronemore, county Kerry, on the night of the 27th ultimo, when Muggar was seriously wounded.

Sir George Young, in a letter to the Pall Mall Gazette, utters some reassuring words in regird to the Irish diffi- culty. He strongly counsels patience, and says it is too much to expect that in five short months the Land Act should have pacified the country. " The present crisis," Sir George adds, "is a crisis only in England. In Ireland matters are running their course—a course which was fore- seen, which we cannot wholly stem, which we can only in- fluence by degrees. In England the question is whether English Liberalism can stand the strain of having done what was right, though unpleasant, and of missing the immediate reward. In political troubles no lane is very long; the turning was by no means expected this year." Major Traill, resident magistrate, writing from Clare- morris, tells a remarkable story of the way in which he was guarded day and night by an armed escort of policemen. He himself and his groom also carry revolvers, and he says he never moves about with less than 25 cartridges ready to be fired in as many seconds, and 34 cartridges in reserve. Major Traill gives this advice to those who, like himself, live threatened lives :—" Let certain death be the method of defence prepared by all objectives' for either the fanatic, the hired assissin, or the tool who may attempt to take the life of his neighbour. The man who attempts nay life and lives to be tried by a jury is entitled to their merciful con- sideration as a brave man." ANOTHER MURDER IN DUBLIN.

At nine o'clock on Wednesday morning the body of a labouring man was found in the river Liffey. His feet were tied together, and there were desperate wounds on his head and body. One of the wounds in the abdomen was so large that the bowels protruded. The deceased has been recog- nised by his mother, who lives in the County Dublin. He has been missing for some time, and it is believed that he was murdered and thrown into the river with a weight at- tached to his legs. The police are investigating the matter. DEFEAT OF LAND LEAGUERS. It was intended by the National party at the North Dublin Board of Guardians to elect on Wednesday to the offices of chairman and vice-chairman persons of Land League views, but a whip was made by the Constitutional Club and all available Conservatives elected and ex-cfficio guardians attended. Fifty-seven members of the Board altogether presented themselves, giving the Conservative party a de- cided majority. Amongst them were Lord Ardilauff and Mr. J. Hamilton, M.P., the latter having arrived from London for the purpose. The result was the re-election to the chair- manship of Mr. Anthony O'Neill, J.P., a supporter of Arch- bishop M'Cabe, and the election of a Conservative to the vice-chairmanship. MURDER IN COUNTY DOWN.

On Saturday night, Thomas Skillen, a labourer, lost his life in Holywood, County Down. William Barre was arrested for his wilful murder. Two other men, named John Connolly and Robert Morgan, were also taken into custody. It appears that after coming out of a tavern, Connolly and deceased had an altercation of a party nature. Barre, who was close by, went into his own house and brought out an old barrel of a rifle and struck Skilien, inflicting serious in- jurie on his skull, from the effects of which he died. EXTRAORDINARY SHOOTING OUTRAGE IN DUBLIN.

Another mysterious shooting affray occurred in Sackville- street, on Saturday night, at eleven o'clock, near the O'Connell Monument. At the time mentioned a shot was heard, and a man shouted, "I am shot; there is a bullet in my leg." A crowd immediately collected, and the young man, pulling up his trousers, showed that he was bleeding profusely. He was at once conveyed to the hospital, where, on examination, it was discovered that there was a hole in his trousers similar in all respects to a bullet mark. There was also a wound in his leg three-quarters of an inch in depth, but no sign of a bullet in the leg. Tho injured man is stated to be John H. Blackwell. and his age about 26. Blackwell is detained in the hospital, but his wound, though serious, is not considered to be dangerous. Much excite-, rnent prevailed in Sackville-street, which was crowded at the time, and the rumour went abroad that another infQrtner had 4:.,en shot,

div.head: FROM MENTONE
div.p: FROM MENTONE

The Queen, accompanied by Princess Beatrice, left Men- tone at half-past ten on Wednesday morning for England via Cherbourg. Her Majesty's gunboat Cygnet and iron- clad Inflexible, at anchor in the roadstead, fired royal salutes and maßned yards at the moment of Her Majesty's depar- ture from the Chalet des Rosiers. Both vessels were dressed with flags. The Mayor of Mentone, the British Vice Con- sul, Captain Fisher, commanding the Inflxible, and the officers in command of the soldiers and gendarmes specially stationed at Mentone during the Queen's stay, attended at the railway station to take leave of Her Majesty, who ad- dressed a few words to each, thanking them for their atten- tion during her visit.

Before fearing Mentone the Queen presented 3,000 f. to the poor, 1,5000 f. to the charitable institutions, a set of diamond studs to the Mayor, a portrait of herself and the Princess Beatrice to the English Consul, a diamond pin to the Consul's son, a diamond ring to the local postmaster, a watch-chain to the station-master, a gold pencil-case and 'pin to the under station-master, and a ring to the commis- saire of police.

div.head: TRADE NOTES.
div.p: TRADE NOTES.
An increase of wages amounting to 10 per cent. was granted to the block chain makers in the Staffordshire dis- trict on Saturday.

The number of failures in England and Wales gazetted during I the week ending Saturday, April Bth, was 226, The number in the corresponding week of last year was 261, showing a decrease of 352 being a total decrease iu 1882, to date, of 462. —Kenzp's Mercantile Gazette. The lock out of the Chorley self-actor spinners was an ac- complishe3.. 'tact from Monday, the notices of the employers cl",ise their mills expired on Thursday night. The original Cause of the dispute arose through the spinners at Messrs. Snietburst's not being able to make sufficient wages, owing to the bad preparation of the raw material. A portion of the spinners struck in consequence, and when their notices ex- pired the remainder followed their example. Messrs. Smet- hurst agreed to and actually did effect a remedy, when the spinners made the demand by indicator. The firm refused to grant it, and they were supported by the whole of the master spinners in the borough, with the result that unless Messrs. Smethurst's workmen return to their employment the whole of the spinners would be locked out. This has now been done, and a large number of weavers and others engaged in the preparation of the raw material are also thrown out of employmeßt. FARMING AND THE CORN TRADE. The Mark-lane Express says :—" The past week has been a season of ' drought, the searching easterly winds having taken up all surface moisture. The appearance of the young crops has net been improved thereby; in fact, everything stands in need of warm rain. The supply of native wheat to the country markets has again been of an irregular character, deliveries in some cases having been ample, whilst in others they have been very meagre. The markets have been quite of ad holiday character, and very little business has been re- ported. In some few cases an improvement of 6d. to Is. has been effected for prime samples, but trade has generally ruled firm in the provinces, against very limited and feeble demands. Flour has moved quietly into consumption at un- changed rates, the supply being ample. The occasional namples of fine malting barley on offer are saleable. For other articles there is no change to note. Trade tor foreign wheat off stands in London, Liverpool, and the chief pro- • vincial markets, has been almost nominal during the few business days of the past week, the consumption having been provided for during the previous week." TRH LABOUR MARKET.—The labour market is at present a good deal affected by the Easter holidays, but remains on the whole in a fairly satisfactory condition. Round Sheffield collieries are on half-time, and in several other districts miners are not fully employed. In several quarters, how- ever, there is a movement amongst the colliers to ask for an advance in wages. At Birmingham the hardware branches are fairly well employed, and some extensions of works are being made. At Newcastle-on-Tyne both the shipbuilding and brickmaking industries are busy, and at most of the northern ports both shipbuilders and marine engineers have plenty of work in hand. In Staffordshire the iron chain- makers have obtained an advance of ten per cent. in their wages, and throughout the north engineers are asking for a return to the higher rate of pay current a few years since. The textile trades generally are fairly employed, though at Bradford business is dull. At Kidderminster both the carpet and the rug trades are busy, and a good deal of overtime is being worked. The agitation for reduced hours amongst railway servaßts continues, and in the metropolis shop assis- tants are still pressing their demand for legislative inter- ference on their behalf. Emigration to the United States continues on a large scale, and a movement of unemployed labourers to Canada is under discussion. Contracts for railway extensions in Natal have been made.—Labour News.

Tili LANCASHIRE IRON AND COAL TRADES: MAN- CHESTER, WEDNESDAY.—With the Easter holidays and the quarterly meetings coming so close together, business in the iron trade of this district has been practically suspended during the past week. Prices nominally are quoted about the same as last week, local and district braids averaging about 475. to 48s. per ton less 21 for delivery equal to Man- chester, and bars at about £6 15s. to £6 17s. 6d. per ton. Both pig and finished iron makers are working on nith old orders rather than push for new business, but where sellers have to come into the market prices are decidedly against them, and it seems to be generally anticipated that finished iron will have to give way upon the rates which are at present being quoted. The engineering branches of trade continue generally well employed with orders in hand, but low prices are still complained of, and the influx of new business or of inquiries is not so great as it was a short time back. The coal trade of this district has been exceedingly quiet during the week. Nominally the market may be said to be without change, with all classes of round coal bad to move and lying heavily in stock. The pressure to sell on the part of needy holders of stock causes prices to be very irregular, but the average quotations remain at about 83. 6d. to as. for best coals, 63. to 7s. for seconds, and ss. to ss. 6d. for common round coals. - Inquiries for gas-making coals are now coming into the market. The best qualities of Lancashire screened gas coal are being offered at about 68.61 to 7s. per ton at the pit mouth. Engine classes of fuel meet with a more ready sale than round coals, but con- sidering the present very limited production of slack supplies are fairly plentiful, and prices do not as yet harden to the extent anticipated. Burgy at the pit month averages about 4s. 6d. to 55., good slack 3s. Pd. to 4s. 3d., with common sorts offering at from 2s. 6d, to 3s. 3d. per ton. The shipping trade continues dull, and both at Liverpool and Garston exceedingly low prices are quoted to secure orders.

div.head: POLITICAL ITEMS.
div.p: POLITICAL ITEMS.
The farmers of county Down have decided to invite Mr. T. M. Healy to contest the county at the next election, in conjunction with the Radical candidate, Mr. Hans M‘Mordie.

Lord Colin Campbell, M.P.,replying to one of his Argyll- shire constituents, who asked why he di ol not vote for the Government on the closure, says that closure by bare majority would be dangerous and hostile to the interests of the Liberal party. If the Liberals used this power they must expect from the Tories such retaliation as would still further degrade the house, . _ _

Mr. J. SI. Maclean, of Chiswick, who was lately invited by the Oldham Conservatives to contest the borough at the next general election, in company with Mr. Smith Taylor- Whitehead, has written to Mr. Samuel Taylor, president of Oldham Conservative Association, consenting to do so. He says he feels honoured by the invitation, to which he could not reply sooner, because he had to take formal leave of the Elgin Boroughs Conservatives. A Bristol paper having suggested that Mr. Errington's expenses in coming from Rome to vote for the cliture were paid out of the secret service fund, the secretary of the Fish- ponds Liberal Association asked if the statement were true, and received the following reply from Mr. Hamilton "Mr. Gladstone directs me to refer you to the declarations on this subject made by Sir Charles Dilke in the House of Commons, which are quite conclusive. At the same time I am to point out that those who made the allegations ought to give tlie grounds on which they base them." In response to the invitation to Mr. Dillon,M.P., at present in Kilmainham, to allow himself to be put in nomination for the first vacancy in the representation of Birmingham, that gentleman expresses himself highly complimented by the offer, and will give the invitation due attention. In any case, he says, on the first possible opportunity he will visit that town, and address his friends on the political situation. Mr. Parnell has been invited to accompany Mr. Dillon. Mr. Jacob Bright, M.P., presided on Wednesday evening at a lecture delivered at Wilmslow on "The Franchise and the Land Laws," and spoke in support of the extention of the franchise ha the counties. He expressed an opinion that instead of an extention of the franchise leading to the economical errors feared by Mr. Goschen it was very likely to teach economical truth to the superiors of the agricultural labourer. It would, he believed, ultimately lead to an im- provement in the condition of agricultural labourers, and might result in those who would be thereby enfranchised challenging the wisdom of the peculiar land laws of this country.

At Holywood, county Down, on Saturday night, an "altercation of a party nature" occurred among several men, and one of them, named William Barre, struck another, named Skillen, on the head with a rifle barrel and killed him.

On Wednesday night, about half-past nine o'clock, while a policeman and a man named Holland were standing drink- ing at the counter of the public-house of Mr. Thomas M‘Gowan, at Keadue, county Roscommon, shots were fired in at the open door by two men, one armed with a rifle, the other with a blunderbuss. The bullet and slugs failed to hit anyone. The police barracks is about 10 yards from the house, and there are 30 extra police stationed in and around the village. M'Crowan was recently " boycotted " for some unknown reason, and his horse was shot in broad day light abeut two months ago. Mr. Turner R.M., ond a large party of constabulary, proceeded to Keadue, and arrested on sus- picion a returned " American " named Devlin and a tramp named Carty.
