div.head: ISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: ISCELLANEOUS.

At the Easter Vestry Meeting at St. James's, Hatcham, on Tuesday, there was a repetition of the noisy proceedings of the last few years. Dr. T. A. Elias, a well-known medical practitioner in Southport, died with awful suddenness on Tuesday while visiting a patient. Lady Harriet Scott Bentinck, who succeeded in 1879 to the Ayrshire estates of the late Duke of Portland, has just died at Naples, in her 80th year. Sir Richard Gilpin, Bart., who was for many years one of the representatives of Bedfordshire in the House of Com- mons, has just died in his 82nd year. On Tuesday, Sir Henry Lech, the retiring governor of the Isle of Man, and Lady Loch were presented with addresses in the ancient metropolis cf the Island, Castletown. Ellen Robinson, sentenced to death at Omagh Assizes for the murder of her child, has had her sentence commuted by the Lord-Lieutenant to penal servitude for life. Mr. William Cockerel', of Cambridge, barrister-at-law, of the South-Eastern Circuit, has been appointed Recorder of Sudbury, Suffolk-, vacant by the death of Mr. T. H. Naylor. Arrangements hays been made to hold a general confer- ence of agricultural labourers in May for the purpose of urging upon the Legislature the necessity of an early consi- deration of the county franchise question. It has been decided, the Army and Navy Gazette under- stands, not to bestow any honours •n• rewards on the officers, non-commissioned officers, and men who took part in the action at Majuba Hill. On Monday morning a prize fight took place in a field at Tottenham between two labouring men named Wright and Watson, for a stake of £lO a-side. Twelve rounds, occupy- ing 35 minutes, were fought, when Wright gave in. The fight, which was uninterrupted by the police, was witnessed by a large number of spectators. A stone weighing half a ton was removed from the Man- chester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway just in time to prevent a train from Manchester being wrecked aL Neepsen- den, near Sheffield. It is stated that a dozen men were seen rolling the stone on the 'hie ten minutes before the train was due.

During the past week the West Cornwall spring mackerel fishery was very successful. The catches ranged trom 2,060 to 4,000 per boat, one night some of the boats having up to '7,000. Prices were firm, and ranged from 255. down to 13s. 6j. per six score. Nearly all the fish were forwarded by rail for the Paris, London, and principal provincial markets. The official programme of the Irish Exhibition to be opened in Dublin, in August, was issued on Saturday. The exhibits are classified under six heads, namely, raw material produced in Ireland, articles manufactured in Ireland, machinery suitable for Irish industries, Irish 'home and ,cottage industries of all kinds, art work by residents in Ire- land, and a loan collection of paintines, sculpture, carriages, china, plate, lace, embroidery, and antiquities. A shocking accident, resulting in the death of Miss Rutter, of Huddersfield, and injury to Miss Lattimer, of Bradford, and Mrs. Webster, of Barnsley,lms occurred at Silkstone Fall, near Barnsley. The ladies awompanied Mr. Webster, a confectioner, in a pheeton to Silkstone Fall to visit a relation. In returning the horse Wok fright. Mr. Webster fell out of the vehicle, and the ladies jumped from the conveyance. Miss Ilutter fractured her skull, and died instantly. Tim HATTON Gs,unrrr ROBSERY.—The Court of Appeal of Brussels has decided the demand of extradition made by the French Government in the case of Watson Henry nil- ton and Cora Fulton for a robbery cormnitted at Paris. They are also the presumed authors of the Hatton Garden rob- . bery. After hearing the public proseettor and counsel for the prisoners, the Court decided on granting the extradition, which, however,uannot be definitive before the decision of , the Minister of Justice. _ _ _ _ _ _

A BRAVE PEAT.—At a meetir.g of the inhabitants of Halesowen, on Tuesday, Lord Lyttelton, on behalf di Her Majesty the 'Queen, presented William Hinton, Inland Revenue officer, with the Albert medal for his bravery in entering a burning building and rescuing a large quantity of blasting powder. It Was stated that through Hinton's bravery the block of buildings was prevented from being destroyed, and the lives of several persons saved. Hinton, in responding,-said he risked his own life to saveothers. An interesting case arising out of the revolt against "ex- traordinary tithe" has occupied an East Sussertench of magistrates for several days. A farmer who is charged with assaulting a bailiff who levied a distress has been,committed for trial at Lewes, where, no doubt, a good deal will be heard on the question. The bailiff was fined for assaulting the farmer's daughter. ' SHoCKING ACCIDENT NEAR BAKEWELL : TIVO PERSONS KILLED.—On Monday afternoon an accident, by which two persons lost their lives, occurred at Padley, near Bakewell. A carriage belonging to Mr. Haigh, of Sheffield, was con- veying a party of excursionists, and when near a place called Froggatt Edge it overtook a traction engine, and in attempting to pass it the horses took fright ana ran up the bank on the side of the road. The vehicle was overturned, and Ben Dakin Littlewood, aged 21, and Miss May Cook- smith, both of Sheffield, were killed on the spot. EXFLOSION ON A STEAMER: THREE IAI ES LOST.—A. ' dreadful boiler explosion has taken place at Amlvrch, Anglesea. The small screw steamer Noah was towing the sloop Victoria out of Atulwch Bay, when the boiler of the steamer exploded, killing three men on board her. The ste liner was so seriously damaged that she immediately sank. One of the men killed was named Nicholas Petters, 1 and the other, named Owen Pritchard, was a diver from Holyhead. The owner of the steamer is Mr. Jones, of Fagwr, Amlwch.

EVPRAORDINARY LETTER TO MR. GLADSTONE.— Mr. Barlow Smythe, whose sister-in-law was murdered in West- meath, last Sunday week, has written a letter to Mr. Glad- stone, laying the guilt of the deed of blood at his door, sup- ported as he is " by the 'No rent' M.P.'s, the Press, and some Irish bishops." 141 r. Smythe further states that the terrorism in his district is so great that no one dare expose the assassins who, even if caught, would escape after the farce of a trial by jury. Mr. Gladstone, in reply, expresses his deep and heartfelt sympathy with Mr. Smythe on the occasion of this, terrible outrage, adding that it will be readily understood why the charge made ic his letter is not noticed.

Tim WORKINGTON MURDER—On Tuesday, Maynard James Harrison, aged 17, was brought before the Working- ton magistrates charged on remand with the wilful murder of Lucy-Sands, aged 16, at Workington, on the Ist Decem- ber, and burying her under a stone heap. The principal part of the proceedings was the reading of the depositions of some :30 witnesses in the case for the prosecution, and amending some 3f them. The case hiving closed for the prosecution, Mr. Paisley, who appeared for the accused, briefly addressed the court, arguing that the evidence was not sufficient to commit the prisoner upon. The magistrates, ho,kever, after a 10 minutes' adjournment, decided to com- mit the prisoner for trial at the assizes. ENGLAND AND IRELAND.—A remarkable debate, Mr. Justin M'Carthy, M.P., in his work tells us, took place in the House of Commons on the 16th March, 1868, on the condition of Ireland. Mr. John Francis Maguire, an Irish M.P. of high character and great ability and earnestness, stated:—"l hold the geographical situation of England and Ireland renders a separation of the two countries impossible. I have often expressed my belief that even in the-event of a war between England and some foreign State—the American Republic, for instance—and even in the event of England losing temporal possession of Ireland, one of the conditions of peace which the foreign Power would most freely accept would be the handing back of Ireland to Great Britain. To my mind, then, separation is a result not to be seriously thought of. But I accept cordially the saying of Grattan, that 'if the ocean forbade separation, the sea denied union.'" Mr. Maguire was in favour of domestic legislation for the internal affairs of Ireland. DEA.TII OF MR. D. G. RosErri.—Mr. Dante Gabriel Rosetti, the well-known poet and artist, died late on Sunday night at Birchington, near Margate, where he had been stay- ing for some -weeks. He had been in failing health for some time past. Mr. Rosetti wo the son of Mr. Gabriel Rosetti, the commentator of Dante, and was brother to Mr. William Michael Rosetti, the critic, and to Miss Christina Rosetti, the poetess. He was looked upon by many as the foremost exponent of the-so-called "resthetic school, both in art and poetry. He was born in London in 1828, and early in life exhibited decided artistic tastes. He has been chiefly before the public as a designer for the better class of illustrated works, and his name has been associated with those of Madox Brown, W. Holman Hunt, Millais, and others. In 1861 Mr. Rosetti published a work entitled "The Early Italian Poets," and in 1870 a volume of poems. THE FIRST NEAVSPAPER AND THE FIRST ALWERTISE- MENT.—The first paper in Britain published at stated inter- vals for the dissemination of intelligence, was the TVeekely .71-ewes, the first number of which was published in London on the 23rd of May, 1622. It was destitute of advertise- ments, and indeed contained very little news. The first ad- vertisement appeared on the 2nd of April, 1647, in Number Thirteen of a weekly paper called Perfect Occurrences of Every Dale iournall or, Parliament and other Moderate In- telligence—a name that would make our newsboys frantic— and relates to "A Book applauded by the Clergy of Eng- land, called The Diune Right of Church Government." For oeveral years booksellers were the only advertisers, but as the newspapers began to circulate more among the less edu- cated classes, other kinds of advertisements appeared, and the :columns gradually assumed a more business-like aspect. The Mercurius Politicus of September 30th, 1658, con- tained the first trade advertisement, which relates the charms of the new "drink called by the Chineans tcha, by other nations tay alias tee."—All the Year Round."

WINMEIS OF THE VICTORIA CROSS.—The London Gazette announces that the Queen will confer the decoration of the Victoria Cross upon Lieutenant Henry Lysons and Private Edward Fewer, second battalion of the. Cameroniaus, for conspicuous :bravery in Zululand on March 28, 1879, during assault of inblobane mountains. Sir Evelyn Wood ordered the dislodgment of certain Zulus from strong natural caves, commanding a position in which some wounded were tying. Some delay ocourring in the execution of the order, Captain the Hon. Ronald Campbell, Coldstream Guards, followed by Lieutenant Lysons, aid de camp, and Private Fowler ran forward in the most determined manner and advanced over the fallen boulders and between the walls of rocks leading ,to the cave in which the enemy lay hidden. It being possible for two men to walk abreast, the assailants had to keep in single file. Captain Campbell arrived first at the moiath of the cave, from which Zulus were firing, and there met hi death. Lieutenant Lysons and Private Fowler im- mediately dashed at the cave, from which led several sub- terranean passages, and, firing into the chasm below, succeeded in forcing the occupants to forsake their strong- hold. • Lieutenant Lysons remained at the cave's mouth some minutes after the attaet uutil Captab Campbell's body , was carried down the slopes.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 15, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 15, 1882.

It has been proposed that the Lord Mayor of Dublin shall convene a meeting to decide upon a memorial to the memory of the lately deceased poet, Denis Florence M.‘Carthy. A serious poaching affray has occurred on Lord Middle- ton's estate near Mallon. A gang of poachers was surprised by the keepers, and a fight ensued, in which the poachers used their guns. Two of the keepers were wounded with shot. The two men Cartwright and Hudson, who engaged in a prizefight at Hendon recently, had another encOunter on Wednesday, near Hatfield. Twenty-one rounds, occupying 85 minutes, were fought without interruption, when Cart- wright was declared the winner. At Rowley, on Wednesday, Henry Heath, cattle dealer, was fined £lO And costs for neglecting to report the existence of six cases of swine fever upon his premises. It was stated that through recklessness of cattle dealers swine fever had spread through two counties. On Tuesday, at Salford Sessions, Mr. Higgin, Q.C., sent a carter named Rowlett to prison for 18 months for kicking his wife with clogs. The learned chairman said he wished "those brutal weapons called cloga were done away with," as they "seemed to be constructed for being used as weapons of the most offensive and horrible kind."

Mr. Bushby, the Worship-street police magistrate, has sent a married woman, named Mary Ann Waller, living in Hack- ney Wick, to hard labour for six weeks for an infringement of the Infant Life Preservation Act by having more thanone infant under the age of one year for the purpose of nursing apart from their parents. Denis Florence M'Carthy, the Irish poet, died on Good Friday, at his residence, Merrion Avenue, Dublin, sur- rounded by members of his family. Mr. M'Carthy was 62 years of age. His best known works are translations of Calderon; original Irish poems, including the "Ode" on O'Connell," The Voyage of St. 'Brendan," and the song of "The Voice and Pen."

Of the eight men charged at the Chester Quarter Sessions, on Tuesaay, with having taken part in the attack on the procession of the members of the Salvation Army, on the 26th ult., five were convicted and the others acquitted. The five who were convicted were bound over to appear to receive judgment when called upon. The Recorder told them if they conducted themselves properly in future they would hear nothing further of the charge, but if they should be guilty of a similar offence they would be sentenced to lenthened terms of imprisonment. THE YALDINGr MYSTERY.—A new enlisted soldier, named George Euban, has given himself up to the police at the Curragh, stating that he was an accomplice of Esther Pay in the murder of the little girl Georgina Moore. Inquiries are on foot as to the antecedents of Eirban, whose " confes- sion " is made in circumstances which will cause it to he received with suspicion. The soldier states that some time in September last he, in company with Esther Pay, put a wire with a brick attached round the neck of the child, and that they threw her into the Medway, near Yalding, Kent. He says that he will tell all when r. t upon his trial for the Murder along with Pay. FIZ/ZIITIML ACCIDENT TO InoN'evORICERS.—Ott TLICSCiay afternoon, while James Edinberough and William Allen were feeding two furnaces at the Staveley Ironworks, near Sheffield, with coal and ironstone, there was a sudden out- burst of flames from the feeding holes of the furnaces, com- pletely enveloping both men. Every particle 'of clothing was burnt off them, and they bath presented a terrible sight. 'Edinborough was the most injured on the lowe part of the body, but Allen's back was literally roasted, ee.nd the skin bung in shreds. They were 'both removed to the Chesterfield hospital, and are in a critical state. In the" Correspendencetetween the Science and Art De- parinent and the Treasury as to the Organisation of the Normal School of Science and the Royal School of Mines," published as a Parliamentary Paper by Command, we find the following remarkable passage: "The Committee of Council, having carefully examined into the whole ques- tion, have come to the'ronclusion that it will, in all pro- bability, be found eventually advisable to move the entire 1 establishment now in armyn-street to South Kensington, and they, have been strengthened in thiscpinion by further communications they have had with Professor Huxley OR the subject of the fossil collections in his charge, and the nature of the space Tecuired for their exhibition." A STAGE ILLESION BY MRS. LANGT,RY.—" Oars" is to be finally withdrawn from the Haymarket, and it will not again be played by the Bancrofts, whose rights over all Robertson's comedies will shortly lapse. It may, perhaps, now ,do no harm, a London correspondent remarks, to explain that the song Mrs. Lengthy is supposed to eing in "Ours," and for which some of her critics have praised her, is not really delivered by Mrs.'Langtry. That lady has no singing voice. But the piano is placed close against the scenery, and Mrs. Langtry, turning half-face to the audience, and realty play- ing the accompaniment, moves her lips in agreement with the words, while another lady well-known in musical life sings behind the scenes. The illusion is complete, and it has deceived some of the most experienced critics. FEMALE EDUCATION IN IRELLND.—Mr. Giaktolle has replied to the memorial from the meeting presided over by the Archbishop of Dublin in favour of the advancement of female education in lreland :-10, Downing-street, April sth. —Rev. Sir,—l am directed by Mr. Gladstone to acquaint you that he is in receipt of the resolution relating to the Intermediate Education Act, which you have done him the honour to forward in behalf of those persons -specially in- terested in female education in '7ereland who held a meeting at the Alexandra College last month. Mr. Gladstone is sorry to learn that the fund provided by the Act is found to be inadequate to meet all the demands which are made upon it. He is afraid that fresh legislation, if desirable, must in a great degree depend upon the general state of parlia- mentary business, which is now so seriously hampered.-e--I am, 4:tc., E. HAMILTON. NARROW ESCAPE OF THE DUKE OF SrTHERIAND FROM DROWNING.—An accident occurred to the Duke of Suther- land on Friday afternoon, while he was boating on the lake in front of Trentham Hall with a number of guests. His Grace, who chose a boat with a sail, had not been on the water long 'before a sudden gust of wind capsized the small craft, throwing the Duke into the water. Being an excellent swimmer his Grace kept himself up till rescued by a servant, who, seeing his perilous position from the shore, imme- diately put ,eff to his assistance, The accident, which was witnessed by the Marquis of Stafford from the shore and the occupants of other boats, who were too far off to render any aid, created much alarm, but an hour after the accident the Duke reappeared among his guests, none the worse for the immersion.

THE OATH QUESTION.—At the Hull Borough Session, a singular incident arose in connection with the empanelling of a common jury. Mr. Champney (the Clerk of the Peace) had called twelve gentlemen into the box, and was proceed- ing to swear them according to the usual form, when Mr. Guy Hayler rose and said he had a religious objection to take an oath.—The Recorder (Mr. W. C. Beasley, Q.C.) : What is your objection? Are you an atheist ?-111r. Hayler: I am not an atheist.—The Recorder: I am very glad to hear it.—Mr. Hayler-: lam a believer in the Trinity, but J have an objection to taking the oath. lam willing to make an affirmation.- -The Recorder: That opens up a nice qt.estion whether I can allow you to affirm. I don't think the law will allow it.—Mr. Champney (to Mr. Hayler): We won't raise the question. Come out of the box.—The Recorder: I think the law will have to be altered before we receive an affirmation from yon.—Another gentleman was then railed into the box and sworn, and Mr. Hayler was released by the Clerk of the Peace from further attendance. EXTRAORDINLRY NO-RENT DEMONGTRATION IN THE HIGHIANDS.--A Skye correspondent sends to the Dailfr Nots the following particulars of an extraordinary scene on the estate of Lord Macdonald, at Nortree, in the Island of Skye: "The tenants on Balmeanach, Peinehoran, and Gedin- taillear have refused to pay rent, and as there was no pros- pect of their doing so his lordship resolved to put the law in force. On Friday, a sheriff's officer was instructed to serve summonses on twenty or more refractory tenants. For some time a regular system of watching the holdings by sentinels has been adopted to give warning of the approach of strangers, and when the officer and his party made their appearance the populace were immediately summoned, about 200 responding to the call. Upon the sheriff's officer mak- ing known his errand he was seizsd, the summonses taken from him and burned before his eyes, and then he was coolly told to return where he came from, or it would be worse for him. The agitation is spreading rapidly and assuming alarming proportions."

WHOLES&LE POISONOUS HOT CROSS BUNS. - On Good Friday, great excitement was occasioned in Inverness by the fact that about 100 persons became ill, with symptoms of poisoning, after eating hot cross buns. On the west side of the river Ness whole families were taken alarmingly ill after breakfast. In the Central school 12 children, and in the Markinch school 15 children were attacked with severe sick- ness, and had to be placed under medical treatment. In one house, in Kenneth-street, a whole family were rendered pros- trate for hours. In most cases the symptoms passed off in the course of three or four hours, and at night most of the patients were better. The poison has been traced to the buns, and, it is conjectured, must have got accidentally mixed with the spice. The superintendent of police estimates the numb2r of persons affected at 150, and the affair has been placed in the hands of the county Procurator Fiscal. The baker states that the buns were made of precisely the same materials as his bread, the spice excepted, so that the presence of the deleterious matter in the buns is attributed to its existence in the spice. Samples of the spice will be obtained from Aberdeen, where it was originally procured, and submitted for analysis.

ANOTHER SWINDLER. -At the Leeds borough quarter sessions, on Monday, before Mr. J. E. Barker (Recorder), William Darnton, 60, described as a gardener, was indicted for having obtained various sums of money, amounting altogether to about £BO, by means of fraud. By means of forged letters aided by undoubted bodily infirmity, the pri- soner succeeded in imposing upon many of the charitAbly- disposed persons in Leeds, as he had before done in London, where he raised £l5O. These letters described the prisoner as "the bravest man in England," and detailed how he had rescued a captain, his wife, and two children, from a sink- ing ship, saved the crew of a life-boat from drowning, in which feat it was said he had both his legs and three ribs broken, and that in many other instances he had rescued persons from drowning. The prisoner produced three medals, which he said had been given to him as re- wards for saving lives. So successfully was the fraud carried out that he got letters inserted in the Scarborough and Whitby newspapers drawing attention to his case, and asking for assistance. The prisoner forged a letter in the name of a Captain Godfrey, whom he had saved, and when letters were sent to the captain inquiring whether the state- ments were true, replies were received which were proved to be in the prisoner's own handwriting. Amongst other names the prisoner forged that of Mr. John Bdrran,M.P. for Leeds. The prisoner pleaded guilty and admittzl three previous convictions for felony. The learned recordsr sentenced him to eighteen eilendar months' hard labour.

Lord Roseberry on Wednesday opened an International Fisheries Exhibition in Edinburgh. A soldier's wife, travelling from Fort George to Edin- burgh, gave birth to a child in the midnight train between Forres and Dunphail. Both mother ar.d child are doing well.

The death is announced of Mr. George Foster, of Sabden, in the 87th year of his age. Mr. Foster was associated with Cobden in business, and held kindred views to his on most political questions, A manager for a corn firm, who is in custody at Birming- ham on a charge of embezzlement, is stated to have acknow- ledged taking £l,OOO to cover losses sustained in betting. In one evening he lost £l2O. A New York telegram says :—The ship Novara, from London and Newcastle for San Francisco, WaS butriCd ?J. Sea on the 13th ultimo. The captain and first and second officers and 17 men are missing. Mr. Edwin Waugh, the "Lancashire poet," being in ill- health, has been advised to make a lengthened sojourn in the Island of Rum, which lies between Oban and Storloway, and for that purpose he has left home. From an official return just issued,it would appear that the tonnage of British shipping entered and cleared at the ports of the United Kingdom has been steadily increasing of late years. As compared with 1840, it has multiplied nearly seven-fold.

On Wednesday, upon the mate of the tchooner Sophie, lying in the Prince's Dock, Hull, entering the cabin of the vessel, he discovered the master, Neils Rasmussen, upon the floor, he having evidently been dead some time, being quite cold. He was lying at full length, a rifle being upon the top of his body. Stornoway advices state that the cod and ling fishing is a total failure. Many fishermen have not landed a single ling this season, and it is calculated that there has not been a poorer fishing season for the last fifty years. The loss to the fishermen on the islandof Lews alone cannot be set down at less than £20,000. Intelligence was received in Sunderland on Wednesday night of the supposed murder of George Dunn, mate of the barque Squando, of Liverpool, whose body was washed ashore at Guano Islands on the 20th February last. The captain and steward of the vessel have beeh arrested on the coast on suspicion. The Squando sailed from Cardiff for South America nine months ago. Four ladies were nominated for seats at the Barton Regis Board of Guardians, Bristol. The votes were counted on Wednesday, and showed that all four were elected—Miss Clifford, for Wrestb-ary-on-Trym, at the head of the poll by several husdreds; Miss Winkworth and Miss Woollam, for Clifton, both at the head of the poll; and Mrs. Prentice, widow, for St. Philip's. At a meeting of the Nottingham Town Council, on Wed- nesday, a letter was read from the Lord Chancellor, appoint- ing Mr. Goldschmidt,the Mayor,and Messrs.Leavers,Gripper, and Hill, members of the borough bench, and adding that as all those gentlemen were of the same political opinions, he would not be willing to add any more names, unless those of men di' ' fferine• from them in politics. The town clerk was appointed clerk to the magistrates. Much political excitement prevailed at Cheltenham, on Wednesday, consequent upon the election of poor-law guar- dians. Of fifteen guardians on the past board eleven were Conservatives. This year they proposed to yield up one seat. The compromise, however, fell through, and four out of six wards were contested, resulting in the return of fourteen Conservatives. A lady candidate was nominated'by the Liberals but was cicleated. Mr. Gladstone gives a denial to a report current that the Covernment would he vwilling to amend the closure resolu- tion in the direction ,of requiring a two-thirds majority to ,close a debate. It is pointed out that strong safeguards have been attached to the exercise of the closing, power, and under these circumstances Mr. Gladstone regards the fears of the Opposition as akin to those which "they have ex- perienced on the approach of all great and beneficial changes in our laws which have made this country illustrious." The Press Association is informed that the convict Lam- son has written what purports to be a diary of his move- ments just before the date of his visit to Wimbledon, but some of the statements are utterly improbable. Some im- portant evidence has been gathered from four servants the convict kept at Rournemouth, all of whom aver that whilst in his service they believed him to be insane. This evidence will be forwarded in due course to the Home Office.

Sarah Built, a domestic servant, charged at Manchester with maaslathter, lost her situation when she became a mother, was turned out of her lodgings when her money became exhausted, and walked the streets for three days and nights with the child in her arms. The child died from ex- posure the fist night, and the girl carried it about for the remainder of the time. At the inquest the,coroner asked the jury to return a verdict of manslaughter, tut they declined; and the maestrates, taking the same view, discharged the prisoner. AN UNFOGNDED REMOUR.—A report was received in London on Wednesday from Hong ROES,' stating that a rumour was current there to the effect that the Richmond, United States flagship on the China station, had been lost at sea. It was said that the ship was aleoutloo days over- due on the passage from Panama to Yokohama. She had between 500 and 600 men on board. Inquiries at the Ad- miralty, Whitehall, however, showed that from advices just received there from New York the Richmond had arrived at Yokohama, but upon what date is not stated. M. Sert RGEON ON PIGEON Setoomee.—Mr. Spurgeon, in a letter to Z. T. Markley, of Eastbourne, in reference to the latter's steggestions in the public prints in favour of the sub- stitution of artificial for live birds at shooting contests, says: "My judgment is heartily with you as to the brutality of pigeon-shooting matches. I cannot make out how people who are in other matters kind and gentle can frequent these butcheries. lam still very unwell, and hardly like to think of the woes of this creation. I cannot just now do or say anything worth doing or saying, and so I must leave the cause of the dumb in the hands of such good pleaders as yourself." The Governor of the Isle of Man (Sir H. B. Loche) on Wednesday received a number of farewell addresses. In re- plying to one from the Douglas Town Commissioners, he re- ferred to the many marked improvements which had been carried out by the present Board, notably the new street and the Loch. Promenade, and be advised the Board to pro- vide a place where visitors could find shelter on wet days, where they could listen to music and otherwise amuse them- selves. The rant of a place of that kind had, he said, the effect of drivir,g away a great number of people long before they otherwise would go. , A RAILWAY CARRIAGE ON FIRE.—On Tuesday night, as a Great Northern excursion was returning from Skegness to Leeds, the roof .of a first-class compartment was observed by the occupants to be on fire. There was no means of direct communication with the guard or driver, but after a good deal of shouting from the window the driverls atten- tion was obtained, and the train, which had been travelling at the rate of 30 miles an hour, was brought to a stand and the flames extinguLehed by buckets of water. The fire is supposed to have been caused by some waste being dropped on the roof when the lamp was lighted. A hole about a foot in diameter has been burned through. The libel case arising out of the recent election contest in the Carnarvon Borougks was before the local magistrates on Wednesday. Among the witnesses called for the defence was Mr. Justice Watlain Williams, who said that so far as he was aware no promise was made to Mr. Sorton-Parry in 1880 that he would be selected as the Liberal candidate for the boroughs at the next vacancy. It was suggested by the defendant's solicitor that the criminal proceedings had been instituted in order that Mr. Darbishire's mouth mieht be closed pending the election. The bench decided on dismiss- ing the case, leaving Mr. Sorton-Parry to pursue his remedy in the civil courts. Considerable interest has been awakened at Mari-en by the discovery of the elopement of two well-known people. One of them occupied a position in the orchestra at the local theatre, and the other is the wife of a well-known publican. The musician was not 30 years of age, but the partner of his flight was rapidly approaching half a century. Still her charms appear to have been substantial, inasmuch as the husband was in good circumstances, and the woman possessed herself of a decent sum of money before her de- parture. The young man had been lodeing at the public- house, and has used the opportunities thus afforded to him of ingratiating himself into the good graces of his landlady. His success is proved by their flight. Their whereabouts has not yet been discovered, but the husband has invoked the aid of the police to recover his ducats and his wife. The couple had no children. A bill to amend the Irish Land Act was issued on Thurs.- day. It is backed by Messrs. Parnell, M.Carthy, Healy, Sexton, and Redmond, and contains :provisions :for staying proceedings to enforce payment, pending the fixing of fair rent, for enacting that no rent shall be made payable on the tenants' improvements, and fur enabling leaseholding tenants to apply to have fair rent fixed. The principal clauses are those dealing with arrears of rent and purchase of holdings. It is provided that in case of the holdings not exceeding £3O annual value, the tenant is willing to pay the year's rent falling due after August 22nd, 1882, but is unable to pay antecedent arrears, then the Land Commission may make a grant to the landlord not exceeding half such arrears. The Lend Commission may advance the full pur- chase money to tenants desirous of purchasing their hold- ings. The quarterly meeting of the Birmingham trade, wtich rules prices in all the midland and southern districts of England and Wales, was held on Thursday, and was at- tended by producers, merchants, and consumers from Lon- don, Liverpool. and North of England, South Wales, and all the midland districts. A very satisfactory tone prevailed, the market being quieter than at any time during the last twelve months, and prices in nearly all departments as low as the medium of last year. The reductions in the value of copper, tin, and spel ter have completely unsettled business, and anticipating a further decline, buyers refused to give out orders except at prices which consumers as a rule were unable to accept. At a meeting of the plate members repre- senting South Wales and Staffordshire, under the presidency of Mr. J. W. Flower, of Neath, it was unanimously decided to curtail the production of the plates 15 per cent, during the whole of the ensuing year. Tin plates were at least 2s. 6d. a box lower than the maximum of three months ago. Merchant bars were 10s. a ton lower, realizing £7 a ton free on board Liverpool as against £7 10s. earlier in the year. Mart bar firms nominally adhered to last quarter day prices of £7 10s. a ton at works, but sales were not affected except at from ss. to 7s. &I. a ton less. Sheets sold at £7 a ton for singles, being 103. a ton less than three months ago, and in some instances even less, money was accepted. Nail rods were in steady demand, in consequence of the activity in the patent nail trade. German wire rods, free on board Liverpool, only realised £8 a ton, equivalent to £7 55. at Antwerp, these prices being £1 a ton less than in July last. The pig iron standard was unaltered, but common melting iron was sold at 40s. and under.

A serious outbreak of scarlet fever has occurred at Green- field, near Oldham. In one house alone three persons have died, and a number of others have been attacked. The workpeople of the Office of Works and Lord Chamberlain's Department have begun the marriage prepar- ations within St. George's Chapel, Windsor, preparatory to the Marriage of the Duke of Albany. Francis Gore, labourer, was convicted at Aberdeen on Thursday, of culpable homicide in February last, at Law- rence Kirk, when he killed his father by striking him with a spade during a quarrel. The sentence was 14 years' penal servitude,

According to the Tageblatt, the German Emperor, on hear- ing of the appointment of Baron de Giers as Minister for Foreign Affairs in Russia, exclaimed, "Heaven be thanked ! Ina we can again hO,pc that peace will last for a time." Prince Bismarck, it is said, forlYarded a most cordial con- gratulatory telegram to the new Minister. A Conservative gathering has been held at the residence of Mr. tivedale Corbett, near Neston, the object of which was to introduce Captain Cotton, who has been selected as the Conservative candidate for West Cheshire at the next election, in consequence of the retirement of the Hon. W. F. Tollemacle, the senior representative. We learn that since January, 1881, the committee of the Cobden Club have circulated 730,000 publications, chiefly in support of the principles of Free Trade. Since the formation of the club in 1863 it has issued 1,300,000 books, pamphlets, Sze., in furtherance of the economic views of Richard Cobden. From all parts of the world testimonies to the value of these publications have been received. The list of persons detained under the Protection Act, on April Ist, includes 511 prisoners, of whom 2S are reasonably suspected of murder as principals, and seven as accessories; eleven of treasonable practices, 24 of shooting with intent to murder, and others of arson, intimidation, unlawful assembly, 4tc. At the vestry meeting in connection with Peel Church, Little Hulton, the vicar, the Rev. C. F. Roberts, announced that an anonymous donor had generously given him .C 416 7s. Id. with which to extinguish the debt remaining on the church, and which so recently as last Christmas amounted to £1,336. At Middleton, on Thursday, a whole family, named Tay- lor, consisting of father, mother, two sons, and one daughter, were charged with drunken anedisorderly conduct. A con- stable stated that he saw the defendants in Little Park, near to where they reside, creating a great disturbance and rous- ing the whole neighbourhood'. They were all of them very drunk. The whole family was sent to gaol for fourteen days, in default of paying the fines. About eight o'clock on Thursday morning a'young woman apparently about twenty years of age was observed to jump into the reservoir of Messrs. Cross, at Doffcocker, near Bol- ton. Assistance was prtnured, but an hour elapsed before the body was recovered. The name of the deceased is not known, but she appeared from her dress to be an operative. The reservoir is known as "Lover's Lodge," from the num- ber of romantic suicides that have taken plane there.

rOUNDERING OF ANEW YORK STEAMER: 50 LIVES LOST. —lnformation received from Lloyd's states that the new iron steamship America, 2,118 tons register, owned by Messrs. E. Carr and Co, homeward bound from New York, with a valuable cargo of produce, has foundered at sea with all hands. She left Sandy Hook on the 30th January, and was due here about the middle of February last, but since sailing she has not been heard of. The vessel was only built six months ago at a cost of some £35,000. We learn -that the negotiations between the post office authorities and the representatives of the leading railway companies with a view to the establishment of a parcels post are proceeding. There is, it is added, no foundation for the statement published in one of the morning news- papqrs to the effect that the railway companies have prepared a special series of returns as to the parcels traffic for a complete fortnight, by way of furnishing data as to the plantto be provided by the post office authorities in carry- ing cut the parcels scheme. A great meeting was held in Gloucester on Thursday night to protest against the proposed disfranchicement of the borough. The Mayor presided; and the principal speakers were Mr. Price (railway commissioner, and for- merly M.P.), Mr. Monk, lii.P., Sir Michael Hicks-Beach, M.P., Baron de Ferrieres, M.P., &c. A resolution was passed protesting against the Attorney-General's proposal as unduly severe, and that it punished the innocent with the - guilty. Sir Michael Hicks-Beach consented to take charge of a petition praying that the disfranehisement be referred to a Select Committee, and that the memorialists be heard by counsel and witnesses.

A GIGANTIC SWINDLE.—A gigantic swindle, involving a loss of £lOO,OOO is said to have just come to light in New York. A ship named the Richard Robinson lately arrived in that port with 7,500 .bales of silk and hemp, consigned to bankers who had made large advances. It was subsequently discovered that, as a matter of fact, there were only 2,500 `bales of silk on board, the remainder of the cargo consisting Of inferior matting. 'lt is stated, moreover, that this is not the only cargo nponwhich large advances have been obtained under similar false pretences, and the losses consequently sustained in New York will be of a serious character. The goods were shipped at Hong Kong by a firm styled Vogel Bros., professing to be connected with a Henry 'Vogel in New York. Needless to say, when the true state of the case transpired, and instructions were telegraphed for the arrest of Vogel at Hong Kong, it was found that the bird had 1-aown.

div.head: MRS. RIPPON ON THE DRESS OF THE PERIOD.
div.p: MRS. RIPPON ON THE DRESS OF THE PERIOD.

The following is a continuation of the article ou dress, from the pen of Mrs. Rippon, wife of the Rev. Thomas Itippon, Wesleyan Minister, Warrington : There are many who would fain believe that the hips are the proper points to support the skirts upon. The testimony of medical men is clearly and indisputably against this. One says, "No description can give an adequate idea of the evils consequent upon wearing skirts hanging from the hips." Another says, "Women carry their clothing sus- pended mainly from the hips, and as the clothes press by their weight upon the soft fleshy walls, they cause dicplace- ment of the internal organs." The pelvic cavity lying between the waist and the hips is formed by the union of the two bones, commonly called hip-bones, with each other in front, and with the lower part of the spinal column be- hind. In the lower part of this cavity are situated sensitive organs. Above these organs are 23 feet of intes- tines lying loosely in the abdominal cavity, with no great support from above. These lower organs are joined together by the folding over and around of the membrane called peritoneum, so that whatever displaces one will affect the others to a certain extent. There are some ligaments which hold them in position, but they will yield if too great or too long-continued pressure be exerted from above downwar& In this way some of the diseases peculiar to women are brought about. When this weight of clothing is supported only by the hips, it has a tendency to press down the intestines, and their wight must then fall on the organs below. These, in their turn, are forced to yield. One of the rules for treatment of diseases of this nature is "Remove all weight from the hips." Recent experiments by a well- known physician of New York show conclusively that con- tinual pressure brought to bear upon the stomach of animals causes their death more quickly than when applied to any other organ. The Austrian soldiers wore a leathern belt round their waists to suspend their pantaloons. Disease of the kidneys spread so alarmingly among them that atten- tion was drawn to the subject, and it was decided that the closely-buckled strap was the cause of the disease. It was at once decreed that suspenders should be used instead. It is a pity that the investigation did not extend to women's clothes, for undoubtedly the weakness of mothers will trans- mit itself to their offspring. The peasant women of Austria work side by side with the men, lay railroad iron, dig sewers, mount ladders with brick or mortar. Their dress is adapted in length at least for their work, reaching a little below the knees, where it is met by long boots. No corset cramps their waist, and they are free from internal distor- tions caused by boue and steel pressure. A lady M.D., who has evidently carefully studied the matter of compressing and depressing, was present at the post mortem examination of several of these peasant women who had been killed in the falling of several houses where they were employed. She say!. "Now. I thought, I shall once at least have an oppor- tunity of seeing the iaternal organs of women normally adjusted. To my utter astonishment it was quite the reverse."

_ "I acknowledge that these peasant women were over- burdened by hard labour, but many of the abnormal condi- tions I saw were dependent simply upon this fact—that heavily quilted or home-spun skirts had been worn from childhood; and that these had rested upon the hips, with each band drawn about the waist and tied by strings. It has been said that the injury caused by bands about the waist is obviated by wearing corsets beneath them. You need but a moment's reflection to see this cannot be so. The pressure of the bands help i to adjust the steels and bones ' more closely to the yielding portions of the body. As no support is given to the corsets at the shoulders, and the skirts are not attached to them, they can furnish no relief whatever to the weight of garments resting upon the hips, and they add greatly to the unremitting downward pressure upon the lower organs." Instances could be multiplied of the ills caused by wearing heavy skirts resting on the hips, were this a fitting place to give them. lam glad and grate- ful to learn that so many doctors are turning their attention to the subject of women's dress; if they who see so much of its evil effects would enlighten their patients, many now Ignorant would at once see the necessity for a change. Dr. Jackson says, "All modes of dress that injure the human body, or make the wearer uncomfortable, are strictly within the province of the doctor, and he should never lose an Opportunity to benefit his patients by teaching them the evils to be avoided by a sensible reform. The protest of one Physician may do much; but what an incalculable amount of good could be done if the whole profession as with one I voice would unite in decrying all the forms of dress which torture mankind, and bring on the innumerable diseases that shorten life and render it miserable." "If woman is to fulfill the high trusts that shall be given her, she must i emancipate herself from the engrossments of fashion, must be clothed in garments that contribute to her comfort, and I must cast aside those that destroy her health When the leading women of the age, and those blessed with position or influence, come to see that a cultivated mind in a healthy body is more to be desired, and better calculated to lead to honour and esteem, than the most costly or elaborate clothing, women will turn their attention to this higher sub- ject, and nil: then make it easy for others less favoured to follow in the same pathway." To be continued.
White lies roll themselves into cocoons and next year come out fall-fledged whoppers.

div.head: LYMIT
div.p: LYMIT

CHURCH • OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY.—OR Easter Monday a festival was held by the Oughtrington branch of the above Society. About six hundred assembled at Sandy-lane school at twelve o'clock, and walked to Heat- ley station to meet the band. They then returned in pro- cession through Heatley to Sandy-lane school, and marched through the parish. At four o'clock they proceeded to the church, where a short service was held, and an address was delivered by the Rev. J. H. Acheson, M.A., rector of St. Peter's, Chester. Tea was served in the girls' school at half-past five, after which a public meeting was held, and addresses were given by the Rev. J. H. Acheson, Rev. A. F. Johnson, curate of St. Andrew's, Manchester, and others. The proceedings were most enjoyable throughout.

WIGAN. THE PURITY PRINCIPLE.—On Saturday an extraordinary election took place at Wigan to fill the vacancy in the re- presentation of Svvinley Ward in the Town Council, caused by the appointment of Mr. James Smith (C) to be an alder- man, in the place of the late Mr. Alderman Gregson. The candidates were Mr. J. C. Mawson (C) and Mr. M. Benson (L), and the poll was declared as follows :—Mawson 308, Benson 287, majority for the Conservative candidate, 21. The contest was a quiet one, and the poll only small, which may be accounted for from the fact that the election was fought on the purity principle. WIGAN FREE LIBRARY.—The fourth report of the Wigan Free Library has been published, and contains some in- teresting figures. The number of volumes in the Institution is 25,333. The number consulted in the referance depart- ment has been 6,160, whilst 58,746 have been issued from the lending library. The attendance on Sundays both in the newsroom and reference department remains about the same as during last year-9,991 persons have visited the newsroom and 260 the reference department.

div.head: GOLBORNE.
div.p: GOLBORNE.

PRI3IITITE METHODIST CHAPEL.—On Good Friday a public sandwich tea meeting was held in the above place of worship. A goodly Jambes partook of tea, (tc., after which a service of song was given entitled, " Uncle Tom." The chapel was crowded. After tea the choir did _lull justice to the service, the congregation being much pleased at the admirable manner in which the songs were rendered. Mr. Thomas Ball officiated as reader. Mr. R. Yates presided. The meeting was a decided success. INDEPENDENT METHODIST SUNDAY SCHOOL.—On Good Friday a tea meeting was held in the school in connection with the Independent Methodist Chapel. A fair number sat down. After tea speeches were delivered by several of the members, and anthems were sung by the choir. The meeting was a most enjoyable one. The proceeds will be devoted to the defraying of the expenses incurred in re- furnishing the vestry of the chapel. SUNDAY SCHOOL SERMONS.—On Sunday last two ser- mons were preached in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Lowton-road, Golborne, afternoon and evening, to crowded congregations. -An address was also given in the morning to teachers, scholars, and friends by Mr. S. Heyes, of Lowton. The sermons were preached by Mr. T. Rawlinson, of Widnes. All the services were much appreciated. Mr. .1. Taylor presided at the harmonium, and Mr. William Entwistle officiated as leader of the choir. The singing and playing was excellent, and altogether the Lowton-road folks had a very good day. Collections during the day amounted to upwards of £9.

div.head: FRODSITAM.
div.p: FRODSITAM.

Urrrox Cauracn, SUTTON WEATER.—The anniversary services at this place of worship were held on Sunday last, when the sermons were preached by the Rev. John Yonge, of Warrington. PRIMITITE METHODIST CHAPEL, FRODSHAI& BRIDGE.— A public meeting was held in the above chapel on Good Friday, when addresses and recitations were given, the speakers being Mr. J. Darlington (chairman), Mr. James Beard, Mr. Henry Limbert, Nr. William Booth, and the Rev. D. Schofield. A collection was made at the close in all of the trust fund. EASTER HOLIDAYS.—That Frodsham has lost none of its popularity was evidenced by the large number of pleasure seekers who visited the town on Good Friday and bank holiday. The weather was everything that could be de- sired and the country, which is just budding into foliage, was a refreshing sight, particularly to those who do not live in the midst of rural scenery. Extensive preparations had been made by the Veal caterers for the entertainment of the visitors, but the road to the hills was inconveniently crowded with standings and doubtful attraction for enticing the coppers from the speculative juveniles. We were glad, however, to see that the order to "move on "was promptly given, as it would be a sad mistake to allow the country lanes to be used for a fair gathering with all its noisy accompaniments, and particularly on such a solemn commemoration day as Good Friday. In previous years there has been some rough play practiced, but on Friday there was an absence of the usual brawls, and although there were certainly a few who were inebriated with some- thing stronger than their own verbosity, they had the good sense to keep quiet.

WIN SFORD. CONCAMT AT WINSFORD. - A concert was given in the Winsford Town Hall, on Monday evening, in aid of the rifle volunteers of the town. The chairman was Dr. Okell, the corps surgeon, and the accompanist Mr. E. Singleton. The vocalists were chiefly Misses Dodd and Hickson; Messrs. Pennington, G. Hamlet, J. Hamlet, T. Hamlet, and Mr. Timperley. The band did good service under Mr. Hulse.

Good Friday and Easter generally as far as Winsford is concerned has passed off with lig usual interest. The Fry!, Methodists had their usual entertainment, for the Sunda'' scholars and their parents and friends, in the shape of reci- tations and music. The manner in which the pieces were said mostly did credit to their trainers, while the music passed off in capital style. Miss Buckley presided at the organ. Then there was the concert on Monday, of which we have spoken; while the Salvation Army have had what is mostly as rich an enjoyment night by night to them.

WINSFORD LOCAL BOARD. The electbin of four mem- bers of this board took place last week end, when there were 11 candidates for the honour. Only in one ward, that of Wharton, was there no contest, no more fitting person than Mr. S. W. Cross being found, and he was also the retiring member. In the Gravel Ward there were three—Mr. Hoyle, the retiring member, who polled 213 votes; Mr. Dierden, 170; and Mr. Mess,l9 ; so the old member took his seat. On the opposite side of the Weaver' in the Swanlow Ward, four put up, viz. :—Mr. J. Hulse, the retiring member, who polled 270, Mr. E. Pickstock 206, Mr. BrereCon 112, and Mr. Smallwood 45; so Mr. J. Hulse sits once more. In the Vale Royal Ward Mr. Hewit, the retiring member, got 81 votes, Mr. C. Daggatt 136, and Mr. J. Dean 76; so Mr. C. Daggatt takes the place of Mr. Hewit, and constitutes the only change for Winsford this year. Out of 1,706 voters about 340 filled papers wrongly. SALT TRADE.—A strong association of the trade on a self- regulating and most durable basis was unanimously formed during March, and Tuesday week the annexed prices were established :—Common salt, us; butter salt, 12s 61 ; Cal- cutta salt, is 21, and Is 21 including mats, 13s; chute stoved, 14s; handed squares, 17s; best fishery, 14s; second fishery, 13a; factory tilled, including sacks, 26s 6d ; best Prussian rock, 6s; picked lumprock, 98 6d. Ground rock for agricultural and chemical purposes: First quality fine, Sc; rough do., 7s; rough riddlings for ship salting; 6s 6d; soiled agricultural, 7s. The probable future will be easily inferred from the following facts :—(1) A large spring de- mand is upon us. (2) A very large increase of consumption in India has already ensued on the excellent reduction of the salt duty by 30 per cent. effected in Calcutta on March 11. Supply will be wholly restricted during April. (3) As the salt canal (the Weaver) is to be closed for repairs from April Bth to May Ist, and a considerable stoppage of works will be permanently effected by the scheme cf the association. In fine, the manufacturers are resolved on recouping themselves for the serious losses incurred at the late low prices. The prospect is both brilliant and solid, and the next month's notice will probably show a large addition to the prices above. Some particulars of the exports may be gathered from these figures:—To the United States was sent 27,325, as against 33,777 in March, 1881, but though less than last year it is still much beyond any previous March; to British America 7,506 has not been surpassed since 1878, nor ever before ; West Indies and South America, 1,630 is likewiSe in advance if we except last year, which reached 2,415; Africa has taken less 2,712 this year (in March) than in 1881 and 1878, when it rose to 3,03 and 2,774 respectively; Calcutta has largely risen, 27,383—1a5t year it was only 16,769. (4) Australia has done less, only 775, against 1,795 last year; Prussia, 8,209, while last year 1,795; Russia, 1,078, against 871; Baltic ports, 4,330, against 2,073; France and Mediter- ranean, 283, vice 76; coastwise in our British Isles, 1,300, against 1,575; for Newcastle, 120, vice 575; for rest of Eng- land, 2,392, against 860; Scotland and Ireland, 139, as against 112; while Holland has taken 2,741, against 2,375; and Belgium 5,120, against 3,756; which summed up makes a grand total from the Mersey during March of 109,296 tons, against 92,142 in March of 1881,

• NEWTON AND •EARLESTOWN. Rumour here is busy in speculating upon the great event of next week, when the High Sheriff is going to give the Volunteers and his workmen a grand dinner in the Town Hall on Wednesday evening, r..nd a breakfast to some hundreds of friends and acquaintances on the Thursday, before he goes to Wigan with the Town Council. THE EASTER HOLIDAYS.—At the printing works on Friday and Saturday at ths Viaduct works extended from Thursday night till Monday night, and at the Vulcan foundry till Tuesday night, during which time the lake was a centre of attraction to thousands of visitors from far and near, and the inevitable rounds or rings were a noticeable feature at the base of Castle-hill, where dancing was kept up with spirit to the strains of a concertina, and the jolly old waterinan bad a fair share of their patronage. It is highly to the credit of the chemists in Earlestown that they have given notice to the public that their pieces of business will, after the 1.6. h instant, be closed on Sundays —except on emergency—when medicines will be dispensed at their private residences, as is the custom of all the m. li- cal practitioners in :Newton and Earlestown. This con se, we may hope, will be followed now by the quasi toffy sh.s, where growing youths may also buy cigars which they are in the habit of lighting at the docr of the Sunday schools in defiance of all seemliness and moral restraint. THE VESTRY MEETING.—OR Tuesday evening in the Town Hall was but thinly attended. The church accounts iv,re audited and passed. Some difficulty seemed to be expEri-

•- alp enced in obtaining the requisite amount of money to meet the expense of repairing St. Peter's Church, the belfry bein in a dangerous condition. 060 is promised and partly coieg lected, but the estimated cost will be £esoo, including architect's fees, and it was thought undesirable to begin operations until the full amount had been subscribed. At the close of the meeting a statement of accounts was read by Dr. Watkins, who is secretary to the Dean School Charity Trust, and who had been advised that this was a technical proceeding needed to give them validity. We understand that at least two scholarships will be competed for in June or July next by the boys in Newton and Earlestown. I.O.G.T.—HorE or EADLESTOWN Looos.—The weekly session of the above lodge was held on Monday evening last in the lodge room, Bridge-street. There was a good attend- ance of members, considering the holidays. After the open- ing ceremonies the report of the Lodge Committee waS received, when it was unanimously resolved that the next session be held in the Wesleyan Schoolroom on Saturday, May 20th, the rooms having been arranged for. It was also resolved to invite the co-operation of the various temperance societies in Earlestown, in arranging for a general can vasS for signatures to a petition in faveur of the Sunday closing of public-houses In England. The lodge closed at 8-45 to enable the members to partake of a coffee supper, as per pro- gramme. About 40 members were present. A very enjoy. able evening was spent. THE EASLESTOWN WESLEYAN BAND OF HOPE.—The first annual festival of the Earlestown Wesleyan Band of Hope was held on Good Friday in the Wesleyan schoolroom; and it is satisfactory to know that the proceeds met the expenses incurred. Mr. P. M. Campbell took the chair at the after meeting, and a programme of music and recitations was interspersed with addresses by the chairman and Mr. E. D. King, secretary for the Chester Union of Bands of Hope. The opening hymn "Sound the battle cry," led by mernbert of the choir, and chorus was followed by a prayer by Mr. Newman, when Mr. Graham read a letter from Mr. Simpson, of Liverpool (lately candidate for Parliamentary honours in Preston), explaining his inability to be present, as announced, atid as he fully intended to be but for an untoward accident and a long standing engagement to lay a foundation stone itr Preston; and, further, that the gentleman whom he had bespoke as a substitute for him had unexpectedly died. But Mr. Simpson very kindly promised to give the committee a lecture in aid of the Band of Hope to make up for any shortcoming of his. Thus thrown on their own resources, and the Secretary and many other friends being unavoidably absent, Mr. Gilmour read the secretary's report which showed that they were making steady headway and had a sovereign in hand, the nucleus of many more let us hope. Miss Stanfield, Miss M. Walton, Mr. T. J. Gilmour, and Mr. Haynes sang the quartet," Drive from us the mortal foe," when the Chairman delivered his address, in which he said that less wine and spirits are consumed by the work- ing classes now than were imbibed ten years ago; and that habits of temperance have been of late years gradually gain- ing ground among us. There was an improvement in pub lic opinion on the subject, but the opinion of society was always against it, for drinking was a vicious habit of long growth, and wherever public-houses multiply their evil effects were proportionately increased. It was no slight matter to allow the centres of this sort of influence to be multiplied without restraint. The great hope of diminishing drunkenness must, he said, be by education, and that not merely the education of schools but of a public opinion developing from year to year, so that intemperance might become as rare among the poor as it had become among the rich. The chairman then proceeded to speak of Sunday closing in general and par- ticularly in Scotland, Ireland, and Wales, and throughout England no hoped before long, for public opinion was setting in that direction strongly. The chairman next dealt with local option, the bill prohibiting payment of wages in public-houses, and the habitual drunkard. A recitation by John Pickett, "Drunk again," followed; and Mr. Porter sang "Be thou faithful unto death," which was encored. Mr. Stansfield's violin solo was also encored. Misses Parr and Jones sang " The convent bells ;" and then Mr. King delivered a most interesting address on total abstinence. A dialogue on the virtues of water, by Miss A. M. Clare, T. Robinson, and T. Clare, was followed by a pianoforte solo by Miss Greenall, who accompanied, and was enthusiastically encored. Miss Sides sang "Far away," and Mr. John Parr gave a recitation, "The bellman," in emulation of "Pop Joe ;" and, in reply to a hearty encore, "A sister's last words," a real feat of memory, and very well delivered. Mr. Haynes sang "Arm, arm, ye brave," and. "Rocked in the cradle of the deep ;" and T. Robinson a. recitation, "The drink demon dethroned." Mr. Ne wine n proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. King, and the singers and reeiters, which Was eteanded by Mr. Porter, and acknowe 'edged by Air. King. Mr. Walker proposed, in a few words, a vote of thanks to the chairman, which Mr. King seconded, and the meeting of soma 203 concluded with some notidca- tioh by Mr. Graham. .

SALE OF WORK AT EIRLESTOWS.—A sale of work was held in the Congreg ttional School on Thursday afternoon, to assist in paying off the debt of 1,00), which remains on the new church building. The Rev. J. Allatt, in opening, said there seemed to be more room than company,- but those present would understand that this was an effort to wipe off some of the liabilities, and that whatever they looked upon, whether water-colour drawings, wax-work, or painted screens, was the work of friends, to whom they were greatly indebted ; whilst all the things were marked at reasonable figures, and they might be sure of getting theirlmoney's worth. He then declared the sale open, and hoped it would meet with the success which it deserved. Among those present were Mrs. Josiah Evans and neice, Mrs. Allatt and the Misses Allatt, Mr. and Mts. John and Misses Evans. Mr. and Mrs. Glover and the Mimes Glover,Mr. and Mrs. Camp- bell, Rev. J. Peake, Miss Peake' Mrs. Dobson, Mrs. and Miss Tait, Miss Lilly Holmes, Mrs. Pritchard, Mrs. Lomas, Mr. , John Owen, ic., etc. The room was tastefully laid out, and Mr. and Mrs. Allatt must have bestowed a great deal of time and attention in making everything look so very nice. The first stall on entering contained some bead work, brackets, vases, and a charming basket-of wax flowers, the work of Miss Minnie Tait, which was very much admired, and we hope brought a good price. Also four hand-painted screens by Miss Lilly Holmes, very beautiful work, and well worthy of a pupil of tha Warrington School of Art as she is. At the same stall was a view of Glen Helen (Isle of Man), a sketch from nature, by Carl Henry Bod- , mer, formerly of the Polytechnic, in Zurich, now principal draughtsman at the Vulcan Foundry, and drew general at- tention and admiration. There were also other views, look- ing glasses, brass salvers, dx., brushes books, cushions, , cosies, gold and silver studs, bead pin cushions, opera hoods (Pyrenees wool), anti-macassars, Chinese and Japanese wares, mats and baskets; and at a stall on the right were hats (straw), caps, shoes (cloth), petticoats, embroidery, and babies' dresses innumerable, table and other linen. At a table to the left was a crewel work corner shelf, the work of Mrs. Allates sister Ellen, a real work of art ; card trays, tea trays, satchels, ebony and rosewood walking sticks from Madagascar (the gift of Rev. G-' eo. Peake), carved paper knives. But in the left-hand corner was a stall, around which the greatest interest centred, and where the greatest variety of ladies and babies' clothes and under clothes were to be seal, the result of untold toil and labour of the ladies of the congrega- tion and their sewing classes. The dust covers and cover- lets (patchwork) hung like trophies at the end of the room, and represented an infinite lot of stitching and cross stitch- ing which might have exhausted "a mile" of Mr. John Evans' sewing thread, and which were bought as curiosities and to astonish country friends. Just below and in the centre was the refreshment stall, a flier was well patroaised about tea time; and Mr. George Unsworth had sent a huge loaf of " real jannock," like an immense shield, which might be had for 9d. a quarter, enough to stay the aomach of an alligator, one of which, brought from Madagazcar, was grinning a welcome to the curious in another corner, be- side a heterogeneous collection of warlike and domestic im. plements, 'displayed by Rev. Geo. Peake, who had also another stall on the opposite side of the room filled with rare and curious objects from Madagascar (where he must soon return). Among these was a cemnlete lady's outfit of silver ornaments, and needlework that altoeether puts our finest work of that kind to the blush. Silk, and silk and cotton lambas or shawls (the only garment the natives wear), except manacles, (for domestic slavery is still existent as it was in patriarchal times, but happily British influence prevents their export), divining horns, tobacco pouches (of Gourds) for the tobacco is fine, and is neither smoked nor snuffed, but "stuffed into the mouth." as monkeys do. We must not omit to mention that the refreshment stall was very tastefully decorated with some very tine cinerarias, spireea japonica, and dentzia gracilis, which were also on sale, with primroses, wallflowers and other spring flowere, and that there was a piano to drecourse sweet music during the after- noon.

CONFERENCE OF ELEMENTARY TEACIIERS. • The annual conference of the National Union of Ele men - tary Teachers commenced at Sheffield on Monday. Mr. R. Sykes, of London, the new president, in his opening address, stated that there was an increase of 1,200 members during the past year, and there were now 320 associations with more than 13,000 teachers affiliated to the union. The president deprecated the system of piyment by results and compe- Wive exatninitions introduced by Mr. Lore, and regretted that Mr. Mundella laad adhered to that principle.—The conference was resumed on Tuesday. On the motion of Mr. Scotson (Manchester), a resolution was passed affirming the desirableness of steps being taken to secure the direct re- presentation of teachers in Parliament. In the afternoon is bazaar and art exhibition in aid of the Teachers' Benevolent Fund was opened by Miss Mundella. Mr. Mundella, m.r., was present and delivered a brief speech.—The Union met again on Wedneqlay. The annual meeting of the Teachers' Provident Society was held ; Mr. W. T. Pink presiding. The income was £BOO, and the balance more than £3OO after the payment of expenses. During the year twenty-seven meal-, hers had been admitted. The report, which stated that there was a desire on the part of higher and middle class s2lool teachers to form a similar society, was adopted. The con- tributors to the Teachers' Orphanage and Orphan Fund also met on Wednesday, and the annual report showed that there was a satisfactory increase in the permanent sources of in- come. Tire president said it was important thit the council should proceed with the erection of the Orphanage, and it was said they would do so as soon as £3,000 had been r —The concluding sitting of the coinference was held on Thursday, when Miss Muller's paper on " 0 ver-pi essure was read. It suggested that delicate chil,c.alrenpasshsoeualdthaaltte%d school as half-timers. A resolution ws mixed, girls', and infant schools great injury had been in- dicted by over-pressure, and that little relief was afforded under the new code. The president said the impression he pot from a recent. conversation with Mr. Munde la, was that that right hon. gentleman felt his reputation depended ex the way he set the inspectors to work out the new code.

BOTELER GRAMMAR SCHOOL WARRINGTON. FOUNDED A.D. 1526. Head Master: • The Rev. E. J. WILLOOORS, Late Scholar of St. Catharine's College, Cambridge. Second Master: The Rev. H. G. SMITH, M.A., . Scholar of St. John's College, Cambridge; And five Assistant Masters. The School contains two divisions. The work of the Lower Division comprises a regular course of instruction in English, French, the rudiments of Latin, elementary Mathematics and Science, with Reading, Writing, Arithmetic, Drawing, Drill, and Vocal Music, and all other elements of a sound modern educatim. In the Upper bivision, the choice is offered of a thorough mercantile or high classical course; German and Greek being optional subjects. Eight Free Scholarships. Two Exhibitions to Oxford and Cambridge. The year is divided into three Terms. Capitation fees. everything included, and £3 per term in the Upper and Lower Divisions :espectively. Entrance Fee, £l, next term commences Thurday, April 27th. For further particulars apply to the Head Masten*.

The Land Act has done much to mitigate Of the grievances under which the tenant farmers aka er, and as it extends its operations it will do more aor these who avail themselves of its benefits, still, the country ie in t as teach unsettled as ever.
