different state of affairs, but it appears to be wholly incompatible with the requirenients of the present day. This fact the hon. and learned member for Dundalk, Mr. C. Russell, Q.C., has not been slow to recognise, and in a powerful letter which he has ad- dressed to his constituents he dwells upon the neces- sity of a reform being speedily effected in this direction. His letter has been well timed, and com- ing from one of the most dispassionate, argumenta- tive, and at the same time the most intelligent and learned members which Ireland possesses, is deserving of careful study. Mr. Russell deprecates as strongly as any one can do outrages, and warns his countrymen not to demoralise themselves by resorting to crime; but his greatest hope for the future of the country he points out as lying in the extension of the purchase clauses of the Land Act, and further amendment of the Act so as to deal with the arrears of rent. Mr. Russell's suggestions are well worthy of consideration at the hands of the Government, whose attention they are not likely to escape. Strange to say, at the very moment when the Cabinet are contemplating a change in. their Irish policy, the chiefs of the Conser- vative party are beginning to discover that it is neces- sary for them to change their policy also, and accord- ingly we find a notice given by Mr. W. H. Smith of his intention to move a resolution having for its object the establishment of a system of peasant pro- prietory in Ireland. This move received the counte- nance of Lord Salisbury at Liverpool, on Wednesday, and it seems very much like an attempt to make a bid for the permanent alliance of the Irish members with which the Conservative party have so long been in aollisuon. It would be idle to speculate on the details of such a scheme which requires explaining; but it Imay be permitted to us to say that it is not likely to meet with very general favour coming from such a quarter. The Conservative party is composed mainly ef landlords, many of whom own extensive estates in Ir,land, and a proposal of this nature from that party is at once open to the suspicion that it is put forward with the view of obtaining for the landlords some- thing substantial from the public purse. It may be there is no desire to take an undue advantage, but it is certain that any such scheme matured by the Tory party would not tell favourably in the interests of the tenant. On this point we commend the very perti- nent remarks of Mr. Russell in the letter to which we have referred. In it he shows that Irishmen have nothing whatever to hope for from the Conservative party, and further that a change of Government at the present time—for which the Irish members seem ,to long—would be a national calamity. As we have said the present is the time when all parties should I unite with the Government in their difficulties ; the Conservative party profess to be anxious to do that, but their public utterances do not give us much ground for believing in their sincerity. Rather do they seem to make capital out of Ireland's troubles, troubles, too, which they have been mainly instru- mental in creating and perpetuating.

div.head: LOCAL NOTES.
div.p: LOCAL NOTES.
I understand that within the last few days the agreement for the establishment of a copper works at Widnes has been signed. The necessary land has been taken at Ditton, the
negotiations in regard to the Mill Brow site having fallen through.

At the last meeting of the Runcorn Board of Commis- sioners, a violent attack was made upon Dr. McDougall, who was unable to be present owing to having to attend an in- quest in a case where he had made a post-mortem examina- tion of the deceased. I think most of your readers will be inclined to question thedelicacy of attacking a gentleman in such a fierce style during his absence. Notwithstanding all the speeches which have been made by those members of the Board who were at first, certainly inclined to throw cold water upon the very sensible proposal that Runcorn should have a Free Library, it is quite clear to anyone read- ing between the lines, that several of the Commissioners are exceedingly annoyed that they were not successful in ex- tinguishing those who were on the side of "sweetness and light" in regard to this most important question. Those who spoke so warmly at the last Commissioners' meeting would have immediately seen that it would have been fairer and more courteous to reserve their sarcasms and innuendoes for an occasion when the object of them was present, if it had not been that their usually good judgment was blinded, apparently, by the vexation they were suffering at the re- sult of the public meeting of ratepayers at which they were requested to allow the premises at present occupied for the town's business, to be devoted to the purposes of the library. The first business of importance at the Commissioners' meet- ing was the reading of the minutes of the Public Library Committee' which contained the announcement that Dr. McDougall had been appointed vice-chairman. I was amused and astonished, to read that Dr. Steele, the chairman of the Board, expressed his surprise at the fact that a gentle- who has certainly put himself to an immense amount of trouble with the object of securing to the town the boon of a public free library, had been chosen for such a post of honour. One who had not any personal bias against Dr. McDougall would have been led to think that the appointment was a very natural one; and it outrages one's sense of the fitness of things to read of the chairman solemnly stating tbat he onght to have had the appointment himself! This out Herod's Herod; —it is piling Pelion upon Ossa for Dr. Steele to coolly ignore all the claims of the doctor, and to manifest no more personal diffidence than to say "I ought to have been ap- pointed to that position," in spite of the decision of the entire Library Committee. Would it not have been more discreet of Dr. Steele to have let some other gentleman dwell upon his merits rather than to have indulged in an observa- tion which is open to criticism that self-praise is no recom- mendation? Then Mr. Robert Shaw, who now-a-days acts as a kind of father to many of the older members, though his own connection with the Board does not extend over many years, offered what can scarce!y be described as other than a personal insult to the elected vice-chairman of the committee, by actually proposing that the resolution on the subject should be rescinded, and the Rev. Canon Barclay appointed in that gentleman's place! I wonder what Mr. Robert Shaw would have said if some " friend " of his had served him a similar trick; and I also am led to indulge in a little imagination as to what would have happened if Dr. McDougall had been within hearing of Mr. Shaw's voice. It is really laughable to read that after the opponents of the vice-chairman of the Library Committee had so exposed their "hands," they were quietly informed by Mr. W. H. Linaker, the law clerk to the Board, that the Commissioners, having delegated their powers to the committtee, had no authority to criticise or reverse their proceedings, except so far as related purely to financial matters! The collapse of the speakers who had apparently intended to reverse every decision arrived at by the committee, was complete, according to your report, and- I sympathire with them as to what they must have felt on finding themselves in such a quandary. Mr. Shaw, still in a patronising vein, said that the minutes of the committee were not intelligible, and the Board had a right expect that they should have clear records plhced before them. I believe the Rev. Canon Barclay presided over the meeting of the Library Committee, and matters have arrived at a pretty pitch if Mr. Robert Shaw has to put a scholar like the vicar of the parish right as to drawing up a minute! But the wise man saith that he who is hasty of spirit exalteth folly; and a little more coolness would have prevented Mr. Shaw making such a statement, which I feel sure he will have .cause to regret. So the minutes had to be left as they were; but the warm language did not then cease. Mr. Shaw proceeded to arraign Dr. Mc Dougall for his statements at the ratepayers' meeting, and said that one of these was such as to be "a crime unpar- donable "in his eyes. How the Doctor and Mr. Shaw are to be brought to fall upon one another's necks and give the kiss of peace after this is one of those mysteries which are too deep for my feeble intellect. Mr. Shaw poses as one who refuses to pardon forgetting how much he has himself to be forgiven ! Well, the Doctor must bear up as well as possible under these trying circumstances. Life is full of trials for all. A certain great poet tells of those who had been friends in earlier days yet a little thing parted them, "in a sunny hour" they " fell.off " "Like ships that have gone down at sea, When heaven was all tranqui:ity." Dr. Steele also spoke in bitterness of the majority who were present at the ratepayers meeting and said be understood that they did not vote because they did not really under- stand what was meant by an amendment! This is a cool description of voters, some ot whom, no doubt, helped to place the chairman on the Board. If it be true, your readers will, I am confident, agree with me that the sooner a Free Library is started the better, for these poor benighted rate- payers, to wbotn knowledge has never unfolded her amp le page, " Rich with the spoils of time." Or could this ob- fuscation on the partiof the ratepayers be due to the unintel- ligible character of the amendmeht ? Perhaps Dr. Steele has forgotten that the gentleman who proposed he should be chairman of the Board, was Dr. McDougall! The case of Beasley v. the Runcorn Board of Commis. sioners continues to excite much public interest. Judging from a remark which lately fell from Dr. Steel, the chair- man of that body, he appears to have for some time had an idea that the conduct of Mr Beasley did not really mean any thing in reality, and that he would ultimately withdraw from the legal proceedings he had taken. I regret that I cannot compliment Dr. Steel on his ability to forecast what will happen in the future. It is, quite clear that he is no

div.head: , THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRII
div.p: , THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRII

Achitophel—of whom it was said "his counsel was as if one had enquired of the oracle of God ;"—for it turns out that Mr. Charles Russell, Q.C., the noted leader of the northern bar, has been retained by the plaintiff. I also understand that another famous M.P.has also been secured as "a second string." The case will be heard at Manchester. FLICCUS.

RUNCORN CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH SUNDAY SCHOOLS. —The anniversary sermons of these schools were preached on Sunday, by the Rev. James McDougall, of Manchester; and in the afternoon a service of song was given entitled "St. John the Baptist," by the children and choir. Mr. Wm. Handley acted as conductor. The total collections amounted to

Runom; GOOD TEMPLARISM.—The Good Templar movement in Runcorn has for some years not been in a prosperous condition; and we hear that the Hope of Run- corn Lodge, which was the last association of the kind to survive, has been wound up. EASTER AT WIDNES. —The weather in 'Widnes on Monday and Tuesday, was of a charming description. The sun shone brilliantly, and still the heat was not so oppressive as to render pedestrianism a burden. Thousands left the town by rail and road, and during the afternoon the streets were almost deserted, the long chimneys were almost smoke- less, and the roaring forges were still. The two railway stations presented a busy scene of activity, and the passengers were so numerous that many of the trains were considerably delayed. Large numbers crossed the railway footbridge for Runcorn, Frodsham, Overton, and Helsby.

RUNCORN AND EASTERTIDE. The Easter holidays have been thoroughly enjoyed by the inhabitants of Run- corn. Owing to the advanced season, which is manifested by the rich blossom which clothes so many trees in the sur- rounding neighbourhood, excursions in the country were the order of the day in the casa of many families. Some idea of the railway traffic from Runcorn to Frodsham, Overton, and Helsby, may be gained from the fact that on Monday upwards of 1,000 pazsengers were booked to those places. Runcorn itself wore a very peaceful aspect, though a fair number of visitors came over from Widnes, and the river Mersey was alive with pleasure boats. VESTRY MEETING AT PRESCOT. The annual vestry meeting was held on Tuesday, the Rev. L. W. Sampson (vicar), presiding. There was a good attendance. The wardens accounts showed that the income had beeu .E 258 19s. 7d., and the expenditure £289 17s 3d., leaving a balance due to churchwardens of £3O 17s. Bd. The old wardens, Messrs. W. L. Evans, Henry Cross, A. F. Evans, and J. K. Slack were re-elected. Mr. Henry Cross and Mr. A. Galloway were appointed representatives to attend the Ruridecanal conference. Votes of thanks were passed to the choir for their services during the year, and to the chair- man for his conduct in the chair. RUNCORN IMPROVEMENT COMNISSIONERS. AD• dOURNED MEETING.—On Thursday morning, an adjourned meeting of the Runcorn Board of Commissioners was held at the Town Hall. Dr. Steele presided, and there were also present, Messrs. Norman, Williams, McDougall, Fisher, Handley, Shaw, Briscoe, Haelehurst, Rhodes, Linaker (law clerk), Brookes (secretary), and Barker (surveyor). The meeting was held "for the purpose of considering a request from the Library Committee for the use of the Board-room for the purposes of the Library, for two nights a week, from seven to ten o'clock; and that the Board place the necessary shelves upon the walls."—The Chairman said the matter was one which he thought did not call for much discussion. —Dr. McDougall moved, and Mr. Norman seconded, a pro- position in favour of the requests of the Library Committee being complied with, which was unanimously agreed to.—A brief conversation of no public interest followed as to whether some shelves in the possession of the Commissioners could be utilised.—Dr. McDougall said the shelves had been so frequently used that they were of no value.—Mr. Handley explained that the expense of putting up the shelves would come out of the penny rate.—Mr. Norman moved that Mr. Barker, the surveyor, be instructed to carry out the work required to be done by the committee, in the best manner which suggested itself to his judgment.—M r. Handley seconded the motion, which was passed without dissent, and the proceedings terminated. RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.—The monthly meeting of this Board was held on Wednesday afternoon. Mr. H. Cole- burn presided, and there were also present :—Messrs. T. Norman, Wm. Whittaker, Wm. Littler, James Handley, G. Moss, Peter Briscoe, and Salkeld (secretary).—Mr. Salkeld reported that, in accordance with the order of the Burial Board, he had sent to the Rev. Canon Barclay the copy of the minutes of the Finance Committee, as to the burial of paupers, and had received a reply, which he now read, for- warding the best thanks of the Vicar to the committee for the trouble they had taken in considering the matter, and the courtesy shown him.—The auditors presented their cer- tificates as to the correctness of the accounts and balance sheet, which were ordered to be published in the Examiner. —Mr. Littler brought under the notice of the Board a case of the interment of a fireman. He stated that the body was taken to the cemetery gates on the engine of the brigade, but on arrival there, the mourners were told by Mr. Ford that as he had no instructions about admitting the eagine, it had better wait at the gates. This course was accordingly adopted; and Superintendent Wright, the head of the brigade, had thought it necessary to appeal to him (Mr. Littler), requesting him to bring the facts under the notice of the members, as he considered it only fair the engine should be admitted to the cemetery when it bore the body of a deceased fireman. He had suggested to Mr. Wright that he ihould write to Liverpool and Manchester, and he had done so, and received a reply from the superintendents of brigades in those cities that they had never known any cases •where fire engines had been refused admittance to burial grounds, under such circumstances. The Board were unani- mously of opinion that Mr. Ford had pursued a proper course, but they decided that in the case of any similar funeral in the future the fire engine should be admitted.— This terminated the proceedings.

INDEPENDENT ORDER OF RECRABITES.—MEETING AT RIINCOAN.—On Tuesday evening a public meeting in con- nection with the Independent Order of Rechabites was held in the Bethesda Congregational school-room, Runcorn. There were only about 40 people present, which may, possibly, be accounted for by the fact that the gathering had been very indifferently advertised. The Rev. George Hack (Wesleyan Methodist) presided, and said that though not a Rechabite himself, he thoroughly sympathised with their chief object, viz., attempting to rescue those who were perishing from the traffic in strong drink. He considered that when presiding over a meeting of that character he was just as much doing his Master's service as when he was standing in the pulpit, preaching what was sometimes called "the pure gospel." Teetotalism was, after all, a constituent part of Christianity, inasmuch as it aimed at saving the unsaved. When they looked at the work which the drinking custom was doing, sometimes they were inclined to feel they were en the losing side, but they need only, for one moment, think of what would have become of this country if the total abstinence movement had not been commenced, to see what a great work it had accomplished. That movement had proved a marvellous power for good, and prevented the utter misery and ruin of hundreds of thousands—nay, of millions. The country was fast coming round to the conviction that some- thing must be done with the object of dealing with the liquor traffic, and the churches were all taking this matter up. The Blue Ribbon Army successes were also very cheer- ing, and at the same time astonishing. Parliament was also taking a broader view of this question, and might ultimately be brought to bring it within the scope of practical legisla- tion. God speed the day !—Brother Councillor Hy. Roper (High Deputy Ruler of the Order), who was received with cheers, delivered an interesting speech. He, first of all, compared the results which had been obtained by the work- ing of lodges which did not adopt the teetotal platform, as compared with those achieved by the Order of Recha bites. The Rev. Stenton Eardly, 8.A., vicar of Streatham, made the following statement: —" In 1869 Streatham Foresters' Lodge had 120 members, of whom 22 were abstainers. The amount paid to the sick was £97. Of this the share of the 22 abstainers, supposing an equality of health in both classes, would have been £l7 ss. Bd. The sum received by the abstainers was £2 55." He summed up the result of a seven years' balancing of the Foresters'. Lodge of Streat- ham, thus :—" In seven years the abstaining members of the Lodge, supposing them to have no better health than their non-abstaining brothers, would have received £lBO us. as sick pay. What they did receive as sick money was £56 us., so saving the funds to the amount pf £124." The speaker proceeded to say that now one-eighth of the popula- tion of the United Kingdom were abstainers, and this fact showed that they were making progress. The initiation service of the Juvenile Tent of Rechabites was next con- ducted in public, and appeared to excite much interest.— Bro. J. Dimond (High Chief Ruler of the Order) referred to the admirable work which was being carried out by the juvenile tents. Indeed this was one of the most favourable signs of the temperance movement, as it gave them reason to believe that the future generations of Englishmen would be a far more sober one than the present. The Rechabite Order comprised 40,000 working Tien, and it had a subscribed capital of £280,000, giving a monetary value of .£7 to every member. (Applause.) He was constantly travelling up and down the couritry on the business of the order, and wherever he went he was greatly cheered by the progress it was making. The speaker then drew a humourous picture of the improvement which would be manifest in the state of the country if the vast sum of money now expended in drink were put into trading channels. The progress made in the temperance reforma- tien in Bristol of late had been something astonishing, and there were 80 publichouses to let in that city to-day. (Loud applause.) Let them carry on the glorious work. He ridi- culed the idea of giving any compensation to the publicans for the extinguishing of their traffic, and said it would be far more reasonable to ask the licensed victuallers and beer. sellers tee compensate the women whom they made widows, and the children they had rendered orphans. (Loud ap- plause.) It there were only a law passed to make the pub- licans keep their own paupers, there would soon be an end of the trade. There was one little spot in disturbed Ireland where peace and contentment reigned, and that was afplace called Besbrook where there were no policemen, no gaol, and lunatic asylum, for the simple reason that there was no publichouse in it.—The proceedings terminated with a vote of thanks to the chairman.

RUNCORN BRUNSWICK MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS. —At the weekly meeting, on Wednesday evening, a paper was read by Mr. John A. Smith on "Thou shalt not steal." SERVICE OF SONG AT WIDNES.—On Monday even- ing, a tea party was given at the Lacey-street Wesleyan schoolroom, when about 140 were present. A service of song entitled" Her Benny" followed ; and the choir was composed of about 30 members of the Sunday school, selected from the senior classes. Mrs. T. Robinson was the reader; Miss P Balshaw presided at the organ; and Mr. T. S. Swale con- ducted.

RECHADITE DISTRICT TENT.-011 Tuesday, a district tent of the Winsford and Norley division of Rechabites was held at; Runcorn. Brother Dimond, High Chief Ruler of England, presided, and the following officers were present: —W. Watson, P.P.C.R., Kingsley; T. Reynolds, D.C.R., illelsby ; J. Gunnery, D.D.R. Tarporley ; W. Dutton, D.S., I Norley; H. Hinde, D.T.; and the following delegates : Kelsall, James Williams; Runcorn, R. Evans. Female tents were represented by Mr. S. Wright, of Norley ; and Mr. William Nockett, of Frodsham. Winsford, D. Kitchen; Norley, John Blease; Kelsall, G. Wright; Frodsham, S. Hulse; Weaverham' D. Forster; Tar- porley, J. Rowlands; Kingsley, S.. Parker; Runcorn R. Wilson; Moulton, T. Brookes; Wincham, J. Alcock ; Mihle- vrich, G. Sant; Preston Brook, W. Jones; Helsby, J. Antro- bus: Halton, J. Boardman; Tarvin, W. Duckworth; Northw ich, A. Alcock ; Hartford, T. Birtwistle; Barrow, Thomas Shall- cross; Little Over, J. Dodd; Alprobam, Thomas Cookson; Clotton, J. Henshall. The usual district business was transacted. The increase on the quarter was stated to be 68. TEA. MEETING AT CAMDEN CHAPEL AND SCHOOL, RUNCORN.—On the evening of the 7th inst. about 150 members of this congregatioa sat down to tea, after which a public meeting was held in the school-room, when there were about 250 present. The gathering was presided over by the Rev. J. Nowell, the superintendent of the circuit, who, in the course of his address, alluded to the recent services held in St. Paul's chapel by Mr. Robinson Watson. The chairman, in conclusion, exhorted all present to profit by the services which bad been held. Messrs. Beckett, R. Shaw, and R. Norman briefly addressed the meeting. About 50 " testified" to the good they had received during Mr. Watscn's visit. The proceeds of the tea were devoted to the trust fund, and amounted to about £6. The following friends gave tables :—Mesdames G. S. Hazlehurst, S. C. Beckett, E. Davies, J. Temperley, W. J. Shore, the Misses Norman, Dobson, Chadwick, Speakman, Harrison, Mr. Simpson, and the Nelson-street society class. WIDNES CHORAL SOCIETY'S CONCERT.—The members of the Widnes Choral Society gave their concluding concert for the season in the Volunteer Hall, on Thursday evening. The principals were Miss Emily Stewart, of Liverpool ; Miss Janet Pierpoint, Mr. Joseph Morrison, and Mr. Ernest Batty; and the conductor was Mr. Argent. The proceedings consisted of a miscellaneous programme, which embraced Sterndale Bennett's cantata, the "May Queen." Miss Pier- point sang the recitative, "Now that the tree is drest, be- gone." Mr. Joseph Morrison gave very effectively "Oh, meadow clad in early green." The chorus, "With a laugh as we go round," was rendered in a very spirited manner. The solo, "With the carol in a tree," was given by Miss Stewart, and loudly applauded, and she was also well received in "Can I not find thee a warrant for changing?" Mr. Morrison was very succpssful in "Why do you cruelly frown on and fly me?" Mr. Ernest Batty was beard to much advantage in "Shall a clown that beauty wear ? " The chorus, "Hark, their notes the hautboys swell," was excel- lently given. The second part of the concert was commenced with Haydn's " Minnetto and Allegro, Seventh Symphony," which was sung in fine style. The flexibility of Miss Stewart's voice was admirably shown in the song entitled "The echo." "Vanished years" was beautifully sung by Mr. Morrison; and Mr. Batty rendered the old favonrite, "The Bay of Biscay," with a force and enthusiasm which won him the hearty commendation of the audience. Miss Pierpoint sang "Punchinello" very sweetly; and the pro- ceedings, at which there was a very fair attendance, con- cludedwith the National Anthem.

DRAMATIC( PERFORMANCES AT WIDNES.—Mr. Edward Sansom, late station master to the London and North- Western Railway, at Widnes, has within the last few days produced several dramas at the Volunteer Hall, in that town in a manner which reflects the greatest credit upon his histrionic abilities. On Saturday evening the play was Sheridan's "School for Scandal," when Mr. W. S. Branson, a gentleman who though old in years, has far from lost all his old fire as an actor, took the part of Sir Peter Teazle; Mr. Sausom that of Joseph Surface ; whilst Mr. James Carr personated Sir Harry Bumper ; Miss Alice Finch, Lady Teazle; and Miss C. St. Clare, Lady Sneerwell. On Monday, the "Lady of Lyons" was given, Mr. E. Sansom taking the part of Claude Melnotte, and Mr. W. S. Branson that of Colonel Damas. Mr. Sansom was very warmly received. On Tuesday " Othello " was produced. Mr. Sansom took the leading character, Mr. Branson " lago,'' and Miss St. Clare " Desdemona." On Wednesday evening, Oliver Goldsmith's "She Stoops to Conquer" was put upon the stage. Mr. Branson was Mr. Hardcastle ; Miss St. Clare, Miss Hardcas,tle ; Mr. W. H. Roberts, Hastings ; and Mr. Charles Nickson, "Young Marlow." The two last-named gentlemen were amateurs, and executed their parts admirably, considering this fact. Much credit was du3 to Mr. Nickson, who has never walked the boards before, and he was highly complimented on the success of this, his first effort in matters dramatic. We regret to have to state that though Mr. Sansom went to a very heavy expense in producing the plays, which were presented in a manner which has never before been equalled in the town, the attendance was poor, and the venture, we fear, must involve him in considerable loss.

ADJOURNED MEETING OF RUNCORN RATEPAYERS.-Ort Thursday evening an adjourned meeting of the ratepayers of Runcorn was held in Bethesda Congregational school ; room, for the purpose of receiving the report of the auditors ; as to the Burial Board accounts. Mr. Henry Coleburn, , chairman of the last-named body, presided, and there ; were also present Messrs. Thomas Bowyer, Wm. Sutton ; (vestry clerk), W. F. Salkeld, Win. Handley, Wm. Dobson, George Moss, Dr. McDougall, James Handley, F. J. Adams, Wm. Mellor, and Thomas Cooke.—Mr. Salkeld, secretary to the Burial Board, read the statement of accounts, which will be found in our advertising columns.—Mr. Wm. Handley, as one of the auditors, moved that the accounts be adopted. • , Whilst he and his fellow auditor were examining the I vouchers, Mr. Salkeld showed them everything which it was ' lin his power, and extended to them every courtesy. He and Mr. Mellor were quite pleased with the general correctness I of the accounts, and impressed with the fact that the Finance ' Committee which had been appointed during the past year , haa been of great service to the Burial Board. There were a few matters that the auditors particularly noticed as they ; were doing their work, concerning which it might be worth while to make a brief statement, as many times during the ' past year enquiries had been made at the ratepayers' meet- ' ings as to the position of the Board, and the amount which the cemetery was costing the town yearly. They had heard ; from Mr. Sal keld that the present mortgage debt was £5,850. If they went back to the opening of the cemetery, on the Ist March, 1860, they found that there had been , borrowed for its construction and enlargement, over ! and above the revenue, £8,050. In 1860 and 1861 there was borrowed for the making of the ground £6,250. Then there I was an additional amount of land bought, making the ceme- tery as large again as it was at first, and another £2,000 was I borrowed to pay for the land. When the cemetery was ex- tended in 1875, and the wall and railings set back, the work was done at a cost of £6OO, which sum was also borrowed. I During the last year another loan of £lOO had,been effected, I for the purpose of constructing the mortuary, making the sum of £8,050. Any one looking at the sinking fund ac- count might be surprised at the small amount in the bank, as the cemetery had been open 21 years. There was £33 Is. 3d. actually at call, but this sum was easily accessible, as the Burial Board, with a very wise forethought, had, whilst I the sinking fund had been accumulating, been paying off their loans, as the bank interest was so small as to be a com- paratively insignificant item. £3,100 had been paid off, leaving £5,850. During the past year the whole of the loans had been brought down to the uniform rate of four per cent. The annual payment to the sinking fund drawn from the overseers was £l2O, being a one-fiftieth part of the £6OO. I This sum was arranged as an actual proportion of the mort- gage debt. There was at present a large amount of unen- closed land, which would prove of service to a future generaron ; and the Burial Board had thought it right that the ratepayers of years to come should bear their share of this burden. The whole debt of the cemetery and land would be extinguished in the year 1931; and entil that time the place would continue to be a cost to the town. In con- clusion, he could only express his gratification at the personal part which he took in the erection of the mor- tuary, as it weuld only cost the ratepayers £5 a year, and the original cost be paid off in 50 Years.—Dr. McDougall seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously. He stated that there was one matter which some two years ago caused a little irritation, as a large number of the commu- nity felt they had a grievance in the closing of the cemetery against Sunday funerals. He had every reason to believe that since Sunday interments had been allowed, the day had been observed in so strict and proper a manner that no one could raise any objection, but he should be glad if the secretary could give them any information on the subject, as it would probably be of such a nature as to cause satisfac- tion to those who took a more liberal view than other gen- tlemen of the rights of the working-classes upon that occa- sion.—Mr. Salkeld had great pleasure in stating that the Sunday funerals were very regularly and respectably con- ducted—extremely so. (Applause.)—Mr. Moss explained, as a member of the Burial Board, that it had been decided the ratepayers should have the opportunity of inspecting the accounts for themselves by having them published in the local newspapers.—Dr. McDougall moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Coleburn in very complimentary terms. He observed that it was a gratification to think that they had at least one chairman in the toun who presided over public proceedings with fairness, and yet who, at the same time, always afforded every latitude for the discussion of any question which might be brought forward. (Applause.)—Mr. James Hand- ley, in seconding the proposition, which was carried with applause, said it would be impossible to find a chairman of the Burial Board more attentive or diligent than Mr. Cole- burn.—The Chairman, in responding, said he had not missed a single meeting of the Burial Board since he had been elected—nearly five years ago. (Applause.)—The proczed- ings then terminated.

RUNCORN MERSEY MISSIONS TO SEAMEN. COMING CONCERT.—On Tuesday evening, the boys connected with the well known Indefatigable training ship, will give a concert in the Public Hill, Runcorn, on behalf of the Mersey Missions to Seamen. ELECTRIC LIGHTING LEGISIATION.—The following may be interesting to the Warrington Corporation :—The Board of Trade has issued the correspondence between that department and the Corporation of Manchester, on the sub- ject of the Government Electric Lighting Bill. The Cor- poration, having received a copy of the draft bill, wrote sug- gesting that it should be so amended as to authorise muni- cipal corporations to supply electricity for public and private purposes within their respective districts for the supply of gas. Subject to this observation, the Corporation submitted that in accordance with the report of the Select Committee of 1879 every local authority should be invested with the exclusive right within its own jurisdiction of supplying electricity, the area of supply being in every case co-extensive with such jurisdiction. In reply, Mr. Farrer, Assistant Secretary to the Board of Trade, wrote on the 11th inst., stating that the bill bad been framed in ac- cordance with the recommendation of the Select Committee of 1879. That committee did not recommend exclusive rights of supply being given to municipal authorities; but that municipal authorities should have power to give facilities to companies or private individuals to conduct experiments, and should have a preference prospectively to control the, distribution during a limited period. HILL CLIFFE BAPTIST CTIAPEL.—The annual tea party, in connection with this chapel, was held on Monday last. Tea had been provided in the schoolroom, and there was a good number of persons present. Mrs. Moss, Mrs. J. Grounds, Miss Rowson' and Miss Booth, were the ladies who presided at the tables. After tea there was an interval of an hour, during which those person 'S who had the in- clination could stroll in the pleasant fields by which the old chapel is surrounded, and enjoy the excellent prospect. The weather being beautifully fine this was much enjoyed. Subsequently a gathering, presided over by the pastor, the Rev. Mr. Pilling, was held in the chapel. The Chairman having remarked on the pleasure it afforded him to see so many present, made a few appropriate observations on the subject of consecration, pointing out that it was the duty of every professing Christian to follow in the footsteps of the Saviour, and to have at heart the interests of their fellow men and women. Mr. Goodier then made a short address, in which he spoke of the value of earnestness and perse- verance in all undertakings. The chief feature of the even- ing was the rendering by the choir of the pathetic and touching service of song entitled " Her Benny." The choir have successfully performed the piece on a previous OCCA- aion, And their efforts on the present occasion appeared to give much pleasur.3 to the audience. The Chairman gave the connective readings. Mr. Peter Harristin presided at the harmonium. Votes of thanks were accorded to those persons who had assisted in providing the tea, and who had contri- buted in any way to the success of the gathering. THE NEW HIGH SIIERIFF.—On Thursday next, Colonel McCorquodale, the new High Sheriff of Laneashire, pro- ceeds to Manchester to receive her Majesty's judges, who will then open the Spring Assizes. The High Sheriff has in- vited the Corporation of Wigan and other guests, numbering in all about 250, and comprising in addition the magis- trates of the respective divisions of the county and the New- ton Commissioners, to meet him at breakfast at his residence, The Willows,, in Newton, on Thursday morning. The F Company of the Liverpool Press Guard, of which the High Sheriff is honorary colonel, will parade, under the command of Captain Wood, at Newton at 8-45 a.m., and will be on duty as a guard of honour during the reception of the guests by Colonel and Mrs. McCorquodale. Breakfast will be served in an elegant marquee, and during this the splendid band of the Press Guard will play a choice selection of mnsic. A procession will afterwards be formed, the Mayer and mem- bers of the Wigan Corporation, together with the invited guests; preceding the High Sheriffs equipage, to the boundary of the township, the Press Guard, with their band, forming the guard of honour. The procession will pass through Ashton, and en arriving at Adam's Bridge will be met by the Wigan detatchment of the 4th L.R.V., under the command of Captain Hilton, and here the duties vacated by the Press Guard at Newton will be undertaken by the Wigan volunteers. The procession will march through the principal streets of the town to the London and North- Western station, when a beautifully illuminated address will be presented from the Town Council to Colonel McCorquo- dale, congratalating him on the honour bestowed upon him by the Queen in appointing him High Sheriff of the county. GOSPEL TEMPERANCE MISSION.—BLUE RIBBON ARMY. —The mission begins on Sunday (to-morrow) evening, in the Public Hall, at 8.15. A WARRINGTON MAN FOUND DROWNED AT THELWiLL, —At the Pickering Arms, Thelwall, on Wednesday, Mr, Coroner Ridgway held an inquest on the body of Thomas Taker, 63 years of age, a pin pointer, who resided at 11 Dutton-street. The deceased had been missing from his home since the 21st March. On Tuesday afternoon, a shoe- maker named George Broady whilst walking on the side of the river at Thel wall, saw a body floating in the water. He pulled the body out, and it was identified by William Taker, a letter carrier, as that of the missing man, his father. There were no marks of violence on the body. Previous to his disappearance the deceased, it was stated, had for three weeks been drinking heavily.—A verdict of found dead was recorded.

SUICIDE BY HANGING AT WAERINGTON.—A Case of suicide occurred in Winwick-street, on Wednesir, under circumstanees which seem to point that the rash act was the result of heavy drinking. For a considerable period

Margaret Tickle, 66 years of age, wife of Richard Tickle, flagger and slater, of 147, Winwick-street, had "suffered from a lacerated tongue, and been addicted to intemperate habits." These habits instead of decreasing, appear to have I gained a stronger bold, and during the past fortnight she had been drinking to excess in her own house. On Tues- day night she seemed to be rambling in her mind. The following morning before going to his work at 6.30 her hus- band pave her some tea. At noon, when he returned, he was surprised to find no fire in the grate, and ascending to the bedroom he found the deceased hanging by the neck from the bed rail. he was quite cold and dead. A large box was clese to the bed, from which she had evidently jumped after fastening the handkerchief, which was round her neck, to-the rail. The deceased was only wearing her night dress. An inquest will be held on the body to-day (Saturday). FATAL ACCIDENT AT WIIIIIINGTON.—An accident, which termiaated fatally, occurred at Warrington on Tuesday afternoon to a labourer named John Birket, 25 years of age, re•iding at Farnworth near Widnes. It appears Birket was employed in the telegraph department of the post office, and, with several other men, was engaged unloading some poles from a lurry standing in Liverpool-road.' Whilst thus en- gaged a pcle rolled from off the lurry, striking Birket on the breast and temples, and knocking him to the ground. A spring cart was procured, and he was conveyed with all des- patch to the Infirmary. The unfortunate man, however, expired whilst on his way thither. Tke inquest was held on the body of the deceased on Fri- day, at the Higher Seven Stars, Bridge-street. The coroner was Mr. C. E. Driffield. The post office telegraph depart- ment was represented by Mr. John Doherty, superintending engineer of the north-western district, and Mr. John R. Edwards, superintending enginees, Liverpool.—John Birkett, father of the deceased identified the body.—David Henry Barnwell, at present living at Sankey-bridges, said he was foreman of the gang With which the deceased worked. De- ceased had only been in the gang about three weeks. Witness said there were eight poles on the lurry, and the pole which killed the deceased was the first pole they unloaded. The deceased and two other men mounted the poles to remove one. It was intended to put it from the harry to the ground by two iron bars, but the pole turned, and the thick end coming in contact with the ground, the other end struck the deceased on the chest. The force of the blow knocked him to the ground, and the pole following him again struck him on the temples. The deceased was bleeding very much from the mouth and one ear. The pole was put off in the usual land Weal manner, but there was a hollow place in the butt 'which caused it to turn. There was no neglect on the part of the deceased or the other men. The deceased by turning his shoulder on one side could have escaped the pole. A verdict of accidental death was returned.

PIiIMITITE METHODISM AT LATCHFORD.—To defray the cost of erecting A wall and palisading in front of the Primi- tive Methodist preaching-room, Knutsford-road, Latchford, a public tea meeting and sale of work was held in the build- ing on Easter Monday. It may be interesting to state that the mission was commenced some three years ago by a few earnest belieyers in the principles of Primitive Methodism, and is a branch of the Legh-street Chapel belonging to that denomination. There are 00 scholars connected with the place, and divine service is conducted every Sunday even- ing. The congregation, which is composed entirely of working people, exhibit considerable enthusiasm in the work, and a good number of persons sat down to tea on Monday last. The ladies who presided at the tables were Mrs. Rogers, Mrs. Mather, Mrs. Massey, and Mrs. Stringer. In the evening, after the tea, the sale of work was held. The goods were the residue of the saleof work held at Christmas, when £2B was obtained, and as there was a large attendance the articles were all sold, and a good sum realised. The stall was in charge of Mrs. Copeland, Mrs. Massey, and Mrs. Wright.

THE EASTER • HOLlDAYS.—Brilliant weather prevailed during the Easter holidays, which seemed to be much en- joyed by the townspeople. On Monday, Warrington had a forsaken appearance, e shops were pearly all closed anq very few persons were to be seen in the streeis. Advantagd seemed to have been generally taken of the suspension of business to have a day in the country. The various railway stations were thronged with per'sons anxious to proceed to the numerous pleasure and health resorts in the neighbour- hood, and special trains were required to convey the War- ringtonians desirous of reaching Frodsham, there to enjoy an invigorating ramble over the hills, and the lovely panorama by which they are surrounded. Many others put to the test the resources of the local cab proprietors by their applications for vehicles in which to drive through the quiet and pretty lanes of the adjoining county; while all the bicyclists in the district appeared to have taken to "the road" so continuous was the tingling of bells and the sounding of horns. The day was most favourable for pedestrianism and not a few persons were to be seen saunter- ing through the fields and lanes• near the town; and the beauties of Bank Park attracted even larger numbers than on the previous Friday. On the whole the conduct of the holiday-makers was all that could be desired, and the sobriety of the pleasure-seekers was the the subject of special remark at the Police Court the following day. In the evening 'Professor Acton, the " War- rington Wizard," entertained the visitors with his clever exhibitions of legerdemain. The sale was continued on Thursday and was again fairly successful, only a small number of articles remaining unsold.

TII E WARRINGTON NTJSIOAL Sc-ICIETY'S CONCERT.

The second of the two concerts given during the season by the Warrington Mus:cal Society was held on Thursday evening last, in the Public Hall. The audience, though numerically less than might have been anticipated consider- ing the attractiveness of the programme, fairly filled the building. The reserved portion included a fashionable gathering of the elite of the town and neighbourhood, and many of the Society's subscribers and patrons. The chief item of interest was the sacred cantata, "The widow cif Nein," composed for the recent Worcester Musical Festival by Mr. A. J. Caldicott, Mus. Bac., the second part of the programme partaking of a miscellaneous character. Apart from any considerations of the reception which greeted the public performance, the Society is to be congratulated upon its spirit in taking in hand a new and comparatively un- known work. And the fact that from amongst the mass of compositions of the class oratorio inviting attention, a work from the pen of one of our own countrymen should have been chosen, redounds further to the Society's credit and tends only to increase the public interest in its operations. It is a pity that with the enterprise and taste in musical matters thus manifest in our midst it should have been found necessary or expedient to dissolve the kindred so- ciety which up to the present time has devoted itself to the study and practice of orchestral music and co-operated with good effect with the Musical Society on occasions like this. We noticed with regret on Thursday evening the absence, for the first time, of the general body of these instrumen- talists. The band, with one or two exceptions, consisted entirely of professional musicians. The Misses Henrietta and Marianne Tomlinson and Messrs. Henry Taylor and Bantock Pierpoint were en- gaged as principals in the four essential voice parts. Of the outline and general character of the cantata we may perhaps say a few words before proceeding further. The story of "The widow of Nein " is briefly told in the 7th chap. of Luke. Out of the somewhat meagre materials here provided Mr. Caldicott has himself elaborated a libretto, amplifying the subject by dwelling upon the widow's grief and subsequent gratitude,and by the consolation offered her in the created character of "a Minstrel" the descriptive portions of the cantata being likewise allotted to a second imaginary personage called "The Narrator." The work is divided into three sections,"Tbe Shadow of Death," "Hope," and "The Resurrection," and these heads give the key to the sequence of leading incidents. It can scarcely be doubted that viewed in its entirety the musical composition has greatly advanced Mr. Caldicott's growing reputation. The settirag at once betokens the scholarly hand, many of the moveThents being elaborate in character and construc- tion and indicative of much fertility of contrapuntal resource. The instrumentation is rich and varied and, indeed, is often so far striking as to endanger the vocal solos by its undue prominence. But, coming now to speak of the performance of the cantata, we cannot help remarking that the playing of the instrumental parts was much too heavy to allow the principal vocalists to be heard to advantage, many of the more subtle effects being sacrificed. It is, on the other hand, to be remarked that the voices of the leading singers were each and all rather light in character, and therefore re- quiring especial softness in the accompaniments. The sing- ing of the principals moreover can scarcely be deemed satis- factory, though it is difficult to say how far thisis due to the artistes themselves or is explained, as we suspect it is in some degree, in the fact that music is difficult of smooth vocalisation. But certain it is that many of the solo numbers fell flatly, and were received with anything but enthusiasm. The part of the Widow is, as might be expected, the most prominent one in the score. Some fine passages fell to the lot of Miss Henrietta Tomlinson. "I shall see him" and "What reward shall I give" are contrasted themes, in both of which this lady displayed the requisite flexibility of style, and in these tho only evidences of the audience's approval were manifested. The most attractive number for the contralto is that entitled " Why is thy countenance sad." Of this Miss M. Tomlinson gave an appropriate interpretation, though a tendency to hurry on the part of the band must be noted as ditninishing the effect as a whole. Indeed, we venture to think that many of the numbers scored for the solo voices would have been beard to greater advantage by the adoption of a slower tempo. The ornate character of the accompaniments seem to tender this necessary. And these remarks as to speed apply with greatest force, perhaps, to the duet for contt alto and tenor, "A loving and a contrite heart," a number possessing more than ordinary merit as a composition. Mr. Henry Taylor is in possession of a vocal organ of rather pleasing qualityof tone. His intonation was, however, not alwayg in strict tune. The solo "Weep not for the dead" received due expression et the hands of Mr. Bantock Pierpoint. This, the only op- portunity offered to the bass voice, was, however, to sone extent lost to the singer for want of steadieess and a one- ness between himself and the orchestra. The unaccompanit d quartette for the principals "They that sow in tears" ard the subsequent unaccompanied chorus, were enjoyable in point of the rich and well blended harmony embodied in them. The choral portions of the cantata are, to our thinking, the most meritorious, and they proved likewise the most enjoy- able in performance. The chorus had evidently been well rehearsed, the singing of many of the numbers leaving little to be desired. "In Rama was there a voice heard" is a splendid piece of part writing, and this chorus was heard with fine effect. But it will suffice that we give a general commendation were all is uniformly good. We need only therefore refer to the opening chorus, " Man goeth to his long home," and the con' eluding fugue and chorus as instances in which vocal ifficulties were surmounted with ease. The overture, which is developed at considerable length, was well played by the band, the movement being especially suggestive of the state er. agitatitln in which the leading character is dis- covered. The Funeeal March of Mourners is a striking ' movement, and serves nicely to divereify the 'T.`ork. Mc+ transition ef the theme from the minor to the major key - is happily conceived.

In the -second part of the programme a number of songs, ballads, glees,&c., were introduced, and the artistes, princi- pal and chorus, showed themselves competent to deal most effectually with these classes of compositions. Miss Henrietta Tomlinson was more than ordinarily successful in the bravura scena "Corn e hello" (Donizetti), and secured a well merited recall. Miss Marianne Tomlinson was likewise encored in the sweet ballad, "By the margin of Fair Zurich's waters," which was sung by her with charm- ing naivette and gracefulness of style. Her voice is rather a mezzo soprano than a contralto, and is singularly sweet in quality. Some little enthusiasm on the part of the audieace beginning now to manifest itself for the first time, Mr. Bantock Pierpoint was also constrained to acknowledge a redemand in respect of his spirited rendering of "Speed on, my bark." The various pirt-songs were also well received, the morceau, "When twilight dews," composed by the Society's conductor, Dr. Hiles, being noteworthy for its beautiful simplicity and subdued harmony. The spirited chorus, "A wet slael and a flowing sea," brought the pro- gramme to a close, and the concert concluded at an early hour.

;I:171E "GREENALL FOR -EVER PLACARD„

Sir,—l was very much surprisld, and• not a little amused, to notice that a meeting had been called by some- body, with a view to induce my old friend Sir Gilbert to reconsider.his determination not to stand i again as the Con- servative candidate for Warrington. It s quite refreshing to observe how innocent and gullable the writer of the placard presumes the Tory party to be—although, bv the ;way, John Stuart Mill always called us the "stupid party" —and if we are unable, although the voice may be the voice of Jacob, to discover that the hands are the hands of Esau, we shall richly deserve the designation referied to. There is no person who has read that placard but who can see the transparency of its design, and who cannot fail to discover that it does not emanate from the Conservative party.— Yours, &c., UNITED STATES.

div.head: " GREENALL FOR EVER !"
div.p: " GREENALL FOR EVER !"

Sir,—Magic ;aim' Workingmen vote to a man for that nice old gentleman who has closed his purse to his party, with this difference, that they will show their good sense by doing as they did when they voted for the Guardians. Also remember, ye aforesaid workingmen, that "The Seraphic Doctor" kindly consented to preside at the mmastre meeting last night. What extraordinary self- sacrifice ! Just remember that when the "S. D." puts himself forward as our member. For I believe there is good reason for supposing that Sir Gilbert Greenall will not, al in thee past, sacrifice personal comfort for the public good (sic) by not becoming our recognised candidate, if we show an lan- mistakeable desire not to have him as such. Let the many who have fought for 30 years under the above watchword, S,glit under another and a far better one, not "Salisbury, Greenall, or Northcote for Ever," but let it be "Gladstone for Ever !"—Yours, ANTI-HUMBUG. Warrington, 14th April, 1882.
