div.p: Tatter to the tor.

THE WARRINGION ORCHESTRAL SOCIETY. Sir,—The musical public of Warrington will agree with your correspondent " Attalus " in deploring the dissolution of the Orchestral Society, and many, doubtless, will wonder at the collapse. If you wish, sir', to know the real cause', just invite the following gentlemen to spend an hour with you some evening to smoke a friendly cigarette, and relate their experience in concert giving. Invite Mr. John Chap- pell, Mr. George Woods, Mr. T. M. Pattison, Mr. Newcombe, Mr. C. E. Rowley, and (horrid to relate!) the musical com- mittee of the Workmen's Club. Perhaps it will be instruc- tive to your readers if I venture to draw the curtain, take a peep into futurity, and reveal the details of that interesting gathering. Imagine then, dear reader, the above named gentlemen solemnly assembled; you, Mr. Editor, acting as chairman and general director of the proceedings. Let us take them in the order given. "Now, Mr. Chappell, stand forward; ,toe the line, John, and speak up." "Well, gentlemen, being a pretty tidy hand on the flute, I took in those days, an active and prominent part in musical matters. I was a kind of musical godfather to these two lads here, George Woods and Tom Pattison. (" You were John, bless you ; " from the "two lads.") So I thought I would turn an honest penny by giving Saturday evening concerts. Being a Yorkshirem in, and knowing that there is more ability located there than in all England put together, I brought talent of the first water from that county to my concerts. The result was, the penny was turned out of my pocket to the tune of .£l5 7s. 4d. If you can see your way, gentlemen, towards starting a subscription to refund— "Thanks, John, thanks. Now Mr. George Woods, stand up, and don't get excited." "Much obliged; I can take a hint. Gentlemen, I was, as you all know, destined for the profession, and studied in the sunny land of the Italians. Unfortunately my vocal organ gave way under severe practice, or Lloyd and Maas would have been nowhere. Sims Reeves himself, gentlemen— (Mr. Chappell : "Draw it mild, George.") To the point. Some years ago I started a class in St. Peter's schoolroom, . and gathered around me a goodly number of vocalists and instrumentalists. As the result of our labour, I gave a most saccessful concert in the Public Hall for a local charity, and handed over a few pounds. I then determined to give a still better concert for the benefit of the Infirmary. Assisted by the flower of the town and neighbourhood I gave a rattling good concert, didn't I, Tom? The public, to my intense dis- gust, neither appreciated the object nor the music, and I dropped at that one concert, .ed 3s. 9d. Gentlemen, my blood

boig— "All right, George. Let's see, who's the next? Mr. T. M. Pattison. Stand back,:gentlemen, and let Mr. Pattison be seen." "As a professor in the town, and a shining light in music, (Mr. Newcombe: "Question ") I considered the formation of an orchestral and choral society a very proper undertaking. Moreover,l had been snubbed by the existing Musical Society in some efforts that I had made to get a band together for them. So I want at it, and produced the biggest band and chorus ever known in the town. For two seasons I worked hard and lost both money and flesh. (Mr. Alfred Woods: "Ha, ha !") But not much; not sufficient to prevent me trying again. Tree third season, however, proved an unmitigated staggerer. I gave the " Messiah " at Christmas time in a manner never before attempted in Warrington. (Mr. New- combe: "Oh, oh !") I determined to draw the public or perish, so I engaged a tip-top band, organist, and four prin- cipals, including Madame Patey. Fancy, gentlemen, the finest contralto in the world singing "He wasdespised" and "He shall feed His flock" to a beggarly array of empty benches! (Cries of "Shame, shame ! " during which the speaker sobbed audibly.) Pardon my emotion, but I had to shell out £6B us. gd. I wore a ghastly smile for two months' and even now the bare mention of a concert gives me a cold shake. Gentlemen, I've done." "Come on, come on; the fun waxes fast and furious. Can you add anything, Mr. Newcombe, to this exhilarating theme?" "Only a few words. As an experienced amateur, with considerable musical talent, I have endeavoured, in the sim- plicity of my nature, to educate the masses in the higher flights of musical thought. Suffice it to'3say, my fingers have been burned in the attempt, to my entire and last- ing satisfaction. No more concerts for me, thank you." "Short and sweet. Now, Mr. Rowley, it's your turn." Well, gentlemen, as a Manchester man, I need hardly remind you that I possess far more musical ability and busi- ness capacity than a man born and bred in this smoky hole. . (Mr. Pattison: "You think so, old man.") No, Ido not think so, it is an acknowledged fact. Ask the Workmen's Corn—. (Ironical chedrs, led by Mr. Price.) After being treated in the manner well known to the inhabitants ru. of this smo—, of this town I mean, by a certain seraphic individual and his committee, I naturally believed that, pro- : , perly managed and with suitable talent, weekly concerts a: would pay. At first they promised well, but a lack and alas! I was ultimately on the wrong side .£33 14s. 11d. I hear that the men of light and leading in this smoky ho—in this town, I should say—far prefer the Circus to a good concert; BO although you have now seen the last of me in the Public Hall, you may hear of Rowley'g Royal Equestrian Troupe, • admission threepence.' "„ "Much obliged ior your candid opinion, Mr. Rowley. Perhaps Mr. Alfred Woods will speak for the Committee." "Our only object, gentlemen, was to provide an evening's entertainment for the working classes. Of course, we young fellows enjoyed the thing imtnensely while the concerts were successful, but we soon began to squabble amongst our- selves. The musical director wanted to ride a high horse, to the Committee did their best to sit on him. At length we separated, and gave oar weekly yells in the Workmen's Club; a wretched place for the purpose. When the place happened to be full, which wasn't often, it was a regular black hole,' nearly suffocating the audience. Public in- terest waned, and we were soon knocked into a cocked hat. (Excitedly.) I'll tell you wot it is, chaps. Th' working mon wants none e' yer patronizin' ways, none o' yer penny yells, none o' yer muffins and ginger beer, none o' yer . (Mr. Pattisen "Hold on, Tubbs, my boy.") Give him a good stiff glass o' There, Mr. Woods, suppress your emotion. Well, gen- tlemen, your verdict seems to be that providing good music in Warrington is ah All, with emphasis, "Not worth the candle." W.

EASTER VESTRY MEETINGS. PARISH CHURCH, WARRINGTON. The annual vestry meeting was held on Tuesday in the vestry of the church, when, in the absence of the Rector, the senior curate, the Rev. F. W. Cory, presided. The at- tendance was limited to 13 parishioners.—Mr. Wet. DooLEY, one of the churchwardens, submitted the statement of ac- counts, from which it appeared that the receipts from all sources, including a belence from last year of £5 ss. 4d., amounted to £404 14s. 10d. Of this £32 Ss. had been realised by the voluntary church rate. The balance in hand was stated to be £5 rs. ; but there is a sum of £25 due to the choir and £l2 12s. for tuning the organ. The accounts having, at the suggestion of Mr. Buckton, been examined by Mr. Councillor Francomb, were passed.—Mr. Wm. Dooley was again nominated as the Rector's warden ; and the parishioners appointed Mr. Thomas Moores as their —iirarden in the place of Mr. S. Davies, who resigned office in consequence of the state of his health.—Some conversation next took place me the question of appointing sidesmen, about which a pastoral leer was read the Bishop of Liverpool, and subsequently the following gentlemen were elected to officiate in that capacity, viz., Messrs. John Dew- burst, N. B. Percival, J. E. Wright, John Naylor, Wm. Gill, 'ana James Morris.—On the motion of Mr. Dewhurst, se- conded by Mr. Leigh, a vote of thanka was accorded to tte retiring churchwardens and sidesmen.—A voluntary rate of 3d. in the £ was laid by the meeting, on the proposition of Mr. Dooley, seconded by Mr. Percival.—Messrs. J. R. Buck- ton and S. M. Webster were re-appointed lay delegates, and they will represent the vestry at the ruri-decanal conference. —The vestry clerk, Mr. James Nicholson, was re-elected.— Mr. Councillor FRANCOMB somewhat humourously drew the attention of the g,stry to the inconvenience arising from two editions the old and the new —of "Hymns ancient and modern " being used in the church, and as the result a resolution was passed instructing the ' clergy to intimate to the eongregation that on and after Whit-Sunday only the new edition will be used in the ser- vices.—Mr. BUCKTON inquired if anything had been done with respect to the land which had been allotted to the poor of Woolston by the Inclosure Commiesioners.—Mr. WHITE (who was asking as vestry clerk) said when this matter was before the vestry two years ago, it was ruled by Mr. Nichol- son that it was a matter with which the vestry had nothing to do.—Mr. BIICKTON then explained that four acres of land were allotted by the Inclosure Commissioners to the church- wardens of Warrington and the overseers of Woolston for the use of the poor of Woolston some years ago. They found that instead of a proper oblong piece being marked out and allotted to them containing four acres, that only 31 had been allotted. The other half acre was taken possession of by the people who owned the adjoining land.—Mr. WHITE said the matter would never he settled without litigation, and he added that Meesre. Houghton, who now held the land, bought and paid for it by measurement from Mr. Standish.—Mr. Bucterox said Mr. Standieh did not have it to sell. The land had been all eted to the churchwardens et Warrington and overseers of Woolston, who were the trustees of the four acres of land for the use of the poor, and it was their duty to see after it.—The Rev. CHAIRMAN observed that it bad been ruled the vestry could not enter- tain the matter, and the question dropped without any de- cision being arrived at.—Teere was no other business_

HOLY TRINITY CHURCH, WiRRINGTON. The annual vestry meeting was held on Tuesday evening, the vicar, the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton presiding. The ac- counts showed the rec,iipts for the year to be £233 7s. 9d., and the expenditure £233 15s. 10d.—Mr. HATTON stated that the poor offertory amounted to £36 188. Bd. The ordinary collections had realised £175 13s. sp.—The CHAIRMAN said he believed the offertory last year was not so good in the aggregate as in the past year, although it was better on the ay.-rage. The reason of that was that fewer special appeals had been roade.—The accounts were unani- mously agreed to. Mussrs. R. Siddall and Mr. John Hatton were re-appointed wardens. The following gentlemen were nominated sidesmpti Brandreth, James 'Harding, John Craik, and Richard Hatton. Messrs. Charles White and W. J. Burgess were re-electtd the lay delegates to attend the church conferences, and Mr. H. B. White vestry clerk.— The CuAlamax thought it would bean advantage to him and a help to the parish to have a parish council, and after a short discussion, Messrs. John Hatton, Siddall, Haines, Jas. Harding, BFgess, Sharp, Owen, White, Brandreth, R. Hatton, Craik, and Adamson were selected.—A vote of

thanks was accorded to the chairman and to the church- wardens, and the proceedings closed. ST. PAUL'S CHURCH, WARRINGTON. The annual meeting of the parishioners was held in the vestry at St. Paul's Church, on Monday morning, for the purpose of passing the accounts, appointing new churchwardens, &c. The vicar (the Rev. S. Wilkinson) presided, and there were also present the Rev. E. St. A. Duke, Messrs. T. Jolley, T. Sutton, D. W. Finney, J. Pierpoint, W. D. Jeans (vestry clerk), J. Craik, M. Chorley, Lawless, G. Bebbington (parish clerk), and J. Hough.—Mr. SUTTON said he was not able to give as complete a statement of accounts as he could have wished, because the parish clerk had not kiven him all his accounts up to the present time. However, as nearly as he could make out the income had been £9l us. 40., and the expenditure £77 165. 8,21., leaving a balance of £l3 14s. 81-d. Against this he stated they owed about £5O, which would leave a balance against the parish of £36 ss. 4d., which would be, he thought, a slight reduction upon last year. He had received £l5 on account of pew rents, and £26 9s. 0,-d. as the proceeds of the tea party. The latter amount showed a decrease on the amount received in the previous year, and was owing to the fact that they had had to pay several outstanding accounts which ought to have been debited against the previous tea parties. From the collections for wardens' expenses they had re- ceived £5O 25. Od. On the proposition of Mr. FINNEY, seconded by Mr. PIERPOINT, the accouats as submitted were adopted.—The VICAR then expressed his thanks to all con- nected with the parish for the very great help they had ren- dered, and the courtesy and kindness they had shown dur- ing the past year, as in previous years. It was a comfort to come to the vestry of St. Paul's because they had gentlemen to deal with who were gentlemen in every sense of the word. During the past year, whenever he had had occasion to consult the churchwardens and sidesrnen they had al- ways given their advice and help most kindly and most readily. No parish was blessed with better churchwardens and officers than St. Paul's had, and he thanked them most sincerely for their very valuable help. During the past year they had accomplished a very great undertaking. They had restored the church, as everyone acknowledged, most satis- factorily. The churchwardens and every one connected with the work had given their time, money, and labour willingly and readily, and that had been the means of effect- ing that great work. He concluded by asking Mr. Thomas Jolley to again be his warden for the ensuing year.—Mr. JOLLEY accepted the office, and said he would endeavour to forward the good work that was being done in the parish.— CRACK proposed the re-appointment of Mr. Sutton as parish- ioners' warden. This was seconded by Mr. Pierpoint and carried.—Mr. JOLLEY nominated Mr. C. Ashurst as his sides- man, and Mr. SUTTON nominated Mr. T. Morris, and four additional sidesmen were appointed, via., Messrs. J. Smet- hurst, M. Chorley, W. Lawless, and W. Pollitt. I—ft was decided to continue the fortnightly collections. Messrs. John Pierpoint and D. W. Finney were appointed to represent the vestry at such con- ferences of the clergy and laity of the deanery of Winwick as may be held.—Mr. JOLLEY moved that the duties of the clerk (Mr. Bebbington) should cease from that day. For a number of years there had been paid to the clerk of St. Paul's a salary.of £l2 a year for certain services in the church, and it was in respect to these services he moved that motion. It did not inteifere with Mr. Bebbington's duties connected with weddings, baptisms, &c. They pro- posed to appoint two apparitors at a salary of £4 each per k annum, and by this means they would give greater satisfac- tion to the congregation.—Mr. SUTTON, in seconding the ' motion, said Mr. Bebbington had held the office for a long period [Mr. Bebbington: Thirty years], but the duties were now of a different character to what they were formerly. There had been complaints on the part of pew owners of their seats having been filled by strangers, and they had threatened to leave the church if it was not altered.—Mr. BEBEINGTON said he should feel very much relieved if the motion passed.—The motion was carried.—Messrs. John Hough and Wm. Bebbington were appointed apparitors at the annual salary of £4 each; and Mr. W. Bebbington was appointed to attend the Thursday evening service at an extra salary of £1 per annum. It was also decided that the Vicar should appoint another apparitor at a salary of £4 per annum.—Vetes of thanks were accorded to the church- wardens, the vestry clerk, and the chairman, and the meeting terminated.

ST. ANN'S CHURCH, WARRINGTON. The Rev. J. G. RICHARDS, vicar, presided at the annual vestry meeting held in the above church, on Tuesday. There were also present Messrs. H. J. Gaskell, P. Calvert, C. Calvert, and Dagnall, with Mr.E. Woods (vestry clerk.) The chairman appointed Mr. George Hemment as his warden, and on the preposition of Mr. Dagnall, Mr. P. Calvert was elected parishioners' warden. Messrs. Hewitt, aud W. Richardson were appointed sidesmen, and Messrs. C. Calvert, and S. Looker were chosen as lay representatives at the ruridecanal conferences. The meeting closed with votes of thanks to the retiring wardens for their services, and to the vicar fer presiding. ST. JAMES' CHURCH, LATCHFORD.

The Vicar, the Rev. F. Slater, presided at the annual vestry meeting held on Easter Monday. There were pre- sent Messrs. Bolton, Hutchinson (churchwardens), Worrall. Rigby, Dobson and Atherton.—Mr. BOLTON read the financial statement which showed the receipts of the year to be £231 18s. BP. The general offertory had realised £lOl 19s. 10P. ; special offertories, £66 Is. 2d.; offertories for church expenses, £l6 13s. 9d. The expenditure was £248 Is. 3. which included accounts, left unpaid by the former churchwardens, amounting to £.34 Hs. 7d. There I was a balance due 0 the churchwardens of £23.—The CITAIRMAN expressed his great gratitude to the church- wardens for the more than efficient manner in which they had carried on the affairs of the church, and as Mr. Bolton had expressed his willingness to again serve, he had great pleasure in reappointing him his churchwarden.—On the proposition of Mr. WORRALL, seconded by Mr. BOLTON, Mr. Hutchinson was reappointed people's churchwarden.—Mr. RIGBY remarked that he should like to see the wardens supporting the vicar next walking-day. (Hear, hear.)— Mr. Worrall and Mr. Joseph Taylor were reappointed sidesmen.—A vote of thanks to the chairman and church- wardens concluded the proceedings, which had only occu- pied about 15 minutes, the chairman observing amid laughter that they had no lively meetings now.

div.head: STRETTON CHURCH.
div.p: STRETTON CHURCH.

The annual vestry meeting was held in the schoolroom, on East er Monday, under the presidency of the Rev. Canon Dodd, vicar. Besides the vicar and churchwardens there were present Messrs. Charles Whitby, John Davies, John Sankey, Winstanley, Ellison' Hugh Derbyshire and De Prez. The accounts were presented by the churchwardens, Messrs. Edward Brocklehurst, and John Derbyshire, and the expen- diture was found to be met by the usual voluntary Easter collection, supplemented by a small grant from the offertory. Mr. John Derbyshire was re-elected parish warden, and Mr. De Prez was elected sidesrnan. The vicar nominated Mr. Hewitt as his warden. At the conclusion of the business a cordial vote of thanks was passed to the chairman.

div.head: LYMNI.
div.p: LYMNI.

On Tuesday evening the Easter vestry meeting was held at the Parish Church, the rector, the Rev. Canon Gucst, M.A., in the chair. The accounts showed that the receipts for the year amounted to £llB 13s. Od ,and the expenditure to £l2l 18s. 11d. On the motion of Mr. Ross, seconded by Dr. BRABAZON, the accounts were passed. Mr. Callendar was appointed parish warden, and Mr. T. P. Norris rector's warden for the ensuing year. On the motion of Mr. WHITE- LEG, Mr. Henry Pearson and Mr. Richard Smith were ap- pointed delegates for the parish of Lymm for the ensuing year. A vote of thanks to the vicar for presiding, concluded the meeting.

div.head: Git EAT SANKEY,
div.p: Git EAT SANKEY,

There V/A4a good attendance at the usual vestry Meeting of St. Mary's, Great Sankey, held on Monday, the Rev. E. S. Jackson, vicar, presiding. The following officers were appointed :—Mr. John Cook, churchwarden; Mr. J. C. Ridg- way, minister's warden ; sidesmen : Messrs. George Segar, Alexander Thorpe, Henry Woolfall, and Henry Bate. Mr. Jonas Foster and Mr. Peter Boardman were appointed the re- presentatives to the Ruridecanal conference. Mr. GEORGE SEG.IR proposed, and Mr. Jonx Cot:ix seconded, that Mr. James Hayes be appointed sexton. The proposition was unanimously agreed to.

div.head: RUNCORN PARISH CHURCH.
div.p: RUNCORN PARISH CHURCH.

The Runcorn parishioners held their annual vestry meet- ing on Monday morning, at the Parish Church. The Rev. Canon Barclay occupied the chair, and there were also pre- sent the Rev. T. M. Armsou, and Messrs. John Brnndrit, Wm. Whittaker, Peter Briscoe, Wm. Sutton, and Samuel Oxworth.

Mr, BRISCOE moved, and Mr. WHITTAKER seconded a motion, which was passed, to the effect that the church- wardens' accounts be adoptel The statement showed that the receipts from all sources had been £2OO 4s. 7d., inclu- ding a balance of £29 13s. 101. from last year. The ex- penditure had amounted to £143 Is. 10d., leaving a balance in the hands of the churchwardens of £52 2s. 9d. The CHAIRMAN appointed Mr. John Brundrit, J.P., his warden. Mr. BRISCOE moved that Mr. Samuel Crosby be appointed parishioners' warden. Mr. WHITTAKER seconded the motion, and it was passed. Mr. BRIINDRIT nominated Mr. Whittaker as his sides- man.

Mr. WM. SUTTON proposed, and Mr. BRUNDRIT seconded, resolution in favour of Mr. Peter Briscoe being elected parishioners' sidesman, which was carried. On the proposition of Mr. BRISCOE, seconded by Mr. W.U. SUTTON, it was agreed that Mr. John Brundrit and Mr. Wm. Whittaker be elected lay representatives of the parish at the ruridecanal conferences during the ensuing year. Mr. BRISCOE moved, and Mr. WHITTAKER seconded, the following motion : "That the two seats in the chancel, and the seats on the south side of the nave, be rated at £2 each, and the remainder at each." The resolution was passed. Mr. JOHN BRUNDRIT moved, and Mr. BniscoE seconded a proposition, which was agreed to in favour of the ringers being engaged for the ensuing year at the sum of n, to be paid out of the churchwardens' funds, with permission to collect gratuities at Christmas, as heretofore. Mr. BRISCOE moved that the thanks of the meeting be given to the choirmaster and the choir for their efficient services during the past year. Mr. WHITTAKER seconded the resolution, which was carried unanimously. The thanks of the meeting were given to the Chairman for his services, after which the proceedings terminated. It was stated that the total amount of collections at the church during the year had been £297 6s. Bd. HOLY TRINI l'Y, RUNCORN. The annual vestry meeting in connection with this church was held on Monday morning. The Rev. W. Preston presided, and there were also present the Rev. J. D.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 15, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 15, 1882.

Llewollyn (curate), Menrs. Buckley, Buck, Fisher, Smith, Lea, Sefton, Porritt, Annett, Croley, and Rogerson. The CHAIRMAN said they were called uponl first of all, to elect new wardens and sidesmen. He might say that dar- ing the ten years he had been in Runcorn he had been most fortunate in his wardens, having had those who worked well and harmoniously with him. Last year, on the resig- nation of Mr. J. Smith, he invited Mr. J. Buckley to be his ' wardee. After some persuasion Mr Buckley consented, and a most invaluable warden he had proved. He had been assiduous in his duties, active, zealous, and earnest, and had done very much for the benefit of the church, the members of which were most deeply indebted to him. He was happy to say that Mr. Buckley had consented to be his warden again for the ensuing year, and he considered that gentle- man was conferring a favour rather than receiving one, in so doing. As to the people's warden (Mr. Buck) he was an old and valued friendovith;whom he had long "pulled," and was quite willing to pull again, if he was re-elected. The decision of that matter however rested not with the incum- bent, but with the members of the congregation. It was their right to choose whom they thought proper, as they ' were free agents, with legal privileges. If they thought ' well to re-elect his esteemed friend, Mr. Buck, so and well. He would work with him as agreeably as of yore. If they did not re-elect Mr. Buck, but elected another gentleman, he ' had no doubt that he would be able to work amicably with him. Before sitting down, he could not refrain from saying how much he felt the considerate and thoughtful kindness of Mr. Edward Buckley in providing the handsome and ' tasteful woodwork for the wall at the back of the commu- nion table. The congregation owed Mr. Buckley a debt of ' thanks. In conclusion he begged to thank the retiring war- dens and sidesmen for their kind co-operation and assistance daring the year. Mr. LEI said that as Mr. Buck had done his work so effi- ciently during the past year, he begged to propose that he be re-elected people's warden for the ensuing year. ' Mr. Ponnirr seconded the motion.

Mr. SEFTON proposed, as an amendment, that they should elect Mr. Fisher. He did not take this course through any disrespect to Mr. Buck, but simply because he considered it would be an advantage to the church and congregation to have a little "new blood" introduced amongst the officials. The CHAIRMAN said it appeared to be thought that a change would be advantageous, and he had the shadow of doubt that Mr. Fisher weuld make a very good warden. Mr. JoRN SMITH seconded the amendment, and remarked that it was very undesirable to keep one gentleman in the office of warden for so long a period. Such a plan was really unfair to the other members of the congregation who were eligible for election. Five voted for the amendment, and four for the original motion. The amendment was, therefore, declared carried. Mr. SEFTON moved, and Mr. FISHER seconded a vote of thanks to Mr. Buck. The latter observed that their late warden had always taken a very active part in the advance- ment of any measure which had been brought before the managers and officials of the church. The CHAIRMAN said that Mr. Buck had served him very well during the past ten years, and he must admit that he felt a certain "wrench " in parting with an old friend and official, but still he considered it his duty to bow to the wishes of the congregation. The resolution was carried unanimously. Mr. BUCK suitably responded. On the motion of Mr. FISHER, seconded by Mr. SErroN, Mr. Rogerson was unanimously appointed a sidesman. Mr. ROGERSON moved that Mr. Sefton be elected to a similar post, but he declined, and Mr. Croley, after some 'demur, agreed to accept the position. On the proposition of Mr. LEA, seconded by Mr. SMITH, Mr. Timmins was appointed supernumerary sidesman. . .

Mr. BUCK said they all felt- very much obliged to Mr. Edward Buckley for the kindness he had manifested in several ways to the church, and he proposed that they accord him a hearty vote of thanks. Mr. LEA seconded the proposal, which was agreed to. The CHAIRMAN expressed his pleasure at the improve- ment which had lately taken place in the choir, the members of which deserved every praise for their painstaking and ex- cellent singing. Mr. SMITH, in moving a complimentary vote to the choir, which was carried nem dis, said he was highly pleased with their singing on the previous Sunday. Mr. Smith and Mr. Sefton were appointed to examine the accounts, which showed that the sum collected for church expenses this year had been £56 13s. 9-id.' against £63 2s. skd. in the previous 12 months. The total receipts had been £O4 12s. 2d., against an expenditure of £lO2 ss. 3d., leaving a balance due to the wardens of £7 13s. id. The accounts were afterwards passed, on the motion of Mr. FISHER, seconded by Mr. LEA. The CHAIRMAN said that last year it was proposed they should have offertories every Sunday evening; and he re- gretted to say this plan had not paid as well as the former system, which was rather a strange thing. After some conversation upon the subject, it was agreed, on the proposition of Mr. RouEasorr, seconded by Mr. CROLEY, that the collections should in future be made on the first and third Sunday in each month, and that the col- lection by boxes at the door be abolished. Mr. ROGERSON moved, and Mr. LEA seconded a vote of thanks to Mr. Buckley for his gift of the "corona," which bad been placed in the chancel. The CHAIRMAN, on putting the resolution, which was passed, said the gift of Mr. Buckley had enabled him and his assistants to read the lessons with the greatest ease, whereas that was in previous times work nearly sufficient to cause blindness.

A reference was next made by Mr. PRESTON, in highly complimentary terms, to the painting of a number of illu- minated texts, which had been placed round the church by Mr. Annett. The other day a painter was in the edifice, and could hardly be constrained to believe that the pictures were the work of the schoolmaster, thinking they must have been done in London. Mr. Annett was a man with "some go " in him. (Applause.) A vote of thanks was passed to the last named gentleman, on the proposition of Mr. BUCKLEY, seconded by Mr. FISHER.

Mr. PREsrox said he thought he might describe the church as "a very happy family," for they had got on very amieably during the past twelve months. The proceedings concluded with the passing of a vote of thanks to the Chairman for presidiag, on the proposal of Mr. LEA, seconded by Mr. FISHER.

to have a 82parate parish, then a division could be made. The executive committee had taken this matter into careful consideration, and arrived at the conclusions he had men- tioned, but if the parishioners desired to call a meeting to discuss the question, it was quite open to them to do so. Mr. CHADWICK also wished to ask if the parishioners had been consulted, and, if not, whether it was possible to take any steps to prevent this "desecration," as it was called, of the parish church. The CHAIRMAN: In the first place, the parish elected an executive committee, and they have had this point under consideration, amongst others. That is the only answer I can give to the first question. The "constituents" sent their representatives to the committee, and as the matter came before them, the parishioners have already been represented on the question. As to the course which can be taken by the parishioners, that is open to Mr. Chadwick, who has been appointed vestry clerk, to consider. (Slight laughter). Mr. CHADWICK said he was much obliged to the Chair- man for the information he had given, but he did not think it was right that such an important proposal should have been considered in a hole and corner manner. Mr. WHITE: I don't think it has.

The CHAIRMAN said he should not like it to go to the public that this question had been conducted in a hole and corner way. Previous to it being discussed, it was found that the old church was falling into a state which required repair, and he had notes in his possession showing that in a few years the building would have fallen into desuetude; and his predecessor in the office of incumbent when he heard that a certain sum had been spent in repairing the sacred place, said it was not worth the trouble. Under these circumstances, and considering what had taken place in the past, he scarcely thought it was fair to say that the matter had been done in a hole and corner manner.

Mr. BALMER moved a vote of thanks to the parishioners' warden, Mr. Treacy, sen., for his services during the past 12 months. Mr. Treacy's regular attendance had been most marked. (Hear, hear.) Mr. ATHERTON seconded, and the Rev. W. H. DUGGAN supported the motion, which was passed with acclamation. The CHAIRIfIAN remarked that he wished to pay a tribute to the admirable manner in which Mr. J. B. Imison, his own warden, had performed his duties during the year. The readiness of Mr. Imison to help was shown by the interior of their church. (Applause.) He had pleasure in nomina- ting the same gentleman as his warden for the coming year. (Hear, hear.) Mr. BALMER moved that Mr. Treacy, sen., be elected the parishioners' warden, and Mr. WHITE seconded the motion.

Mr. TREACY said he 'Should be gratified if they would not press his nomination, but the meeting insisted. Mr. TREACY, jun., moved, and Mr. DWERRYHOUSE se- conded an amendment in favour of Mr. Lord being ap- pointed; but only the mover and seconder voted for it, and the original motion was carried. • The next business was the eleetion of 16 sidesmen ; and the Chairman nominated the following:—Messrs. Balmer, Kilcross, Hagley, Jones, Chadwick, Treacy, jun., Atherton, and Briscoe.

Mr. CHADwithc : Mr. Chairman, I think it seems rather too much as if it were a case of "You appoint me, and I will appoint you" at this meeting; and I think it would be well to adjourn it so that we might have a larger number present._

The CHAIRMAN said that if Mr. Chadwick would only compare the number present at that meeting, he would ad- mit it was a very large attendance compared with the meet- ings at many other vestries. Mr. BALMER : I think that as the notice has been up for two Sundays, if people are not here, they ought to be. (Hear, hear.) On the motion of Mr. TREACY, senr.r seconded by Mr. TREACY, jour., the following other sidesmen were appointed: —Messrs. Lord, Whittle, Dsverryhouse, Crabtree, Beacham, Lowe, T. Davies, and Farrant.

late vicar was still in the hands of Messrs. Smith and Son, of Chester, who had been unable to dispose of it, whereupon it was moved by Mr. H. LINAKER, and seconded by Mr. John ASLITON, that Messrs. Smith and Son be requested to return the cloth to Dr. Robinson, churchwarden, who was authorised to dispose of it to the best advantage. ACCOUNTS.—Messrs. J. Pollard and Thomas Davies were deputed to audit the accounts and on their recom'imendation the same were adopted. The following is a summary of the accounts viz. :—Receipts: Balance in hand, £l6 us. lOid.; collections, £BO Os: 3d.; parochial tea, £l9 16s. 2d.; total, £ll6 Ss. 3A-d. Payments: Standing salaries £43 12s. Od. ' • maintenance of divine service £l3 ss. ; sundries, £lO Ss. 9d.; balance in hand, 5:49 2s. 2d.; total, £ll6 Bs. 30.

ENLARGEMENT OF THE BURIAL GROUND.—The Com- mittee appointed at the Easter meeting in 1881, to receive the report of Messrs. Ashton and Garratt, as to the formation of a banal board in accordance with the resolution of the the sth May, 1879, and to consider the advisability of such resolution being still adhered to, presented a report containing the following offers by Mr. W. Hayes, of Ashton Hayes, and Mr. E. A. Wright, of Castle Park, Frodsham :—Mr. W. Hayes, offer :—Ashton Hayek Chester, Mar. 29th, 1882,—Dear Mr. Blogg,—Years ago when I told Mr. Ashton to close with Lord Cholmondeley fcr Harrison's garden for £4O, it was simply that I knew the parish would want it. I thought it too good a chance to miss, not however with any intention to give it to the parish, and if the Burial Board had gone on as subsequently arranged, of course they would have found the money. Should you decide to annex it to the church yard, I shall be glad to subscribe £4O towards your outlay, and trust some scheme will be adopted for the yard to be cared for. I am, yours truly, (signed) WM. HAYES.—Mr. Wright's offer (copy)—Whereas the vicar and churchwardens of Frodsham having acquired from the Marquis of Cholmondeley a piece. of land containing about 3,337 superficial square yards for the purpose of enlarging the bunal ground attached to the parish church as depicted in the plan here- upon endorsed and it is computed that a sum of about £iiso will 4e required for the purpose of draining and build- ing a boundary wall, and in other respects making ths said land suitable for the purpose aforesaid, and in consideration of the premises Edward Abbott Wright, of Castle Park, in this parish, undertaker, to contribute the said sum of .£250 on the following conditions, namely :—That there shall be reserved in perpetuity to the said Edward Abbott Wright, his heirs, executors, administrators, and assigns, the exclu- sive right of interment of themselves, and for such others ' as they may direct in the piece of ground indicated on the said plan, cont ining 313 square yards. That the Church Resto- ratioa Committee be empowered to carry into effect without avoidable delay the drainage and other works necessary. That if there remain any surplus after the necessary expen- diture on the land herein referred to such surplus be applied to the improvement of the present burial ground in such manner as the committee deem proper. That this document be deposited with the parish muniments and a copy thereof be entered in the minutes of the vestry, and it is submitted as an urgent recommendation to the vicar and church- wardens that a plan be made for regulating the position of the graves with reference numbers and that a record be kept of all interments therein. As witness my hand this 10th day of April, 1182. (Signed) E. A. WRIGNT.—The com- mittee recommended that the resolution as to the formation of a burial board passed sth May, 1879, be rescinded, and that the offers of Mr. Hayes and Mr. Wright ba accepted. The committee recorded their opinion that such offers were most liberal, and would relieve the parish of a great difficulty and expense. A discussion ensued as to the conveyance of the land re- quired for burial ground from the Marquis of Cholmondeley, during which it was stated by Mr. Ashton that an under- taking to convey the land had been entered into on the 9th January, 1877, in consideration of the payment by the churchwardens of £4O, and the hearse-house (which formerly stood in Overton, opposite the church) being conveyed to the Marquis of Cholmondeley. The resolution passed by the vestry on the sth May 1879, relating to the formation of a burial board was rescinded, and it was unanimously resolved that the hand- some offers of Mr. Hayes and Mr. Wright be accepted with thanks. -

HOWHY-LANE FOOTPITU.—Mr. Wright, of Castle Park, Frodsham, produced an agreement which had been entered into between himself and Mr. Rigby, in which the footpath from Honey-lane to the hills was reserved to the public in perpetuity. The footpath in question is in substitution for a footpath which formerly divided Mr. Rigby's property, arid Mr. Wright had obtained the agreement, as it was proposed to do away with the footpath altogether, a course which Mr. Wright explained he had opposed in the interests of the public and for priyate reasons. It was resolved that a record be placed upon the minutes that the agreement was pro- duced to the meeting, and the document was ordered to be deposited in the parish chest. Penisyr CHARlTlES.—Harrison's Charity: This charity consists of £lOO which was invested by the late Mr. Har- rison for the benefit of the widows in Overton and Bradley. The account produced showed that 17 widows had received 3s. 9d. each from the trustees, the total amount paid being a 3s. Pd.—Organ Fund: The Vicar reported that the balance in the hands of the trustees was £7l 83., and this sum had been handed over to the Church Restoration Com- mittee, to be applied to the organ fund, which now amounted to £365, but the committee were anxious to raise the wind to the tune of £3OO more.—Overton Sunday School: The accounts produced showed a deficit of £1 143. 911—Gram- mar School: The cash book of the feoffees of this school was produced. The accounts relating to the Frodsham and Stockham Charity, the Girls' and Infant School, and the Provident Club, were not produced.

RESTORATION OF THE PARISH CHURCEL—The Restora- tion Committee presented a report, from which we extract the following :—Since the committee pre- sented their report at the last Easter meeting considerable progress has been made in the work of restoration, and in order to lay before the parishioners a comprehensive ac- count of the state of the work at the present time it has been deemed best to obtain from the architects a special re- port. For this purpose Mr. Bodley visited the church on the 22nd and 23rd March, and his report is appended here- to.—Heating: It is intended to warm the church by means of hot water pipes, the furnace being placed in the vault under the south chancel aisle, and for this purpose the com- mittee have entered into a contract with Mr. Charles Seward, of Preston, amounting to £145 155., which is exclusive of masonry and brickwork. Lighting: Preparation will be made for laying on gas when required ; the architects recommending side lights or brackets in preference to pendants or standards, and this the committee fully approve of. It is proposed to suspend the brass candelabra which swung from the chancel arch, either in the same place or in the chancel.—Organ.—A sub-committee has been formed for the purpose of considering the question of a new organ, and recommending builders who should be asked to tender for the work. A specification for a three manual organ has been decided upon, and some half dozen tenders obtained, and it now only remains to choose a builder. This, however, will not be done until the committee, accompanied by Mr. Riley, the organist of the parish church, have in- spected some of the organs manufactured by the parties who have sent in tenders. It is proposed to place the organ in the easternmost bay of the north aisle, with a vestry for the clergy behind; the corresponding bay on the south side not being considered so'suitable. It may not be out of place here to appeal for subscriptions to this fund, as a large sum is still required to meet the contemplated outlay of about £650, the available funds at present amounting to some £364 17s. sd. MEMORIAL WINDOW.—Mrs. Pickering has very generously provided funds amounting to £4OO (which stands to a separate account in Parr's Bank) to place a stained glass window in the east of the chancel, to the memory of the late Robert Wainwright Ashley and John Rigby Pickering, the subject being the Ascension. Messrs. Burdeson and Grylls, of London, are preparing a design for this. GENERAL—Every effort is being made to push on the work, which to an outsider may appear to progress slowly, but in a restoration of this kind with old walls not in a very good. condition to begin with, many things occur which ace quite unexpected, and, in order to make a satisfactory job, greater outlay has to be incurred and more time taken. It is proposed to complete the interior of • the chancel in the first instance, so far as to render it fit for divine service, all out- side decoration &c. being left for the present. This latter remark applies more particularly to the tower, porches, and emb tttlements on the north aisle, &c. Should the work make satisfactory progress during the spring and summer, it is hoped that the church may be re-opened in the autumn. The state of the finances will be seen on reference to the summary account given below. The bazaar which was held in August last, despite the unpropitious state of the weather, realized the handsome sum of £BlO 14s. 6d., and a sale of work left on hand will be held on the 11th and 12th April by which it is expected a considerable sum will be added to the funds. Subscriptions amounting to £5,742 Os. 7d. have been promised, of this sum £5,208 12s. 7d. has been paid to the treasurer, and it is estimated that at least another £l,OOO over and above that already promised will be required to fully complete the restoration. The committee, whilst thankfully acknowledging much generous aid, think that they are justified in making a more special appeal to the parishioners in order that all may feel that they have bad a share in the restoration of their parish church. The follow- ing is a summary of the accounts, viz. :—Receipts : £6,219 lls. 11d. Payments: Clerk of works, £317 3s. Bd.; private rights, £75 ; dismantling, £BO Os. 60. Rebuilding: Labour, £2,167 16s. 1111 ; materials, £709 10s. ; contracts for roof, £750; sundries, £3l 18s. sd. ; watching, £ll Os. 6d; total payments, £4,151 19s. 10d., leaving a balance in hand of £2,067 12s. id. The architect's report contained a detailed account of the present state and progress of the work and also particulars and estimated cost of work re- quired to thoroughly restore and beautify the "church.—lt was moved by Mr. Thomas Riley, seconded by Mr. H. Linaker, and resolved that the above reports be printed at the expense of the vestry and a copy thereof fozwarded to each subscriber to the restoration fund. CHURCHWARDENS.—A vote of thanks was accorded to the churchwardens for their services during the past year, and the Vicar again appointed Mr. John Ashton as inner warden, and Dr. Robinson was unanimously re-appointed parish- ioners' warden for the'ensuing year. It was decided to adjourn the meeting to the Bth proximo at three o'clock in the afternoon. A cordial vote of thanks to the Vicar for presiding brought the meeting to a close.

There is nothing more nourishing and warming in cold weather than a cup of really good Cocoa, but the difficulty has been to obtain it pure. This may be secured at a cost of one halfpenny for a large breakfast cup by using Cadbury's Cocoa Essence, which goes three times as far as the adulterated and starchy compounds ordinarily sold, the smallest ps,3kut making fowteen breakfast cups of strong Cocoa.--,Advt.

div.p: WIDNES PARISH CHURCH.
LAY REPRESENTATIVES.
Mr. BALMER moved and Mr. TREACY, senr., seconded proposition in favour of re-electing Messrs. James White and John Matthews as lay representatives for the ensuing year which was carried.

div.head: VESTRY CLERIC.
div.p: VESTRY CLERIC.
Mr. Chadwick was appointed vestry clerk on the motion of Mr. TREACY, junr.
THE SITTING ACCOMMODATION.

Mr. TREACY, junr., moved that the Church Council should at the earliest possible day, take into consideration some means of increasing the accommodation 't St. Mary's, either by providing additional seats, or making the church altogether free and unappropriated. Mr. CHADWICK had pleasure in seconding the motion. He had no intention of going over the same ground as last year; and his object in seconding the proposition was merely to keep the matter alive. A scheme with which he had had some little connection might ultimately meet the matter to a great extent. The resolution was passed unanimously. THE NEW CHURCH.

The CHAIRMAN, in reply to a question, said the present depression in trade was holding back the hands of those who were working in connection with the new church; but he thought it probable that the work of erecting the edifice would be commenced in about two months.

A vote of thanks was paf_ised to the Chairman, after which the proceedings terminated. We append the detailed account of the churchwardens for the year :—Receipts: To amount received from offertories (id. added to cancel id. in previous balance sheet), £Bl 5s 10d; to subscriptions received on account of vicarage land, £4O; to net proceeds of annual tea party (as per balance sheet), £39 9s 4d; to ground rent (less income tax), £5 193 3d; to J. Jessop drawback from salary on account of church cleaning (52 weeks at 2s), £5 4s; total, £l7l 18s 51d. Ex-1 penditure : By balance from previous year, £l6 6s 4id; by amount of rent of vicarage land paid Mr. S. White (as per receipt), £4O; by amount of church expenses for current year, £96 3s 7d; by balance in hand of wardens at close of year, £l9 8s ; total, £l7l 18s 51d. REPAIR FUND.—Receipts: To churchwarden Imison for cash advanced by him to pay drainage account, £35 17s 4d; to balance (see credit side), £l9 Os 8d; total, £54 18s old. Expenditure: By balance (as per printed sheet), viz., Churchwarden liaison for cash advanced, £l7 12s 8d; by churchwardens for cash advanced by them, £1 8s Op ; by Henry Mather for drainage of churchyard (as per account rendered), £35 17s 4d; total, £54 18s OP. MR. J. B. IMISON IN ACCOUNT WITH CHURCHWARDENS, 1881-82.—T0 balance in hand of wardens at close of present year paid him on account (as per resolution of vestry, 10th April, 1882), £l9 8s ; to balance (due to Mr. Imison), £34 is ; total, £53 103. By repair fund No. 2 for cash advanced by him, £l7 12s 8d; by repair fund No. 2 for cash advanced (drainage account), £35 17s 41; total, £53 10s.

div.head: HALTON VESTRY MEETING.
div.p: HALTON VESTRY MEETING.

The annual Easter vestry meeting of the parish of Halton, was held on Tuesday evening, in the vestry of the church, and afterwards by adjournment to the girls' school, accor- ding to due notice. The meeting was called for seven o'clock, when the old custom of ringing the church bell was again carried out. The vicar (Rev. J. Lockwood) occupied the chair. The churchwardens, Messrs. Joseph Stokes and Joseph Wallworth Baguley, presented their accounts for the past year, which showed a small balance in hand after pay- ing for everything. The church ley for the year realized £66 7s. W., and the collections £53, besides nearly £3O in support of the choir fund. The wardens for the past two years retired from office, and their places were filled by Mr. Thomas Fletcher Acton, of Sanley Wood, as vicar's warden, and Mr. Daniel Tinsley Baguley, of Stockham, as parishioners' warden. To show their continued interest in the church, Messrs. Stokes and Baguley accepted the offices as -representatives of the parish at the Ruridecanal con- ference. Mr. Albert Woodier, of Halton, and Mr. John Ackerley, of Astmoor, were appointed sidesmen for the ensuing year. The vicar and wardens' kcal charity had been duly distributed, and the accounts audited and found correct. Votes of thanks to the various office-bearers of the last year, and to the chairman for presiding, brought the meeting to a happy close.

div.head: FARNWORTH PARISH CHURCH.
div.p: FARNWORTH PARISH CHURCH.

The parishioners of Farnworth Parish Church held their annual vestry meeting on Monday. The Rev. G. Bond pre- sided, and there were present :—Rev. S. A. Spooner, Major Cross, and Messrs. Eustace Carey, John Brock, J.W.Davies, W. B. Longton, Matthew Taylor, R. Kidd, A. Speakman, Allen, Glover (Cronton), Taylor (Cuerdley), Minton, Mercer, Goff, Hauncle, S. Kidd, and J. Williams.—The accounts, which were passed on the motion of Major CROSS, seconded by Mr. A. SPEAKMAN, stated that the total income for the past year amounted to £l2B 10s. Op. Of this sum £53 10s. 101-d. was from collections for church expenses, and £5O 13s. 7d. from collections for church repairs. The balance in hand was, including some items not yet collected, £4B 12s. 4d.—Mr. Whalley was elected warden for Bold, and the CHAIRMAN, in appointing Mr. Henry Brunner, Vicar's warden, remarked that Mr. Brunner was at present away, and he really did not know what they should have done without the services of Mr. Allen. For the office of warden I for Crouton there was nominated Mr. W. B. Longton.—Mr. HAUNCLE remarked that Mr. Longton was quite a lad and not the person to be placed in such a position, whereupon Mr. W. B. LONGTON proposed that Mr. Glover, the retiring warden, be elected to the post.—The CHAIRMAN observed that the Longton family might be said to have held the office of churchwarden for Cronton from one generation to another. They were deeply indebted to them for what they had done for the school, and the assistance they had ren- dered in other parochial matters.—The resolution was then plat, and Mr. Longton was unanimously appointed.—Major Cross, Messrs. J. H. Davies, H. Roberts, Glover, and Long- ton' were appointed sidesmen.—Mr. BROCK called attention to the state of the Church tower, observing that unless the parish found the money the tower would tumble down some fine morning. The bells wanted turning, and the striking bell was cracked.—lt was understood that a special vestry meeting would be called at some future date to consider the matter.—On the motion of Mr. MATTHEW TAYLOR, seconded by Mr. Kinn, Messrs. Brock and Whalley were appointed lay representatives of the church at the arehidiaconal con- ference.—The following, viz., Messrs. E. Carey, R. Mercer, J. Valentine, J. Goff, A. Speakman, T. Minton, Barker, D. Foster, Johnson, Neil, and W. Newton were appointed sides- men for St. Ambrose Church.—This terminated the business. FRODSHAM PARISH CHURCH. The annual Easter meeting was held at the Parish Church on Monday, when an adjournment was mole to the boys' school, Overton. The following were present at the meet- ing, viz. :—Rev. H. B. Blogg, vicar, in the chair, Messrs. John Ashton and John Robinson, churchwardens, E. A. Wright. Charles Reynolds, H. Linaker, C. E. Linaker, Thomas Davies, Thomas Lewis, Thomas Riley, Henry They, Ralph Bate, Thomas Gorst, Joseph Cunnah, Joseph Knibb, Samuel Davies, Robert Andrews, John Pollard, Samuel Aston, 11. Milner and J. Milner. Mr. J. Ashton (churchwarden), reported that the btack cloth used for. draping the church after the death of the

div.head: annual vestry meeting was held on Monday evening, when the Rev. J. Wright-Williams, the vicar, occupied the chair.
div.p: The annual vestry meeting was held on Monday evening, when the Rev. J. Wright-Williams, the vicar, occupied the chair.

ACCOUNTS. The churchwardens' accounts were presented, and showed that the church expenses for the year had been £B5 53. lota., proceeds of annual tea party £39 9s. 4d., ground rent £5 193. 3d., subscriptions in payment of ground rent for land adjoining the vicarage £4O, making a total, with other items, of £l7l 18s. 51. The credit side of the sheet stated that the balance against the wardens at the beginnikg of the year was £l6 163. 41d., and there had been spent for general. purposes £95 133. 71-A. The balance in favour of the wardens at the close of the year was £l9 Bs. SP. Mr. CHADWICK moved the adoption of the accounts, and said he considered them extremely satisfactory, when they took into consideration the fact that at the commence- ment of the year there was a balance against the wardens of LIG.
Mr. JAMES WHITE seconded the motion, and it was agreed to.

It was then proposed by Mr. WHITE-, seconded by Mr. CRABTREE, and carried, that in acc4rdance with a previous understanding at the Church Council, the balance in hand should be trangerred to the treasurer of the repairs fund

Mr. CIWAVICK said ho had a matter of great importance to bring before the parishioners. He had lately read a re- port in one of the Liverpool newspapers of a meeting at which the Lord Bishop presided—he believed it was one connected with the Diocesan Church Building Society. He noticed that the Bishop spoke very strongly about the inade- quate church sitting accommodation in the diocese, and he illustrated his remarks by a reference to Widnes, in which parish it seemed the parishioners numbered 16,000, whilst there was only a miserable chapel, with sittings for 420 to accommodate them. The Bishop went on to say be was I glad to saw that land had been given for the erection of a church by the trustees of the Leigh estate, on which it was expected that a building would be erected at some future time, which would accommodate a considerable num- I ber of people; and when that was done, the present parish church would become merely a chapel of ease to the new building. What he (the speaker) wished to know was, whether the parishioners could take any steps which would prevent the present church becoming a mere chapel of ease to the new edifice.

The CHAIRMAN expressed a slight regret that Mr. Chad- wick had not spoken to him upon this question privately before bringing it under the notice of a public meeting pf ' parishioners, as it was known that he was always wilting and ready to answer any questions in reference to matters connected with their church. The speaker promised to reply at a later period of the meeting, when he did so by saying that the Bishop had merely stated what he (Mr. Wright-Williams) believed would be the case. The present church at West Bank was one of the most ruinous in the country, possessing a roof which was con- stantly tumbling in. It would be a most unconrteous and unfair thing to the comparatively sparse inhabitants of West Bank, that they should be called upon to entirely sup- port the present building; for if it were decided to divide the parish, such a proceeding • would simply be taking away three-quarters of a•parish to make a new one, and leaving the one-fourth to support St. Mary's in its regular working expenses. They would have observed that the accounts pre- sented at that evening's meeting showed that the whole j body of the parish found it work enough to support the ! church. He had made diligent enquiry into this matter, having consulted the Bishop, the registrar, and several other gentlemen, and they all expressed the opinion that it would be a most unfortunate thing if St. Mary's were cut off at all. He wished to remind them that the proposed chane would be no advantage at all to him; but they must, he thought, admit that it would be a very unfortunate thing for St. Mary's to be cut off, as the building was decreasing in value every day, for obvious reasons. To fasten an old, tumbling-down church entirely upon the people at West Bank, and say that they must support it, would be most un- fair. If the new Parish Church were put on the ground in- tended for the site, and a distinct district formed, not one man in West Bank would have the right to say "That is my church," and they could only attend it upon sufferance. It, however,the parish remained as it was now, and the new build- ing was niacin the Parish Church, then the church at West Bank would be worhed just in the same manner as heretofore- and if the West Bank people afterwards thought they ought

div.head: AMATEUR DRAMATIC
div.p: AMATEUR DRAMATIC
PERFORMANCES AT LATCHFORD.

On Tuesday. and Wednesday evenings last dramatic per- formances were held in Christ Church school-room, Latch- ford, on behalf of the fund being collected for the extension. of the schools. The entertainment was got up by Mr. John White, who, at his own expense, we are informed, caused a very compact and convenient stage, with appropriate scenery, to be erected in the school-room. The pieces selected for representation were " Bombastes Furioso," " Ici on parle Francais," and "Popping the Question " (by the late J. B. Buxton), in which the fotlowing ladies and gentlemen took their respective parts :—Mr. John White, Mr. Dun, Mr. Finlay Dun, Mr. Thurnam, Mr. H. Roscoe, and the ladies, Miss Margaret E. Woods' Miss Constance Broadbent, Miss A. L. Robinson, Miss M. Roscoe, and Miss Nellie Roscoe. The musical portion of the entertainment was conducted most ably by Mr. and Mrs. John Reylolds, Mr. Frank, and Mr. E. Reynolds. Alderman Joseph Harrison, who acted as prompter, came before the curta!n and recited the following prologue, which, we are informed, was written by him for the occasion. It seemed to be well appreciated by the audience and created a good deal of amusement. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, 'fis said that "all tha world's a stage;" then he who treads thereon Must either play himself, or he must be played upon. To play to-night, then, we're resolved, for a noble thing of use, Which necessitates no prelude, and calls for no excuse. We seek alone sincerely our Vicar's work to aid; And if we are successful, then all our labour's paid. Your hands now being emptied for that noble Christian cause No doubt you'll kindly welcome us withyour esteemed applause. To win your praise is our intent, nor deprecate your blame; For what we do is humbly done, in education's name. We ask not of your charity to benefit ourselves; He needs it not who earnestly but labours, digs, and delves. We ask it only for the children—that poor boy or girl, That they may better battle with life's warfare and its whirl. 'fie education, we are told, that forms the youthful mind; Just as "the twig is bent," 'tis said, just so " the tree's inclined.'' Then intellect and culture we cannot well ignore, But to debase the moral feeling, and dishonour it the more. All this you know as well as we, and to dissipate your fears, We seek to move your mirth to-night, not to invoke your tears. Bombastes Furioso first in order makes his bow, Between whom and the " King " there'll be a sanguinary row. Not on the" hazard of a die "Born' sets his life, like "Mr. Toots," • But like St. Crispin, cavalierly, on theidisplacement of his boots. " Mr. Spriggins " next presents himself in Ici on parle Francais, Or " French before breakfast," learnt in a novel kind of way. The fiery Major Reg. Rattan, poor " Spriggins's " beta stoic, he And the lovely Angelina, et hoc genus mune, With " Dubois " included. She, the burden of his song, Will amuse you with their laughter, "side splitting" contra temps. "Popping the question" next in order comes, an ever welcome theme • Of which bachelors love to talk about, and ladies love to dream 'Twill afford you all the "Sport that wrinkled care derides " And involve you in that laughter, which Milton says, " Hair's both its sides," Pope says that" Hope eternal, in the human breast cloth spring," A pretty tuneful sentiment, with a pleasant truthful ring, So we have hoped, and not in vain, or your patronage to- night. We've got it, and your money too, so in that respect we're right. Our modest efforts to augm-,nt, the auriferous little store, Of what the "Vicar" needs so much, jut hinted at before, ** Videlicit." s. d., those useful little tools. With which he may manipulate the completion of his schools. But I find I mu-t away, as our goad friends behind, Are anxiousall toplay their parts, and hoping that you'll find Your wiiling cultivated ears charmed to-night, for certain, By the • Raynoldsonian" orchestra, you see before the curtain. From which 'tis prove 1, sweet music flows, 11 cadences harmun'ous,
In strains as from ' Apollo's Lute," to sooth the most censorious, And you may be pleased to know, we all our own expenses pay, Not a stiver will be taken, from the proceeds of the play,
So our nests me shall not feather, nor has it been our aim, _ _ _

Then, I think with rne you will agree, t'svill be a " paying grime." Both for us, and our good Vicar, whose credit sure is pledg'd For a dozen score of pounds or more, e'en so it is alleg'd, That in sterling win is wanted, so the village gossip runs, And entre 710 US, the Vicar has already had the •4 Duns." Debt clinging to the Parsons, smells nct sweet like the "Laburnum," Turns their reputations sombre, then " White," let's try and " Thurnam." These are "puns," I should observe, as else you might not know it, For in the names, as they're applied, there's little wit to show it. The ladies' names we dare not" pun," he who'd presume to do it Would meet a retribution just, to make him quickly rue it. A "Broad bent "ash plant from the "Woods," on shoulders he would suffer, For "Robin's son" with vigour would-well lay it on the duffer, Until he cried peccam and sheved devout contrition, Kissed Roscoe's law of evidence, in proof of his submission. _ _

But, Aevenons a nos moutons, from which I have digress-ed, The Vicar's aim in this good cause, like "Mercy is twice blessed." This debt for school- extensions, was not incurred at random, He merits not, a Capias ad satisfaciendum ! Which means in more familiar words, a residence in "Limbo," Whera he until the debt be paid, might sit with arms skim)); Then if our aim accomplish'd be, our warmest wish is won, Your greatest pleasure w,rfected,_our simple duty done. _ _

And now my doggereriended, of which you've had enough, Fr me thinks I bear a muttering, "Tis'nt worth a pinch of snuff!' But in kindn,ss you've endured me, I, in gratitude retire, May you spend a pleasant evening. Au revoir ! Au revoir ! There was a numerous and fashionable audience assembled on both evenings. The performance commenced with " Bombastes Furioso," with :Mr. Dun as "Bombastes," a character he sustained with great ability. Mr. John White was hardly less successful as " Fusbos," Mr. Finlay Dun as "King Artaxominous," had a commanding appearance, and his performance was much enhanced by a pleasant and powerful voice. Miss Margaret E. Woods as " Distaffina " looked and acted in a charming manner, and her singing was no less so. This was followed by "Ici on parle Francais." Mr. John White took the character of "Spriggins," to which he did ample justice, and created roars of laughter every time he appeared on the stage. The character of "Victor Dubois" the Frenchman, was sustained by Mr. Dun with considerable ability. The "Major Regulus Rattan "was sustained by Mr. Finlay Dun on the whole very fairly. Miss Constace Broadbent played the part of "Julia," wife of "Major Rattan," with great confidence and sweetness, under the very em- barrassing situations in which she was placed. Miss Mar- garet E. Woods did full justice to the character of "Mrs. Spriggins ;" her acting was worthy of an accomplished pro- fessional. Miss A. L. Robinson as "Anna Maria," the ser- vant of all work to "Spriggins," was irresistibly amusing. 'Miss N. Roscoe as the charming "Angelina," daughter of Mrs. Spriggins was played in an appropriate and lady- like manner. The performance of this piece was a great success. The amusing little comedy "Popping the ques- tion," by J. B. Buxton, was beautifullytdressed and some of the situations were very funny. Mr. Primrose, the old bachelor, was represented by Mr. W. D. Thurnam, and although he played in a gentlemanly quiet manner, as was no doubt intended by the author, still we think he was much too quiet and undemonstrative. The same may be said of the character of "Henry Thornton," represented by Mr. Henry Roscoe. Miss Nellie Roscoe as "Ellen Murray," the affianced of "henry Thornton," had not much to do. but what she did, was done intelligently, and with good taste. The same is also true of Miss M. Roscoe's "Bobbin," the ladies' maid, and the performance of Miss Constance Broad- bent as " Miss Winterblossom," and Miss A. L. Robinson, as "Miss Biffin," the two antique rivals for the hand of Mr. Primrose," both of whom, by a ludicrous mistake believed that they were respectively the especial objects of his affection, until he undeceived them, amid a storm of abuse, that his affec- tion was fixed upon his ward "Ellen Murray," and upon neither of them ; whilst "Ellen Murray" repudiated "Mr. Henry Primrose" as she all along meant to marry" Henry Thornton," to whom, in fact, she was then already married. The scene between the two venerable spinsters in Mr. Prim- rose's drawing room, when he informed them that he would as soon have thought of marrying Adam's grandmother as either of them, was highly entertaining, and brought down upon his head their combined fury. The acting of these two young ladies was strikingly good. The scene between them before the arrival of Mr. Primrose was full of the most laughable equivcque. It would be both difficult and invidious to say which was the best. The two evenings' performances were a very great success, and the pecuniary result we should hope will also be Satisfactory.

div.head: WARRINGTON POLICE COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON POLICE COURT.

SATURDAY.—Before Alderman Burgess and Alderman Chandley. A COMBATIVE TRAMP.—John Davies, a tramp, who said he was on his way from Cardiff to Leicester, was charged with disorderly conduct in the workhouse, and with using threats to James Curry, the porter.—On Thurs- day night at 9-30 the prisoner presented himself at the work- house with a ticket he had received at seven o'clock. The porter charged him with being drunk, when the prisoner pulled off his coat and " swore" he would " stick" Mr. Curry with a knife. He afterwards ran about the street to find a brick, with which he intended to batter Mr. Curry. With the aid of an inmate named George Oldcroft, Mr. Curry seized the prisoner, with the intention of taking him to the police station. The prisoner was very rough, and it was with difficulty be could be made to walk along. In Scotland-road be threw himself to the ground, and a crowd of men and women gathered round, and rescued him. He was afterwards captured in Buttcrmarket-street.—The pri- soner with great volubility accused Mr. Curry cf roughly using him, but not having questioned the statement of a witness, he was committed to gaol for 14 days with hard labour.

MILITARY DESERTION.—James Hennessy, alias John O'Brien, was charged with being a deserter from the 103rd regiment of foot stationed at Salford.—The prisoner pleaded guilty.—lt appeared that when passing on Manchester-road on tlae previous day. P.S. Spinks observed the pilsoner, whose regimentals were torn, and who seemed to have travelled some distance. The sergeant apprehended him on suspicion of being a deserter, when the prisoner admitted that he had climbed the barracks wall at Salford on Thurs- day.—He was remanded to Regent-road Barracks, Salford.
