div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD. The monthly, and last meeting of this Board as lately 'tonstituted, was held on Tuesday afternoon, at the room in Alforde-street. Major Cross presided, and there were also present Messrs. E. Carey, B. Brown, F. H. Pankhurst, F. Heyes, H. Gaskell, jr, Ti Handley, D. Forster, Dr. O'Keeffe, Dr. Booth, T. Shuttleworth, John Mathews, W. H. Kershaw, J. T. Allen (clerk), and J. Dickson (nuisance inspector.) WIDNES SCIENCE AND ART CLASSES. A communication was read from Mr. Jos. Morrison, hon. secretary of the Scienco and Art Classes, stating that owing to the very large number of students they had this year, they would not be able to find accommodation for them in their class-rooms at the examination, and asking for the use of one of the rooms belonging to the Board. Mr. KERSHAW said he could only say that if the students made as much noise as they did on the previous Monday night, in the room above the Board-room, it would be out- rageous. They acted "more like a lot of bicyclists than anything else," and they had to send up to ask them to be quiet. Mr. HETES : I have heard that before, and also that they take lessons in dancing. Mr. CARRY : What time was it? Mr. KERSHAW : Between six and seven. Mr. CAREY : The lecture does not begin until half-past
six. The CHAIRMAN : What reply shall be sent? Mr. KERSHAW : I think I should let them have the use of

the room they require. Mr. Kershaw's suggestion was adoptel • THE LEVEL CROSSING NUISANCE. The CHAIRMAN read a letter from the London and North- Western Railway Company, stating that the directors had ordered certain woras to be carried out which would,in their judgment, tend to reduce the traffic at the Waterloo-road level crossing. Mr. KERSHAW said representations had been made to the committee to the affect that the railway committee intended to put down more sidings at Carter House, and remove the water tank nearer to Ditton, so that much of the traffic would be taken from the crossing. The letter just received did not, howerer, state what alterations where to be executed. He thought they should know this. It was agreed that the railway company should be written to, as to the alterations they intended making. GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE—IMPORTANT STATEMENT AS TO FUEL CONTRACTS. The minutes of the Gas and Water Committee stated that the illuminating quality of the gas during the month had averaged 16 59 candles. Mr. GASEELL, junior, moved the adoption of the minutes, and called attention to the fuel contracts which had been concluded by the Board. At present the committee were in the habit of using coal for the boiler fires, which he con- sidered to be a great mistake, as £375 per year might be saved by the use of slack. Ile did not think any private firm in Widnes used coal for such a purpose; and he hoped that their successors in the management of the Board's busi- ness would give this matter their careful consideration. 111,r. BROWN seconded the motion which was passed. HEALTH COMMITTEE. This committee's minutes contained the report of the Medical Officer of Health, which showed that during the month there had been 101 births, or 48-4 per 1,000, and 35 deaths, being at the rate of 16-8 per LODI 1 hey included 14 of children under one year, or 6.72 ner 1,000, and six of children between one and five years. Pour persons had died from zymotic diseases. The Nuisance Inspector (Mr. Dick- son) had caused the following bad food to be destroyed :- 3061bs onions, 569 oranges, and 81 apples. The committee having failed to obtain the consent of the property owners for the cleaning of certain unadopted streets, it was recom- mended that the committee take steps to have the thorough- fares properly made, with a view to their adoption. The market bye-laws, as approved, were ordered to be printed. The market receipts for March were £lB 15s. sd.' being an increase of £2 10 2d. on the corresponding period of last year. Mr. CAREY moved the adoption of the minutes, which was seconded by Mr. MATTHEWS, and agreed to. The suggestion of Mr. CAREY that the Window Plant Association should be allowed to keep loam at the market, to be supplied to appli- cants by Mr. Shepherd, in his spare time, was approved. HUTCHINSON'S TRUSTEES AND THE BOARD.—MR. COPLAND'S POSITION. The minutes of the joint Highway and Health Committee, were passed, on the motion of Mr. CAREY, seconded by Mr. HEYES. A letter has been received from Messrs. Part, Wood- cock, and Co., solicitors, offering to leave the question in dispute with the Board and the Hutchinson trustees, to a valuer to be mutually agreed upon. It was resolved that the offer be accepted, and the legal firm above named in- formed that the Board would agree to either of the following surveyors being selected as arbitrator :—Mr. H. Linaker, Frod- sham ; Mr A. Hanson, or Mr J. M. Wilson, surveyors, both of St. Helens.—lt was also recommended that Mr. Copland heap- pointed re!sident enginee!, in accordanv, with the specificam tiot,l for the §ewerage lChrn, r spare dine to be tilted up '..11 the office work as usual. Mr. SaurnEwouTtc wished to know if Mr. Higginson would still hold the post of surveyor to the scheme? Mr. CAREY replied that the recommendation of the joint committee had been in accordance with the specification, which distinctly stated that a resident engineer, with certain duties, should be appointed. The specification was upon the table and Mr. Shuttleworth could see it, if he wished to do so. 'Mr. Copland had had a great deal to do with drawing up the plans, and as he knew as much about the matter as any one, the committee considered he was just the man for the appointment. The CHAIRMAN observed that the resident engineer woeld be simply an assistant to Mr. Higginson. 'Mr. Copland would have charge of the works, but Mr. Higginson would have the full power of determining what should be done, accerding to the specification, and he would also have to endorse the certificates.

div.head: HOSPITAL.
div.p: THE HOSPITAL.

These minutes showed that a donation of £4 Os. Id. from the Workmen's Club at Messrs. Sullivan and Co.'s, had been forwarded by Mr. J. Brock, J.P. The following is a list of books, &c., presented to the hos- pital since August, 1881, to March, 1882. Books, Miss Harriet Mather, Rev. Michael Ryan, Mr. T. Whitby. Maga- zines, Miss Deacon, Good Words for 1881, and Mrs. Cooper, the Christian. Copies of the local papers, from the pro- prietors. Mr. H. Wade-Deacon, Illustrated London News and Graphic. Mr. Whitby, Christian Herald. Dr. McLen- nan, papers. Flowers, Mrs. Kenr, Mrs. Thompson, Mrs. Johnson, Mrs. Pattison, Miss Mather, Mr. Gossage, Mr. Jno. " Owen, and Dr. McDonnell. Fruit and vegetables, Mr. T. Whitby and Mr. Gossage. Evergreens, at Christmas' from a friend, and Christmas cards from Mrs. Deacon. Old linen from Mrs. J. L. Muspratt. The thanks of the Board were ordered to be given to the various donors. The minutes were passed on the proposition of Mr. HAND- LEY, seconded by Mr. CAR.EY. FINANCE —IMPORTANT STATEMENT. The Finance Committee's minutes contained nothing of general interest. Mr. HEYES moved that they be passed, and drew attention to the fact that many of the new loans had been taken up at a reduced per centage. He also added that under the old - system, Mr. Thomas Beasley, the late clerk, was allowed 15s. per cent. commission upon all new loans obtained. Mr. Allen, the present clerk, now did this work without any commission, which represented a saving to the Board of between £3OO and £4OO per annum. Mr. GASKELL, Jcec., seconded the motion, which was passed, and expressed a hope that the new Board would see to it that future loans were obtained at as low a cost as pos- sible to the ratepayers. MR. ICERSHAW AND TUE RATEPAYERS' ASSOCIATION. Mr. KERSHAW' as returning officer, prevented the official return as to the late election. He remarked that he had been charged by some of the members of the Ratepayers' Asso- ciation, with having shown a preference to the supporters of the Owners' and Occupiers' Association during the late con- test. . If he had done so, the act had not been an intentional one upon his part. Certainly the members of the last-named body were the first in the field, and they took advantage of the position in which they found him. Perhaps a little jeolousy had crept ieto the minds of the Ratepeyers' Asso- ciation through their members knowing that he was himself a member of the opposition body! However, whatever had been done, the Ratepayers' Association ought to be thorougly satisfied with the way in which the election had gone. Some complaints had been made as to the voting papers not having been delivered properly, and, in reply to this, he had to say that in no one year had they been de- livered properly, as there were scarcely a dozen names in the book from which they had to be taken, spelled correctly. On this occasion he had, as returning officer, to have the .„ assistance of a legal gentleman in conducting the election. Mr. Thomas Beasley, the late Law Clerk, had been chosen for this purpose, he having had the conducting of the elec- tion in his hands during so many years past. He did not think he could have found a better man. The expenses this year had been £64 7s. Bd., ageinst £5l last year; and the refreshments had cost £6 17s. 6d. as clmpared with £4 4s. 10d. last year. The number of voting papers delivered by the police was 4,029, the number delivered by the returning officer 107, total 4,136. Number of papers not delivered through change of residence 1,675, number returned blank 110, void papers through rates not being paid 87, not accounted for 89, num- ber of good voting papers 2,175. A motion was passed sanctioning the payment of the election expenses.

div.head: EULOGIES ON MAJOR CROSS.
div.p: EULOGIES ON MAJOR CROSS.

Mr. KERSHAW rose to move a vote of thanks to Major Cross for the admirable manner in which be had discharged the duties of chairman of the Board during the many years he had been connected with it. He felt utterly at a loss to find words in which to express his opinion of the manner in which their chairman had presided over their deliberations for so long a period. The conduct of Major Cross whilst occupying that position had always been marked by great ability and the utmost courtesy to every member. He was sure that the township never made a greater mistake than they had done at the late election in rejecting him. (Hear, bear.) Widnes had in the past been largely indebted to Major Cross in a variety of ways, which would take him a considerable time, were he to attempt to detail them upon that occasion. He might, however, just say that this had been particularly the case in regard to the Hutchinson Estate, for if Major Cross had not been so intimately associated Nth that estate, the con- nection of the Board with it in bu mess matters would not have been of so agreeable a cha-acter as it had been. Mr. CAREY very cordially seconded everything which Mr. Kershaw had said, as he was of opinion that the manner in which Major Cross had conductel the business of that Board since he had been chairman had been beyond all praise. The

chairman had discharged the onerous and responsible duties of his position with the utmezt fairness agd satisfaction to all the gentlemen who had worked so long with him in dealing with the affairs -of the town. When they looked back upon the long period which Major Cross had presided over them, and the ability and courtesy which had marked his official career, they must all admit they were very much in- debted to him. Not only was this the case in regard to the chairmanship, but especially was it so in respect to the special services Major Cross had rendered the Beard during the last two or three years. A shorto time ago their chairman devoted a great deal of attention to the Board's finances, with the object of getting them into a better state. He knew that Major Cross at that time worked in that building a good many days, and a great parr of many nights; and believed he (the speaker) was quite within the mark in saying that the finances of the Board had never been in so good a state as they were at the present moment. [Mr. HEYES (very emphatically): Never.] In the opinion of the best authori- ties, they were in a better position as regarded their finances than most of the Local Boards in the district. He ought also to add that the whole neighbourhood owed their chair- man a debt of thanks for the way in which he had helped them in connection with the sewerage scheme, in relation to which his disinterested services would long live in their recollection. In conclusion, Mr. Carey observed that he quite agreed that the raiepayers had made a mistake in not again electing Major Cross upon the Board, his retirement from, which he looked upon as a calamity to the town. (Hear, hear.) Mr. HEYEs also spoke strongly in support of the motion. The services of Major Cross in regard to the finances of the town had, in reality, been very mug) underrated by the mover and seconder of the resolation. Some time ago the finances were in a state of confusion, and had it not been for the assistance of the chairman, and the time he spent over them, they would not have been in the condition they were to day. He believed there was not a Local Board in the district whose finances were in the same plain state as those of Widnes; in fact, the auditor and treasurer both expressed that opinion. Dr. O'KEEFFE also spoke to the motion. He said that during the time he had been a member, the greatest courtesy had been shown to himself and every member by their chairman, who had conducted their business in a way which would have reflected the greatest credit upon the model chairman of any local beard or town council in the country. He was extremely sorry that they were about to be deprived of the Mayor's services. The resolution was put by Mr. Kershaw, and carried with applause. - The CHAIRMAN, in responding, said he was sure he felt particularly gratified at the kind manner in which the mem- bers had spoken of his services. Whilst he bad been chair- man of that Board the gentlemen serving with him had at all times been anxious to further the interests of the town- ship, to second everything which fell from the chair, and to carry on the business comfortably and well. He had not the slightest doubt that their successors would do the same. He was one of those who believed there were "as good fish in the sea as ever came out of it," and , that it was a wrong idea that the non-return of any one man could do any harm to a Board like that. At the same time, although it had been his own wish to retire from the Board, yet one did not alto- gether like being turned out after 12 years' service ; and he, therefore, considered that, under the circumstances, the com- pliment they had paid him was ten-fold more valuable than it would otherwise have been. He thanked them all very much. (Applause). The proceedings then terminated.

div.head: WIDNES WINDOW PLANT ASSOCIATION.
div.p: WIDNES WINDOW PLANT ASSOCIATION.

Mr. Eustace Carey presided, on Tuesday evening, over a lecture given in the Simm's Cross Board Schcol, by Mr. John Glover, of Liverpool, on "the cultivation of window plants." There was a poor attendance. The CHAIRMAN said the committee had called them together that evening to hear a lecture 14y Mr. Glover, of Liverpqol, upon the subject of window plant cultivation. The committee had felt that it would be a very useful thing indeed to hear what Mr. Glover had to say upon the subject. Mr. Glover, and the two other gentlemen with him—whom, perhaps, they knew—Mr. Drysdale and Mr. Green, had at each of their exhibitions in previous years had the gre.tlindness to come over and act as judges. They had done so without any remuneration whatever, and the committee felt very much obliged to them. Those gentlemen had still further shown their interest in the society by coming over that evening—Mr. Glover to lecture !mid Mr. Green and Mr. Drysdale to give them .a few hints. The 'LECTURER said it was suggested by Mr. Carey at the last exhibition that something might be done to encourage cottagers to grow window plants successfully, and he expressed a wish that somedody would come for- ward and give a lecture on window plants, or re(l a paper on the cultivation of them. It uas suggested that he should read a pafler op the treatment of window plants, and that Mr. Drys Lie and Mr. Green should join him and give them the benefit of their experience. He thought anything that could be done to encourage an extended cultivation of window plants would be appreciated, for there seemed to be a growing taste for window gardening, which was deserving of encouragement in many ways. It was a great source of pleasure to the house-wife to see her pet plants growing and flowering under her own special care, and it promoted habits of cleanliness, for wherever there were good window plants grown there was sure to be a clean house, as plants would not thrive satisfactorily without cleanliness and attention to their daily requirements. Where the surroundings were favourable to plant life they must also be the same to human life, for there were great similarities with the one and the other. It also afforded as much pleasure to the husband to see the plants growing, as it showed at once that there was care and attention bestowed upon them to attain such satisfactory results ; and when it was a plea- sure to the husband to admire and appreciate the well-grown window plants, it was a greater pleasure to the wife to know that her labours were appreciated by him. The cultivation of window plants also had a tendency to create a love for home, and was a very innocent and creditable source of en- joyment, and was much more economical that seeking plea- sures from home. He then proceeded to give some practical hints upon the soil, watering, and air needed for the suc- cessful cultivation of window plants,'and spoke on the cul- tivation of fuschias, geraniums, petunias, roses, hydrangeas, musk, coleus, and begonias. There were many other plants, he said, that might well be termed window plants, some of which were well understood and successfully grown in that neighbourhood, such as creeping jinny, or wild snapdragon, myrtle, or French nettle. These plants seemed to thrive under difficulties which sufficiently indicated the care and attention bestowed upon them to attain such fine specimens as he had seen grown in the cottage windows in Widnes, and which would compare very favourably with those grown in any other district he was acquainted with. He was sure that some of their favoured neighbours might learn a lesson which they would not easily forget by visiting Widnes, and making notes of the cottage window plants be had m=ne tioned. There were some other window plants that might be grown in a similar way to that he had described, but these he considered were only deserving of secondary con- sideration. • They were baisalms, primulas, calceolarias, cinerarias, and lobelias. He pointed out, in conclusion, that it was better to grow a few plants well than tq attempt to grow more than they had space for, and to give each plant as much light as possible, and to prevent overcrowd- ing. (Applause.) Mr. E. GREEN, of Bank Park, Warrington, spoke of the pleasure that was derived from the cultivation of flowers; and Mr. DRYSDALE confirmed the lecturer's remarks as to the cultivation of plants promoting habits of cleanliness. On the motion of Mr. MORRISON, a vote of thanks was ac- corded to the Lecturer, and to Messrs. Green and Dysdale ; and on the motion of Mr. OAKDEN a similar compliment was paid to the Chairman, and the proceedings terminated.
RESTORATION OF FRODSFIAN PARISH

div.head: CHURCH.
div.p: CHURCH.

The laudable work of restoring the fabric of the ancient parish church of Frodsham is progressing satisfactorily towards completion. At the present time the workmen are engaged upon the chancel, and by next autumn the church, which is at present closed, is expected to be opened. When the undertaking was commenced, it was known it would be no mean magnitude ; and though about £O,OOO has been raised towards the expenses, it is estimated that a further sum of £l,OOO will still be required. This sum is required in addition to the £BlO which was received from the bazaar held in August last, and which was brought to a rather , abrupt termination through the tents being overturned by I the wind. In consequelace of this accident a considerable quantity of articles were left unsold; and these goods formed the nucleus of a two days' sale of work, which was was opened in the Frodsham Town Hall on Tuesday last, with the object of realising a portion of the sum required. There was no formal opening ceremony. The arrangement of the stalls was that usually adopted. In the centre of the hall were arranged four stalls ; on the left side were two others; while running across the bottom was the refresh ment stall. The fair vendors were evidently no novices in the art of stall decoration, for their wares were enticingly displayed. No. 1, the vicar's stall, was in charge of Mrs. Charles Linaker, Mrs. Heron, and Miss Linaker. The most noticeable objects on this stall were a pretty flower stand, made of tinted glass, with a silver bottom ; a beautiful mother-of-pearl shell on a gilt stand, and a minature child's cot. The flower stand was marked 425. There were a number of articles in crewel work with illustrations of various nursery rhymes; a portrait frame to hold eight photographs; and three pictorial maps. Dolls, antimacassars, slippers, kc., completed the stock. A most interesting stall was No. 2, presided over by Miss Simpson, Mrs. Dunsford, and the Misses Simpson. Here were several antique ornaments, some good specimens of Dunmore ware, and a curious jug, said to be considerably over a hundred years old. For female ornamentation there was a Bulgarian necklace made of silver, and set with emeralds, but of such an extraordinary pattern, that we feel the fair stall holders would have a difficulty in disposing of the article. Also from the East were a silver coffee stand set, and a quantity of Maltese lace. The Misses Crosfield, who attended to No. 3 stall, had a well stocked stall of miscellaneous articles usually found at bazaars, , among which were two gipsy tables, a large doll, porcelain inkstand, baskets, sticks, and various articles in needlework. A handsome footstool worked in beads was much admired, and the prettily designed hand screens were very noticeable. As in the other stalls, there was much crewel work in pretty patterns. On No. 4 stall, over which Mrs. Ashton, Miss Tyler, and Miss Davies presided, a large fire screen occupied a prominent place. But the most universally admired articles were a number of hand painted terracotta ornaments. The

ASSAULTING TWO POLICE OFFICERS.—Mary Pipit', Mary Murray, and Margt. Healey, Wm. Fyldes, were charged with assaulting P.C.'s Pitt and Snowden, and there was also a like charge against Owen Shannon, and Peter Finn. John Byrom was likewise charged with assaulting P.C. Anderson, at the same time.—The offences arose out of a case which came before the justices last week. The officers stated that about half past six on the evening of the Ist inst., they were trying to apprehend a prisoner named Finn' when the defendants interfered, raised a croud of about 200 people and struck Pitt in a savage manner. Byrom [ severely treated P.C. Anderson. The chairman said it was remarkable that whenever there was a street row the women inevitably ' interfered, and so got themselves into serious trouble. Each of the female defendants would have is. fine, and Bs. 6d. costs to pay, or, in default, be sent to gaol seven days.—Fyldes, Shannon, Finn, and Byrom were each fined 205., and 9s. 6d. costs, or one month's imprison- ment.—Wm. Dunningham and. Mary Dunningham were charged with causing a breach of the peace at the same time as the row above mentioned occurred. The summons in the case of Mary was dismissed, and the male prisoner was ordered to enter into sureties to keep the peace two months, himself iu £lO, and two sureties in £5 each. GRAVE CHARGE AGAINST A DEAF AND DUMB MAN.— Alfred Moores, a deaf and dumb man, aged 24, was charged with indecently assaulting a little girl named Emily Shaw. The hearing took place in private, and was of a most pro- tracted character, as the proceedings had to be conducted nearly entirely by written questions and answers.—Prisoner, who formerly worked at Occleston's tannery, ultimately pleaded guilty, and was sent for trial at the Quarter Ses- sions. NEW RATE FOR CRONTON.—Mr. James Houghton, assistant overseer, applied to the Bench to sanction a new poor rate of 2s. in the Z for Cronton. The sum uncollected upon the old rate was £5 4s. 3d. MR.BEASLEY'S ACTION AGAINST THE RUNCORN COMMISSIONERS. As this matter is causing great interest in Runcorn and the neighbourhood, we furnish our readers with a summary of Mr. Beasley's amended statement of claim. The docu- ment states that the plaintiff is Mr. Thomas Beasley, and the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners and Messrs. William Henry Linaker, Wm. Brookes, John Parry, Wm. Handley, Finlay McDougall, William Lyon, Matthew Steele, Philip Speakman, George Marshall, Ebenezer Timmins, Thomas Norman, J. J. Speakman, Robert Shaw, George S. Hazle- hurst, James Dobson, J. R Frith, Jos. Williams, J. Meadow- croft, Peter Briscoe, Samuel Collier, and Samuel Taylor the defendants. The first paragraph of the statement of claim , says that the plaintiff is a solicitor practising at Widnes, that the first named defendants are the Board of Commis- sioners for the district of Runcorn, that W. H. Linaker is the clerk, William Brookes the secretary, and John Parry the nuisance inspector of the said Commissioners, and that the other defendants are and were the individual Commissioners. The next paragraph states that as against the defendants Robert Shaw, Philip Speakman, Geo. Marshall, Jas. Dobson, Jos. Williams, and J. Meadowcroft the plaintiff withdraws the action. The statement goes on to show that for upwards of four years the plaintiff occupied as tenant of the Com- missioners, who were the owners, a dwelling-house known as Waterloo House. He gave up possession on the 24th June, 1881, and removed his furniture and fixtures to 125, Church-street, Runcorn. On the 4th July, 1881, the defen- dants W. H. Linaker, W. Brookes, and J. Parry, by the in- structions of the other defendants, "wrongfully, wilfully, and knowingly, and without reasonable or probable cause" applied to the clerk of the Runcorn justices for a warrant or summons against the plaintiff on the charge that he had "feloniously stolen and fraudulently removed from the dwelling-house" certain goods, chattels, and fixtures, the property of The Commissioners, or had received and was in possession of the goods, 41c., well knowing the goods to have been "feloni- ously stolen and fraudulently removed." On the 4th of July the three above named defendants, by the instructions of the Commissioners, appeared before the magistrates' clerk at his office, and "falsely and maliciously, and with- out reasonable or probable cause," charged the plaintiff with being guilty of malicious injury to the property of the Commissioners under pretence of asking for a summons for such alleged injury. On the 6th July, 1881, the defend- ants, by the defendant William Brookes, who acted on their behalf, appeared before the justices and laid against the plaintiff sworn information to the effect that on or about the 24th June, 1881, "divers goods and chattels of the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners," Viz., six door knobs and thtee spindles, two cornice rods, two window shutter knobs, two birch cernice poles, 24 rings, four brackets, one drying rail, two pulleys and cords were stolen, taken, and carried away from and out of Waterloo' House, and that he suspected the goods or some part thereof were concealed in 125, Ohurch- street, and he "prayed justice may be done in the premises ;" and thereupon caused to be issued against the plaintiff and his dwelling-house and premises 125, Church-street, a search warrant. "Thomas Beasley," mentioned and referred to in the search warrant, is the plaintiff. There never was "any reasonable or probable cause" for the laying of the informa- tion or the issuing of the warrant, as the defendants well knew; but the prosecution by the defendants was "wholly malicious and ungrounded." On the 6th July the defendant by John Parry, accompanied by two constables, entered the plaintiff's dwelling-house, and "made a great noise and dis- turbance therein, and remained therein for a long time, and caused damage to the same, and to the character and repu- tation of the plaintiff by searching the said dwelling-house for goods falsely alleged to have been feloniously stolen and there concealed', as the defendants well knew." The plain- tiff had been seriously injured in his personal and profes- sional credit and reputation by the "trespasses, acts, and matters aforesaid," and had had the possession and enjoy- ment of his house disturbed and disordered, and had suffered great distress and pain of mind. The plaintiff had given the defendants notice of his intention to bring the action, and he claimed £3,000 damages. Plaintiff proposed that the action sbeuld be tried at Manchester.

As briefly stated in our last issue, Dr. Kendrick, who, for nearly half a century, has been in medical practice in Warrington, died last week, after a painful illness extending over about five weeks. Dr. Kendrick wae born in the house in Buttermarket-street, now occupied by Messrs. Hesketh and Son, on the 7th November, 1809. He was the eldest son of Mr. James Kendrick, M.D., also a native of Warrington, founder of the Warrington Dispensary, and one of the original members of the Warrington Natural History Society, from which sprang the Warrington Museum and Library. He received his education at private schools in Warrington, and adopting the profession of his father, studied for some time at the old Dispensary in Buttermarket- street. The doctor afterwards proceeded to Edinburgh, where he obtained his diploma of M.D. about 1833, and then returned to Warrington to practice. He was first married on the 21st July, 1837, to Isabella Anne, only child of Robert Berry, merchant, formerly of Port Louis, Mauritius, and afterwards Consul for Sweden and Norway, in China, residing at Macao and Ann Mary, his wife. The said Isabella Ann Kendrick died 23rd July, 1863. By her he had nine children, five of whom survive him. On the 19th October, 1864, he married Martha, third daughter of the late Thomas Green, of Warrington, and sister-in-law of the late Mr. Benjamin Pierpoint, J.P. She died about 1873. In 1874, he "tarried Catherine, daughter of the late William Burgess, of Warrington, and sister of Alderman John Burgess. Although busily occupied by his professional duties, Dr. Kendrick yet found time to study the Roman and other antiquities of the district, upon which he wrote and published many valu Able papers. Some years ago, , when excavations were being made at Wilderspool—the • Condate of the Romans,—he collected, described, and catalogued the relics found, and in 1870 presented them to the Museum. In all matters relating to the literary history • of Warrington, Dr. Kendrick took a special and deep interest. He was assiduous in his literary labours, and the Museum has been greatly enriched by his contributions. ' Amongst his publications are—" Contributions to the early history of Warrington," " Warrington Worthies," "Some account of two Ancient Chess Pieces found at the Moot

A SERIOUS CHARGE.—John Connolly was charged with having, in the month of September, 1880, stolen a purse of three sovereigns from the person of Dennis Dagnall.— Isabella Jones said she was a single woman, living with her mother in Lugsdale-road, who, up to September, 1880, was landlady of the Star Inn public-house. On the 17th of the month named, witness was engaged in the bar, when the prisoner and three ether men, named John byes, John Cunningham, and Michael Adams, came in. Heyes called for liquor, which the prisoner paid for, tendering a sovereign. Two of the men she had named were apprehended imme- diately afterwards for stealing the money from Dagnall.— Superintendent Barker asked that the prisoner might be re- manded until Tuesday, as he was understood to be concerned in the robbery.—The magistrates granted the application.

Hill, Warrington," "A Morning's Ramble round old War- rington," "An Account of Warrington Siege, A D., 1643," "An Account of the Romaq, Station at Wilderspool," " Eyers's Warrington Press, and its Local Associations," In 1868 Dr. Kendrick published a pamphlet on "The War- rington Blue Coat School exposure and its beneficial results," and in the following year a work on "The Roman Station at Wilderspool, near Warrington, the presumed Condate ' of Antoinne." Another publication "On recent discoveries at the Roman site at Wilderspool," appeared in 1871, and was followed in 1876 by a series of "Warrington Local Sketches," and in 1877 by " Memorials of the late Dr. Robson of War- rington." The decea'Red gentleman also occasionally lectured on the history and traditions of old Warrington. In 1877 he presented to the Art Gallery, oil portraits of his father and Dr. Robson, and a life-sized bust in plaster, of his relative, John Kendrick. He shortly afterwards presented to the Museum, a coat, portion of the uniform worn by the Warrington Volunteers of 1798. He also made many other valuable contributions to the institution, and no one can walk through the various rooms without feeling how greatly the town is indebted to him for his liberality. Numerous friends of Dr. Kendrick in 1878 presented his portrait to the town, and to show his appreciation of tills act, the doctor gave to the Public Library over 300 volumes which bore a Warrington imprint. By the generosity of Dr. Kendrick, the Museum has bEcome possessed of an extensive and valuable collection of seals. The doctor was well known as an anti- quarian, and was ever ready to assist inquirers by any in- formation he possessed. He was much esteemed by his literary and other acquaintances, and his loss will be deeply

PRESCOT BOARD OF GrALDIANS. The usual fortnightly meeting of titis Board took place at the Whiston Workhouse on Thursday. Mr. W. Tyrer pre- sided, and there were present Rev. J. Barnacle and Messrs. Leigh, Fisher, Syder, T. Dobell, T. Eatock, J. Leather- barrow, J. Ransom, W. Swift, T. Sadler, W. Gerrard, J. Matthews, W. Birchall, W. Gillbody, G. J. Paris, R. Tuson, Edwin Birch, J. T. Hall, and J. Kenwright. MASTER'S REPORT. The MASTER reported that there were 486 inmates in the house this week as compared with 487 last week and 489 in the corresponding week of last year. There had been seven deaths in the workhouse during the fortnight.

RUNCORN POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before the Rev. E. A. P. Campbell (chairman and Mr. Henry Reynolds. Two LADS FINED FOR STONE TIIROWING.—Two boys named Arthur Lunt and Wm. Shit'land were summoned for assaulting Edwin Griffiths, a youth, the son of Mr. William Griffiths, farmer, Weston.—Mr. Burton appeared for com- plainant, and said that on the 23rd ult. the lad was return- ing from Weston Point, where he had been with some milli, and was in charge of a donkey an 4 cart, when a number of boys, amongst whom were the two defendants, commenced throwing stones at him. One of the stones hit him at the back of the head, and inflicted a wound from which blood flowed rather freely. The two defendants appeared to have been the ringleaders in the outrage, and the father felt it ab- solutely necessary to summon the offenders before the court in order that he might have his son protected.—The com- plainant was called, and supported this statement. —The Chairman said he knew of several cases where the windows of carriages had been broken by young ruffians like the defendants' who would each bp fined 2s. 61 and costs, 11S. HEAVY FINES FOR GAME TRESPASSING.—WiII. Cooke, Joseph Bailey, Joseph Rowlands, and William Snape were charged with having, on the 26th ult., at Sutton, trespassed on land in the occupation of Mr. George Gorst, in pursuit of game; and secondly, with using certain nets to secure it, not having a license.—Tiae last two defendants did not appear, and a warrant was issued for their apprehension. Mr. Thos. Beasley appeared on behalf of Bailey.—George Hargreaves, assistant keeper to Sir Richard Brooke, Bart., said he first saw the defendants on land in the occupation of John Baguley, and they were making in the direction of Sutton. They stopped when they bad reached Mr. Gorst's land, and commencad setting nets over the "harepaths." Wilkinson and Rowlandson went to the far side of the field to "get round the hares," and Bailey provided himself with a good supply of mac :dam stones, with which to drive the hares into the nets. The men afterwards went towards Halton, and he followed them. Mr. Daglish had the right of shooting over the land on which he found defendants.—John Taylor. gamekeeper to Mr. Daglish, was also called.—Mr. Beasley.- contended that Bailey was a respectable man, and he asked their worships to take the view that he was present on the occasion casually, and not for the purpose of joining in any unlawful pursuit.—Having consulted with Inspector Hol- lingwortb, the Chairman said there was a very aggravated list of offences against Cooke, including night poaching, day poaching, trespass, assault, and, in fact, everything which was bad. For the trespass Cooke would be fined £4 and us. 6d. costs, and for using the nets, £4 and Ils. costs, or in default of payment, two months' imprisonment. The money was paid. Bailey was fined 10s. and us. 6d. costs in each case, or 28 days' imprisonment. SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST A BEERHOUSE KEEPER.—Mrs. Jane Baguley, of the Queen's Head beerhouse, High-street, was summoned for having supplied beer to two drunken per- sons.—Sergeant Walley said that on Saturday night, the 25th ult., about a quarter-past nine, he saw two men stagger- ing up High-street. He and P.C. Noden afterwards looked into the defendant's Deerhouse' and observed that the men in question had been served with beer. On speaking to Mrs. Baguley she took the beer from the men, and remarked that she did not know they were so much inebriated when they entered the house.—P.C. Noden gave corroborative evidence. —Maria Collins appeared for defendant, who, she stated, was not well, and pleaded on her behalf .that she had com- mittrd the cffence through ignorance.—A witness was called in support of this statement. —The Chairman said it was a misfortune that defendant and other publicans were too fre- quently so anxious to sell their liquor that they were not careful whom they let have it. Defendant would be fined 20s. and the costs, 15s. 61—The names of Thomas Nolan and Thomas Riley were then called out in court, they being charged with having been on the defendant's premises in an intoxicated condition. Neither of them answered, and war- rants were issued for their apprehension. THURSDAY.—Before Mr. C. W. Hazlehurst (chairman) and Mr. John Brundrit. NEW Poons' BATE.—On the application of Mr. Sutton, assistant overseer, the magistrates granted a new poor rate of 91 in the for Runcorn. The arrears of the old rate were £5 Bs., and the present one is expected to realise £4,832 6s. 4d. A DISORDERLY Womaar.—Catherine Kernealy, formerly of iNiorthwich, was convicted on the evidence of Sergeant Mcrris and P.C. Morris' of having been drunk and dis- orderly in the Queen's Head beerhouse, on the previous afternoon, and had to be forcibly ejected.—She was frned 10s. and costs.

We are sorry to hear that the Archdeacon of Warrington has not been well. Mr. Cie:). Hazleburst, of Chesterfield, has been appointed auditor for the Warrington, Prescot, and other Unions. WESLEYAN CHAPEL, SANKEY BRIDGES.-A service of song, entitled " The basket of flowers," was rendered on Monday evening, in the Wesleyan Chapel, Sankey Bridges by a choir of 50 voices and the following instruments (under the leadership of Mr. Walter Brough) :—Harmonium, W. Tomkinson ; first and second violins, W. Phillips, T. Tron- ter, and Whftfield ; violincello, C. Ball; flute, S. Tomkin- son ; cornet, T. Armstrong. The chapel had a gay and ' festive appearance by several choice plants and profusion of of flowers. The part songs and solos were giv,en by the Misses George, Taylor, and Spark; Messrs. J. Taylor and Travis. The committee secured the able services of Mrs. Garnett, of Hall Nook, Penketh, to give the connective readings. , On taking the rostrum on her arrival evoked , hearty cheering and rounds of applause. She had with her a basket of beautiful flowers, and placed it on the reading desk. Her reading was pleasing and effective. The service was well attended, and throughout gave great satisfsction.

not do that. When you made arrangements with Mr. Shearer this was over, or close upon it, It is a shocking thing for this woman to have caused her death, and to have been driven to it by you or by some mis- take of yours. It is a shocking thing.—ln answer to a juryman the witness said he had not turned the deceased out of the house.—The Coroner said his answer must be taken with a reservation. If this woman was not turned out he never knew one who was. The door was locked and she was unable to enter the house.—Permission was given to Mr. Alban Boyle, of Manchester-road, the brother of the deceased, to question the witness. In reply to Mr. Boyle's questions, the wi ss said he had a policy of £lOO in the 1-'ruclential Assurance Company on the life of the deceased. He effected it four years ago in order Lek make provision for her death.—Mr.Boyle : But surely you had sufficient money then in case of her death? I don't think so.—Not four year's since! Did she ever threaten to expose you how that policy was effected? In which way, sir ?—Was it effected properly? For anything I know.—Was she ex- amined by a doctor? I believe so, but I don't know whether it was Dr. Fox, or a doctor from Widnes.—Didn't Dr. Fox examine her and refuse to pass her? I believe so, but a doctor from Widnes came.—Did that doctor see her? I cannot tell; I was at my work.—Kr. Boyle: The deceased told me this policy had been effected fraudulently. (To witness.) Did you ever kick her off the steps? No, I did not.—Did you ever illuse her? I have not illused her these two years.—You have illused her In times gone by? Yes. I have struck her in self-defence.—You have never struck her when she has been sober? When she has aggravated me I have.—Have you ever struck or pinched her privately in the bedroom? She showed me marks on her arms and said you had caused them. They were caused by her tumbling —The marks that I saw could not have been caused by tumbling. She gave me to understand that she had gone through systematical illusage in private. You could not face to do it in public. What was she doing with a cut lip the other day ?—Witness said one day at noon she was striking him and he struck her in self defence.—Mr. Boyle: Did you ever keep her without money ? No. If anything she has had too much.—Do you recollect the time I lived with you when you kept her without wages? I remember that time, and she had money then, although I kept the house.—Did you give her sufficient for the daily means in a morning and I then reckon her up to the farthing every night ?—Witness: Every night !—Mr. Boyle: You have had many a row over a halfpenny in my presence.—Witness: Yes, at the time she was taking drink.—Never mind what time. It has caused much unpleasantness; did it not? Yes, because I thought she was " doing " me.—When did she pawn things? I can- not say.—Did you never give her occasion to pawn? No. I don't know that I have.—Did not you think she would pawn things when you kept her without wages? I did not think so.—Well I do. When you missed these things did not you threaten to kill her? No. Such a thought never came into my head.—James Monks, rope and twine manu- facturer, Arpley Fields, who said he was a distant relative of the deceased, deposed to the deceased sitting on a form on the river bank near his works. She was very low spirited, and looked very poorly. He lead known her all her live, and was not aware that she was addicted to drink. Had anyone asked him if she was a drunken woman he should certainly have replied "No."—Edward Jeffries and Alfred Cooper having been examined, the Coroner addressed the jury. After a short consultation the jury returned a verdict to the effect that deceased committed suicide whilst tempor- arily insane, adding: "And they further say that in their judgment there has been, and perhaps for a considerable time past, an amount of harshness exhibited to deceased by her husband, John Speakman, which they cannot but deem exceedingly reprehensible on his part."

div.head: FUNERAL.
div.p: THE FUNERAL.

In perfect accord with the quiet unpretentious character of the deceased was the unostentatious funeral which took place on Tuesday morning last. The mournful procession left the house in Bold-street, -,liertly after eleven o'clock, and consisted of the hearse, three coaches, and several private carriages. In the first coach were the widow, Miss Ken- drick (laughter), Mr. Berry Kendrick and Mr. Robert Ken- drick (sons), and Masters Alfred Kendrick and John Harding (grandsons of the deceased). The second coach contained Mr. end mre. John Tl.rding awl naugnter or the deceased), Mrs. Berry Kendrick (daughter-inlaw)' Mr. ; James Rigg (nephew), and Masters James Ken- drick and Kendrick Harding (grandsons). In the third coach rode Mr. John Burgess, Mr. George Burgess,Mr. W.J. Burgess,and Mr. John Hatton. Then followed a carriage containing Mr. C. S. Burgess and Mr. John Laverock ; Mr. Beamont's private carriage containing Mr. Beamont, the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, and Mr. T. S. Smith, M. 8.; the car- riage of Mr. J. G. McMinnies, M.P., with drawn blinds; car- riages in which rode Dr. White and Dr. Spinks, Dr. Sher- ratt, Dr. Fox, Dr. Joseph, the Rev. R. Filcher, 8.A., Coun- cillor Monks, and Mr. Chas. Chorley,_Mr. R. Pierpoint, Mr. J. C. Sutton, and we also noticed Councillor Brown, Coun- cillor Caldwell, Mr. J. E. Wright, Mr. Walton, Alderman Harrison, Alderman Webster, Councillor Broadbent, Mr. W. Longshaw, Mr. C. Madeley, Mr. 'l'. Woods, &c. As the cortege slowly made its way to Padgate signs of the respect in which the deceased gentlemen was held were observable along the route in the drawn blinds and partially closed establishments. Soon after twelve PadgateChurch was reached, and the coffin, preceded by the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton and the Rev. W. H. Williams (vicar), and followed by the mourners, was carried into the ivy-clad church where the usual service was held. Afterwards the body was borne to the grave on the south side of the edifice, and the burial service having been read by the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, in this sequestered burial ground, in the presence of his family, the local members of the medical profession and a few friends, the mortal remains of the late Dr. Kendrick were lowered with the greatest reverence to their final resting place. As the coffin was lowered into the grave the relatives of the deceased covered the lid with a number of beautiful wreaths. The coffin was of brown oak, with ebony moulds and sunken black silk velvet panels, and heavy brass mount- ings. It was supplied by Messrs. S. E. and R. Johnson, Bridge-street. On the brass plate on the lid was engraved in Old English and Roman letters the following :—" James Kendrick, M.D., Died 6th April, 1882, Aged 72 years." ' Mr. Laverock, of Bridge-street, had charge of the arrange- ments.

div.head: SUICIDE OF A WO\IAN AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: SUICIDE OF A WO\IAN AT WARRINGTON.

Under somewhat melancholy circumstances, a woman named Maria Speakman committed suicide at Warrington on Tues- day afternoon. The deceased, who was 38 yeaas of age, was the wife of a bookkeeper named John Speakman, living , at 46, Golborne-street. For some time back, according to the report of the police, the deceased and her husband have lived unhappily together, in consequence of her intemperate habits, and their relations to each other had become so un- pleasant on the 4th inst., that the deceased left 11,-_T home. She never afterwards returned. On Tuesday afternoon the deceased was sitting on the river bank near the rope works, for sometime talking to Mr. Monks. Afterwards she walked along the river side in the direction of, Walton. When she arrived at the spot known as Mondock Bay, she took a seat on a large stone lying there, and for a few minutes gazed in the water. Then rising she took off her bonnet, placed it on the ground, and jumped in the river. She does not ap- pear to have made any cry, bat a youth named Edward Jeffreys, who was standing on the bank, saw her commit the rash act, and he informed two men named Alfred Cooper and Thomas Bachhouse of the occurrence. With the aid of a rail, the men succeeded in drawing the deceased to the bank, but life wasthen extinct. The body was removed to the Higher Seven Stars, Bridge-street. The inquest on the body was:held at the Higher Seven Stars, Bridge-street, yesterday morning, before the county coroner, Mr. C, E. Driffield. John Speakman, the husband of the deceased, said on Tuesday at noon he met the deceased in Crown-street, and she asked him what he was going to "do in it." 'Witness replied that she must go to the work- house. The deceased then turned round and left him, say- ing, "You will remember this to the day of your death." The sane afternoon he heard of her death. On the 4th inst. witness missed some articles, and at breakfast that day he said if the pawn tickets were not produced at dinner she "would have to go out." When he came home at noon the de- ceased was missing. On Good Friday he went to Liverpocl and in consequence of a telegram be received from his nephew, Joseph Gibbons, he returned at nine o'clock that night. The deceased was standing at the house with the door handle in her hand; he unlocked the door and entered, but kept the deceased outside, telling her that as she had gone away of her own will she must stay away. In a short time the deceased went round to the back, and smashed a pane of glass. She asked for her clothes, and he gave them to her through the broken window. The following evening she returned to the house, and asked for some lodging money. Witness told her she had some money, and she must go to the workhouse. He had made arrangements with Mr. , Shearer, the relieving officer. They had been married 17 years, and the unpleasantness had arisen through drink. She had been drinking very heavily for the past two years. He had contemplated breaking up his house and living in lodgings.—The Coroner: But you did

THE RESIGNATION OF THE ASSISTANT OVERSEER FOR WIDNES. The following letter was read : Farnworth, Widnes.—To the Chairman and Guardians of the Descot Union.—l keg to tender to you my resignation as assistant iNerseer for the township of Widnes, and take this opportunity to thank you for the kindness you have shiwn me durinw my term of office. I extremely regret thit the t.,e-u- -?hip shoutd be so much In arrears, but I have been unable, single-handed. to cope with the difficulties that have presented themselves.—J. S. Mum% The Rev. J. BARNACLE: With respect to that I wish to remark upon what has been very strongly put to me by the ratepayers of Rainford. I ask you whether Widnes or any other district—which is backward in its payments—whether it affects the rates of any other parish. They seem to think it does. I shall be very glad to find that it does not. The CLERK: It does not effect or increase the rates of another parish when one is in arrear. It is simply carried forward in the next account of that parish. Mr. LEATHERBARROW was understood to say that it might be more urgent on the other townships. The CLERK: We are now owing tradesmen between £3,000 and £4,000; with the asylum bills it will, perhaps, come to £6,000. We have not money in hand to meet these bills, so that we are working on the tradesmen in the owing, and not on the ratepayers. Mr. LEATHERBARROW : I should like to ask if Mr. Rigby could reconsider his decision and remain with us a short time to give us assistance. Mr. MATTHEWS : I think Mr. Rigby had fully con- sidered the matter, and contended with it as much as he could ; and I think it would be a relief to him for us to ac- cept his resignation. Mr. LEATHEIZIARROW : He is here ; we might ask him the question. Rev. J. BARNACLE : Won't it be a great difficulty to get a successor under the circumstances. Mr. FIDLER : We can always find gotnebody in the greatest difficulty. The bIAIRMAN : Should we ask him to reconsider it? What do the Guardians of Widnes say about it? I hear he has got another appointment. Mr. BIRCIIALL moved, and Mr. PARIS seconded, that the resignation be accepted. This was carried. The CHAIRMAN : It has been said to me that one gentle- man has already bzen appointed. If it is so it is not worth advet ti sing. Mr. FIDLER : One gentleman! He has not had my vote, anyhow. (Laughter.) On the motion of Mr. PARIS it was decided to advertise. Mr. LEATHERBARROW : It has been hinted to me that if the resignation be accepted Mr. Guff will be sure to be ap- pointed. If that is so I will move an amendment that no advertisement be inserted. The CHAIRMAN: That cannot be put unles.s the motion which has just now been carried, be rescinded. Mr. LEATHERBARROW: It Will save other candidates corn- ing into the field when you have another man cut and dried for the post. I give notice of motion that a. fortnight hence Mr. Goff, the relieving officer, be appointed assistant over- seer for Widnes. That will save people the trouble of applying.

THE REY. THOMAS RIPPON ON THE SALVATION ARMY.

The Bev. Thomas Rippon, Wesleyan minister, Warring- ton, writing in yesteiday's Times on "The Salvation Army," says :—Circulars lately received by many friends, begging for aid towards the cost of a training institution for the Sal- vation Ar aiy, and signed by several influential Wesleyan ministers, prompt me to call the at- tention ofour readers to a few facts. These they may easily verify ,in a small pamphlet published by Win. Booth, at the head-quarters 101, Queen Victoria-street, London, and containing orders and regula- tions for the Salvation Army.. From pages 11, 12, &c., I learn that the army aims at becoming a permanent religious body, in addition and in scarcely disguised antagonism to existing churches. Before lending our aid to the establish- ment and enrichment of such a body, we ought to know something of its principles and constitution. The Salvation ' Army is an absolute and permanent monarchy. "The general for the time being is recognised as having absolute control over the Army and all it possesses" (p. 11). "Each general is to ppoint his successor, so that there shall always be one person having power and authority" (p. 12). The only parallel to this despotism known to me is the General of the Order of the Jesuits. And, in spite of the effectiveness which frequently accompanies, for a time, absolute rule, I cannot doubt that, like all other despotisms, it will soon either break down or work ill. Strange to say (p. 94), though all self-rule, which is the glory of England, and all voting against the executive are forbidden, yet, like Louis Napoleon's prefects, a commanding officer is encouraged to show his " skill" by " causing his force at times to vote for that which he wishes them to do." A masked feature of the orders and regulations is a constant spirit of hostility to other churches. Nearly all the references to Christians, even without a qualifying adjective, are in a depreciatory tone. As to ministers, Mr. Booth warns his officers "to be

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

The Rev. Canon Pearson, Canon of St. George's Chapel, Windsor Castle, died after a short illness at his residence at Sonning, on Thursday night. Jewels to the value of 00,000, the property of ladies of the Imperial family of Brazil, have been stolen, and no trace of them has been discovered.

The Empress Eugeine and suite arrived at Dover yester- day morning from London, and left by mail steamer en route for the south of France. About fifty copies of United Ireland seized on Thursday at Kilkenny were yesterday returned by the police, who stated they had received instructions not to interfere further with the sale of that paper.

Yesterday, the 25th anniversary of the birth of Princess Beatrice, the youngest daughter of Her Majesty, was observed at Windsor with the usual rejoicings. Leon Pellzer, alias Vaughan, has now, it is understood, made a full confession of the murder of the advocate Bernays at Brussels.
A labourer, named George Sanderson, aged 50, suffering six months' imprisonment in Durham Gaol for assault on a little girl, was found hanging quite dead in his cell yester-
day worßing.

The Mayor of Heywood (Alderman Isherwood) yesterday morning received a letter from the Home Office stating that Sir William Harcourt had acceded to the request of the Town Council of Heywood for a borough bench, and that he has requested the Chancellor of. the Duchy of Lancaster to issue the commission.

Dr. Ernest Ganz, the Socialist leader whose extradition ilLw been applied fur by the Dutch Orvvetunient and granted after some legal proceedings, was escorted to Rotterdam yesterday morning by an English detective. A large number of Socialists assembled at the Liverpool-street Station, London, to witness his departure. - -

The Marquis of Lorne gave a grand balls at Montreal, on Tfmrsday night. His Excellency has been presented with an address for transmission to the Queen, signed by 30,000 Canadian women, congratulating Her Majesty upon her recent escape from assassination. A tramp, who gives his name as Horan, from the Queen's County, was arrested on Thursday night charged with being implicated in the murder of Mrs. Henry Smythe, on the 2nd instant, at Barbaville. The prisoner, who admitted he was in the wood at the time the murder was committed, has been remanded. Mr. Childers, secretary for war, yesterday paid an official visit to the Royal Military Suhool of Music, Kneller Hill, Twickenham, and after making a complete tour of the build- ing, and expressing his satisfaction at the way the establish- ment was conducted, left for tovin about four o'clock. At the annual meeting of the South Lincolnshire Conser-

vative Association, at Boston, yesterday, a letter was read from Sir Welbey Gregory, M.P., announcing that he should not contest Devon at the next general election owing to ill health. Mr. G. Finch Hatton is mentioned as his probable successor.

div.head: GENERAL STRELNIKOFF'S MURDERERS.
div.p: GENERAL STRELNIKOFF'S MURDERERS.

A Central News telegram from St. Petersburg, yesterday. says :—The Messager Officiel states that Baron Jomini has ascertained that the two murderers of General Strelnikoff, namely, Jelvakoff, a student, and Khaltourtne, a peasant, are the two men who have long been wanted in connection with the Winter Palace explosion.

div.head: DASTARDLY OUTRAGE AT A COLLIERY.
div.p: DASTARDLY OUTRAGE AT A COLLIERY.

A dastardly act was found, yesterday morning, to have been perpetrated at the Bentley Road Colliery, Darlaston• When the workmen had assembled to descend the pit they discovered that the winding ropes in the shafts had been cut in such a manner as to be useless. Had it not been for the timely discovery, the probability is that several lives would have been lost, as the ropes would have broken when the men got into the c3ge.

ASSAULTING AND THREATENING THE POLICE. At the Altrincham Police Court yesterday morning, Patrick 11I‘Glore was charged with being drunk and dis- orderly. On Thursday during the hearing of a case, the pri- soner became very violent, and threatened to run a bayonet through Constable Robinson's heart. He was fined ss. and costs. At the same court, John Fletcher, said to be a mem- ber of the Chester Salvation Army, was sent to prison for two months, with hard labour, for assaulting the police.
FRAUDULENT PRACTICES AMONGST JEWELLERS.

Yesterday the Birmingham recorder sentenced a manu facturing jeweller, named Thomas Merson, to one month's imprisonment, without bard labour, for disposing of pro- perty obtained on credit, otherwise than in the way of trade. Within four months previous to his bankruptcy the priso- ner had pawned about £4OO worth of goods which had been supplied to him by other jewellers. The recorder, in passing sentence, said the practice was stated to be a common one in the trade when bills had to be met. This prosecution, which was the first of its kind, was instituted to put an end to the custom, and in future all such cases would be most severely dealt with. It must be thoroughly understood amongst traders that, if previous to bankruptcy, they pawned stock for which they had not paid, they committed an offence under the Bankruptcy Act.

THE CONSERVATIVE LEADERS IN LIVERPOOL. Shortly after noon yesterday, Lord Salisbury and Sir Stafford Northcote were present at a luncheon given in their honour at the City Hall, Liverpool, by the members of the Junior Conservative Club. Lord Lathom presided, and a very distinguished company assembled. On their arrival the Opposition leaders were greeted with enthusiastic demon- strations, and on behalf of the Club Lord Salisbury was presented with an address of welcome, expressing the deep sense of his great services which the members entertained, and their regard for the House of Lords as a safeguard of constitutional liberty. Another address to Sir Stafford Northcote thanked him for his efforts to maintain freedom of debate and other constitutional privileges.

1882. TO BREEDERS OF WAGGON HORSES. That Dark Brown Waggon Horse LORD BEACONSFIELD, the property of Mr. LONGTON. Eceleston Grange, will serve Mares during the season at his own stable, Holt-lane Quarry, Whiston, at the following charges :-21 each Mare and 2s. 6d. the Groom, if paid at time of serving ; if left for collection -21 10s. each Mare.

MARES WILL BE SERVED at the Stables of Mr. Jorug WILSON, at No. 2, Ford-street, Liverpool, by any of the well-bred Waggon Entlies in his possession, including • TRITE BRITON," "BROWN PRINCE," and "BLACK PRINCE" (who are so well known for the quantity and quality of their stock), at a fee of £l, and 38. the groom, if paid on or befare June 24th; and £l. 108., and 3s. the groom, if fur- ther credit be given. On Wednesdays and Saturdays, between April Ist and June 24th, an Entire will be in attend- ance during the afternoon, and after six o'clock each evening. " WAXWORK " will serve mares at hirrown stable, Wood- lane, Little Wootton, during the season. On the above condi- tions owners of mares will have the privilege of using any horse if they desire a change. No business done on bundays All mares tried must be paid for.

LANCASHIRE INDEPENDENT ,COLLEGE. THE GRAND ARTISTIC COUNTY BAZAAR will be held in ET. JAMES'S HALL, MANCHESTER, on TCESDAY, MAY 2YD, 1882, and TEN FOLLOWING- DAY-S. The Hall will be transformed so as to represent a GERMAN MEDIEVAL TOWN. From the Designs and under the Direction of MR. ALFRED DARBYSHIRE, F.R.1.8.A. The Painting of the Scenery being in the hands of MR. ROBERT POLLITT. The Building of the Town by 1 Mr. JAMES REILLY, of the New Globe Works, Cornbrook. There will be TWENTY-FIVE STALLS, representing the various contributing Churches and Congregations,. ke. Full particulars of the OPENING OF THE BAZAAR, on TUESDAY, MAY 2, will be duly announced. Tickets my be had from Me..srs. Roberts and Son, 19, Bridge-street; or at the cflices of John Nunnerley and Co. ArplPy Station, Warrington. CONTRIBUTIONS, Either in money or articles, will be thankfully received by the Secretaries, by the Members of the Local Committees, or at the Bazaar Offices, 80, Howarth's Buildings, 5, Cross-street, Manchester. All communications to be addressed to WM. M. ECKERbLEY, Assistant Secretary. 80, Howarth's Buildings, 5, Cross-street, Manchester.

The REVERSION in FEE SIMPLE expectant on the decease of Ann Ashton, in one 18th share of an estate known as ' Mile's Green Estate,' situate at Audley aforesaid, containing an area of 36 acres. The property is let as follows :—George White occupies house, and about 20 acres of land, at £7O; Robert Berke, house and shop, and about 16 acres, at £45; William Eardley, house and butcher's shop, at £25 ; Henry Edwards, cottage, at £6 10s.; and another tenant a cottage at £6 10s. ; the total yearly rents amounting to £153. MR. GEORGE JAMES HEALEY will SELL BY AUCTION, at the VICTORIA HOTEL, WIGAN, on FRIDAY next,the 21st day of April,lBB2,at three o'clock in the afternoon, unless previously disposed of by private treaty, the ALBION IRONWORKS, situate at Aspull, near Wigan, in the county of Lancaster, late in the occupation of Mr. Edward Hale. The prerni<es are bounded by the Leeds and Liverpool Canal, and the Springs Branch of the London and North-Western Railway, and immediately adjoin the collieries and blast furnaces of the Wigan Coal and Iron Company, and are in close proximity to other large collieries. There is a branch canal, and there are sidings to the railway, all of which run into the works. The area of the land upon which the works are situate is 11,966 yards, and the same is held for the residue of a term of 999 years, commencing on the 12th May, 1869, subject to the yearly rent of £75 16s. Od. Upon the land are the usual erections, plant and machinery necessary for the production of 250 tons of puddled bars and 260 tons of finished iron per week. The premises are sold as a going concern, and the purchaser will take all fixed and loose plant, machinery, and effects now on or about the premises. The lease contains no restrictive conven- ants as to user of the land, and the lessee has full powers to re- m ,ve or take away any erections, buildings, or machinery now or hereafter to be erected or placed thereon. For further particulars and cards to view apply to the AUC- TIONEER, King-street, Wigan, and 18, Acresfield, Bolton; to Mr. WILLIAM CHALK, Millgate, Wigan; to Mears. PEACE, ACEERLEY, and Co., solicitors, Wigan; or to MESSRS. SCOTT & ELLIS, Solicitors, King-street, Wigan.
